ch00.anchor: the Volunteers ever went into Korea
ch00.note: The Chinese People's Volunteers, the name given to the PLA forces China sent into the Korean War (1950–1953).

ch00.anchor: the deepest secret in the world
ch00.note: The author's framing thesis: that the intelligence and security services, being the profession of secrecy itself, are the most hidden part of any state — and that China's, and the CCP's in particular, are the least known of all. The chapters that follow are his attempt to open them.

The Nationalists, or Kuomintang (国民党, Guomindang), the party founded by Sun Yat-sen and led from the mid-1920s by Chiang Kai-shek. It unified China under its rule in 1928 and governed the Republic of China until its defeat in 1949, when it withdrew to Taiwan. Throughout this book it is the CCP’s chief rival, on the open battlefield and the hidden one alike.

The Chinese Communist Party (中国共产党), founded in Shanghai in 1921 and, from 1949, the ruling party of the People’s Republic of China. Its abbreviation, CCP, is used throughout this book; its intelligence and security services are the book’s subject.

ch00.anchor: Stalin and Roosevelt both misread their intelligence
ch00.note: The author means the two great intelligence surprises of 1941: the German invasion of the Soviet Union on June 22, which caught Stalin unprepared despite repeated warnings, and the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, which caught Roosevelt’s United States off guard. He sets Mao Zedong’s handling of intelligence against these famous failures — a claim the reader should weigh as the author’s own.

ch00.anchor: In the largest civil war of all
ch00.note: The Chinese Civil War of 1946–1949, the final round of the Nationalist–Communist struggle. It ended in Communist victory, the founding of the People’s Republic in October 1949, and the Nationalists’ retreat to Taiwan.

The People’s Liberation Army (PLA), the Communist armed forces. The same army had been the Red Army until 1937 and, in the war against Japan, the Eighth Route Army and the New Fourth Army; it took the name People’s Liberation Army in 1946–47, during the civil war described here.

ch01.anchor: their first reaction is a startled cry
ch01.note: Tewu (特务), literally “special service” or “special affairs.” In modern usage it is the ordinary word for a secret agent, and in both parties' propaganda it carried the menacing charge of the enemy's spies and secret police. The chapter's opening argument is that the word began as a neutral one; see the author's word-study below. Where he discusses it as a word it is kept as tewu; elsewhere it is rendered by sense.

ch01.anchor: Juntong agents had so fearsome a name
ch01.note: Juntong (军统), the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission, was Chiang Kai-shek's military secret service under Dai Li; it and the party-run Zhongtong are the CCP's chief adversaries through this book. Both are treated at length in Chapter 2.

ch01.anchor: Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun!
ch01.note: Mao Zedong's most quoted dictum, spoken at the August 7 Conference of 1927. The standard English rendering is preserved here.

ch01.anchor: the August 7 Conference
ch01.note: An emergency conference of the CCP Central Committee on August 7, 1927, held after the collapse of the first Nationalist-Communist united front and the Nationalist massacres; it set the Party on the path of armed uprising.

ch01.anchor: three rooms above and three below
ch01.note: Shikumen (“stone-gate”) houses are the terraced townhouses of early-twentieth-century Shanghai and other treaty-port cities, built around a small courtyard behind a stone door-frame — the characteristic cover for underground work.

ch01.anchor: an "adventurers' paradise."
ch01.note: A stock epithet for interwar Shanghai, whose foreign concessions lay outside Chinese jurisdiction and drew spies, gangsters, and refugees alike.

ch01.anchor: "Three Heroes of Longtan"
ch01.note: Li Kenong, Qian Zhuangfei, and Hu Di (龙潭三杰). Planted inside the Nationalist agent chief Xu Enzeng's own apparatus, their warning after Gu Shunzhang's 1931 defection allowed Zhou Enlai to move the CCP Center to safety — the episode this section recounts. Corroborated: the story is standard in both official and independent accounts of CCP intelligence.

ch01.anchor: Notice of Wu Hao and Others Leaving the Communist Party
ch01.note: The “Wu Hao Incident.” “Wu Hao” was a Zhou Enlai alias; the notice was a Nationalist forgery meant to suggest he had defected. It resurfaced decades later, during the Cultural Revolution, as material used against Zhou.

ch01.anchor: the "AB Corps,"
ch01.note: The “Anti-Bolshevik Corps,” an alleged counter-revolutionary network. The scholarly consensus, and now the CCP's own official verdict (quoted by the author later in this section), is that the organization was largely a fabrication and that the purge conducted in its name killed thousands of innocent Red Army members on confessions extracted under torture. Contradicted, as a real conspiracy of the scale charged.

ch01.anchor: the "Futian Incident"
ch01.note: The December 1930 mutiny at Futian by Red Army officers resisting the AB Corps purge. Mao Zedong's own role in initiating and driving the Jiangxi purge is documented and is more central than the author's emphasis on “devolved” authority suggests; independent historians treat the episode as a formative act of intra-Party terror. Partly corroborated / the author's framing is partisan.

ch01.anchor: "coerce, confess, believe,"
ch01.note: Biru gong xin (逼供信): to extract a confession by force and then believe it. The phrase became the standard shorthand for the method that drove the purges' self-multiplying “confessions.”

ch01.anchor: three foreign letters, "GBW."
ch01.note: The source prints the badge letters as “GBW,” then identifies them (below) with the Russian GPU. The letters as printed do not match a transliteration of ГПУ (GPU); rendered here as printed, with the discrepancy flagged. Either the badge or the author's reading of it is inexact.

ch01.anchor: the three provinces of Jiangxi, Fujian, and Zhejiang
ch01.note: As printed. Geographically this is doubtful: the Jinggangshan base straddled the Jiangxi-Hunan border, and the later Central Soviet Area lay chiefly in Jiangxi and Fujian; Zhejiang was not part of either, and the figures given describe the larger Central Soviet Area rather than the small Jinggangshan base. Contradicted by the geographic record; rendered as the source has it.

ch01.anchor: seized and strangled the Communist leader Li Dazhao
ch01.note: The source dates Zhang Zuolin's raid on the Soviet embassy and the execution of Li Dazhao to 1928. In fact both occurred in April 1927 (the raid on April 6, the execution on April 28). Contradicted; rendered as printed.

ch01.anchor: Red Star Over China
ch01.note: Edgar Snow's 1937 book, the first sympathetic Western account of the CCP, based on his 1936 visit to the Shaanxi base. The author's point is that Snow's changed view of the Communists owed something to his interviews with the security chief Zhou Xing.

ch01.anchor: the "sword and shield."
ch01.note: The paired emblem — sword for the offensive intelligence arm, shield for the protective security arm — echoes the insignia of the Soviet security services and is today that of China's Ministry of State Security.

ch01.anchor: the Xi'an Incident had broken out
ch01.note: On December 12, 1936, Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an to force him to halt the civil war and resist Japan. Its peaceful resolution, brokered in part by Zhou Enlai, produced the second Nationalist-Communist united front.

ch01.anchor: the Marco Polo Bridge Incident
ch01.note: The clash at Lugouqiao, southwest of Beijing, on the night of July 7, 1937, conventionally taken as the start of the full-scale War of Resistance against Japan (the Second Sino-Japanese War).

ch01.anchor: a Li Zicheng
ch01.note: Li Zicheng (1606–1645), the rebel leader from Mizhi in northern Shaanxi whose peasant army took Beijing in 1644 and ended the Ming dynasty — the author's portent for a movement rising out of the same poor country.

ch01.anchor: the third armed uprising of Shanghai's workers
ch01.note: The third of three armed workers' risings the Communists led in Shanghai in 1926–27; in this one, on March 21, 1927, the pickets seized the Chinese-administered parts of the city just ahead of the arriving Northern Expedition. It was the high point of Communist labor power in Shanghai, and the target of Chiang Kai-shek's purge three weeks later.

ch01.anchor: On April 12, Chiang Kai-shek engineered a coup
ch01.note: The April 12 Incident of 1927, Chiang Kai-shek's sudden turn on his Communist allies in Shanghai: with the help of the Green Gang, his forces disarmed the workers' pickets and massacred Communists and labor organizers. It shattered the first Nationalist–Communist united front and opened the “white terror” that runs through this book.

ch01.anchor: slipped away to Wuhan
ch01.note: Wuhan, the great tri-city (Wuchang, Hankou, Hanyang) on the Yangtze in Hubei, was in 1927 the seat of the left-wing Nationalist government still cooperating with the Communists, in rivalry with Chiang Kai-shek's rump at Nanjing. That alliance too collapsed in July 1927.

ch01.anchor: the Nanchang Uprising of August 1
ch01.note: The August 1, 1927 revolt at Nanchang in Jiangxi, when Communist-led units of the Nationalist army mutinied after Chiang's purge; it is reckoned the founding of the Communists' own armed forces, and August 1 remains the army's founding day.

ch01.anchor: Borodin, head of the Soviet advisers
ch01.note: Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), the Comintern's chief political adviser to Sun Yat-sen's Nationalist Party and its Soviet-backed government from 1923; when the alliance broke down in mid-1927 he was recalled to Moscow.

ch01.anchor: before Xia Douyin raised his Yichang mutiny
ch01.note: In May 1927 the Nationalist general Xia Douyin turned against the left-wing Wuhan government and marched his troops on the city from Yichang, up the Yangtze; the revolt was beaten back short of Wuhan.

ch01.anchor: When Xu Kexiang mutinied at Changsha on May 21
ch01.note: The “Horse Day Incident” of May 21, 1927 (named for the telegraphic code-character for the 21st), in which the Nationalist officer Xu Kexiang launched an anti-Communist coup at Changsha, capital of Hunan, killing large numbers of Communists and peasant activists.

ch01.anchor: the 24th Division, commanded by Ye Ting
ch01.note: Ye Ting (1896–1946), a gifted Communist commander who led troops in both the Nanchang and Guangzhou uprisings of 1927 and, in the war against Japan, commanded the New Fourth Army. He died in the April 1946 plane crash that also killed Bo Gu and Deng Fa.

ch01.anchor: The First National Congress of July 1921
ch01.note: The founding congress of the Chinese Communist Party, held in secret in Shanghai in July 1921; when police interrupted it, the delegates finished on a pleasure boat on South Lake at Jiaxing, in Zhejiang — the “Red Boat” of later Party lore.

ch01.anchor: Yang Yin, of the Guangdong District Committee
ch01.note: Yang Yin (1892–1929), an early Communist labor and military organizer in Guangdong; he was arrested in Shanghai and executed by the Nationalists in 1929, together with Peng Pai.

ch01.anchor: the assassination of Liao Zhongkai
ch01.note: Liao Zhongkai (1877–1925), the leading left-wing figure of Sun Yat-sen's Nationalist Party and architect of its alliance with the Communists and the Soviet Union; his assassination in Guangzhou in August 1925 was a blow to the party's left.

ch01.anchor: on the Beijing-Hankou Railway, at the Anyuan mines
ch01.note: Landmark early Communist-led labor actions of the 1920s: the Beijing–Hankou railway strike of February 1923, crushed in the “February 7 Massacre”; the Anyuan coal-miners' strike of 1922; and the great Canton–Hong Kong strike and boycott of 1925–26, one of the longest strikes in history.

ch01.anchor: In the First United Front of 1924
ch01.note: The first Nationalist–Communist alliance (1924–27), formed on Comintern advice: Communists joined the Nationalist Party as individuals while keeping their own organization, and the two cooperated in the Northern Expedition until Chiang Kai-shek's 1927 purge tore the front apart.

ch01.anchor: the Green Gang and Red Gang of the lane-ways
ch01.note: The Green Gang (青帮, Qingbang) and Red Gang (红帮) were the great criminal brotherhoods of the lower Yangtze, dominant in Shanghai's docks, opium, and rackets. The Green Gang, under bosses like Du Yuesheng, supplied the muscle for Chiang Kai-shek's 1927 massacre of the Communists.

ch01.anchor: The National Government's Songhu Garrison Command
ch01.note: The Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison Command, the Nationalist military authority responsible for security in the Chinese-administered districts of Shanghai; a chief instrument in the hunt for the Communist underground.

ch01.anchor: members Peng Pai and Yang Yin were arrested
ch01.note: Peng Pai (1896–1929), pioneer of the Communist peasant movement and founder of the short-lived Hailufeng Soviet in Guangdong, sometimes called the “king of the peasants.” Betrayed by an informer, he was arrested in Shanghai and executed in 1929.

ch01.anchor: under the chairmanship of Song Qingling
ch01.note: Song Qingling (1893–1981), widow of Sun Yat-sen and, as such, a figure of great moral prestige; she used it throughout these years to shelter and rescue Communists and left-wing activists, and after 1949 became a vice-chair of the People's Republic. One of the three famous Soong sisters.

ch01.anchor: Ren Bishi, a member of the Central Political Bureau
ch01.note: Ren Bishi (1904–1950), a senior Communist leader who made the Long March and, in the 1940s, ranked among the Party's five chief secretaries beside Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai; he died young in 1950.

ch01.anchor: After Luo Yinong went to his death
ch01.note: Luo Yinong (1902–1928), a leader of the Communists' Jiangsu and Shanghai work; betrayed by a turncoat couple, he was arrested and executed by the Nationalists in Shanghai in 1928.

ch01.anchor: "Six Gentlemen of the Chou'an Society"
ch01.note: The Chou'an Society (筹安会) was the propaganda body got up in 1915 to promote Yuan Shikai's scheme to make himself emperor; its six promoters, Yang Du among them, were mocked as the “Six Gentlemen.” Yuan Shikai (1859–1916), the strongman who had become president of the new Republic, briefly proclaimed a monarchy in 1915–16 before dying in disgrace. That the monarchist Yang Du secretly joined the Communist Party late in life is one of the book's quieter curiosities.

ch01.anchor: had saved Chiang Kai-shek's life during the Eastern Expedition
ch01.note: The Eastern Expeditions of 1925, in which the Whampoa cadet army marched east from Guangzhou to crush the warlord Chen Jiongming. In one reverse the young Communist officer Chen Geng is said to have carried a beaten and despairing Chiang Kai-shek to safety — a debt Chiang later chose not to repay in kind.

ch01.anchor: with Deng Yingchao serving as the cipher clerk
ch01.note: Deng Yingchao (1904–1992), a leader of the early women's movement and Zhou Enlai's wife and lifelong political partner; she became a senior Party figure in her own right in the People's Republic.

ch01.anchor: the backing of the Comintern representative Mif
ch01.note: Pavel Mif (1901–1939), the Comintern's man for China, who at the January 1931 plenum pushed his protégé Wang Ming and the Moscow-trained students later mocked as the “28 Bolsheviks” into the Party leadership. Mif himself later perished in Stalin's purges.

ch01.anchor: in the May Thirtieth Movement he had charged in
ch01.note: The May Thirtieth Movement of 1925, a wave of anti-imperialist strikes and protests across China touched off when British-officered police in Shanghai's International Settlement shot dead Chinese demonstrators on May 30.

ch01.anchor: When the Northern Expedition reached Anhui
ch01.note: The Northern Expedition (1926–1928), the military campaign launched from Guangdong by the allied Nationalists and Communists to defeat the northern warlords and unify China; its success, and the split between the allies during it, set the stage for all that follows.

ch01.anchor: the leading men of the New Culture Movement
ch01.note: The New Culture Movement of the 1910s and 1920s, an intellectual ferment that attacked Confucian tradition and championed science, democracy, and writing in the vernacular; out of it the Communist Party was born. Hu Shi (1891–1962) was its leading liberal, the apostle of vernacular writing and pragmatism, who later broke with the left; Chen Duxiu was its radical, and a co-founder of the Party.

ch01.anchor: a band of May Fourth stalwarts from Anqing
ch01.note: The May Fourth Movement began with the student demonstrations of May 4, 1919, protesting the Versailles award of Germany's Chinese concessions to Japan; it broadened into a national cultural and political awakening that many take as the seedbed of the Chinese Communist Party.

ch01.anchor: Chen Yun, a member of the Central Political Bureau, took over
ch01.note: Chen Yun (1905–1995), here a young Politburo member briefly running the Special Branch; he became the Communists' foremost economic planner and, in the 1980s, one of the small circle of Party elders who steered — and at times braked — the reform era.

ch01.anchor: the fourth "encirclement and suppression" of the Central Soviet Area
ch01.note: The Nationalists mounted five “encirclement and suppression” campaigns (围剿, weijiao) against the Jiangxi Central Soviet between 1930 and 1934; the Red Army beat back the first four but lost to the fifth, which forced the Long March.

ch01.anchor: In January 1933 Bo Gu and the rest of the provisional Central Political Bureau
ch01.note: Bo Gu (the Party name of Qin Bangxian, 1907–1946), a Moscow-trained leader of the “28 Bolsheviks” who headed the provisional Party Center in the early 1930s. His and Li De's rigid tactics cost the Central Soviet its base; sidelined at the Zunyi Conference, he died in the 1946 air crash.

ch01.anchor: The Autumn Harvest Uprising forces led by Mao Zedong
ch01.note: The Autumn Harvest Uprising of September 1927, a Communist peasant-and-soldier revolt on the Hunan–Jiangxi border; when it failed as a bid to take cities, Mao Zedong led its survivors up into the mountains at Jinggangshan, a turn toward rural, guerrilla revolution.

ch01.anchor: joined up at Jinggangshan
ch01.note: Jinggangshan, a remote massif on the Hunan–Jiangxi border where Mao Zedong's and Zhu De's forces united in 1928 to build the first durable rural Red base; it is enshrined in Communist memory as the “cradle of the revolution.”

ch01.anchor: at Yeping in Ruijin, Jiangxi
ch01.note: Ruijin, a town in southern Jiangxi, served as the capital — the “red capital” — of the Chinese Soviet Republic from its founding in 1931 until the Long March began in 1934.

ch01.anchor: with Li Lisan, a member of the CCP Front Committee
ch01.note: Li Lisan (1899–1967), an early labor leader who in 1930, as effective Party chief, forced a disastrous line of premature urban insurrections — the “Li Lisan line” the Party later repudiated. He survived long years in the Soviet Union and died in the Cultural Revolution.

ch01.anchor: On December 11 the CCP launched the Guangzhou Uprising
ch01.note: The Guangzhou (Canton) Uprising of December 11, 1927, a Communist attempt to seize the city that held it for only three days before being crushed with heavy loss of life; the short-lived “Guangzhou Commune” is counted the last of the party's three 1927 risings.

ch01.anchor: The CCP's Sixth Congress, held in Moscow
ch01.note: The Communist Party's Sixth National Congress, held near Moscow in mid-1928 — the only Party congress ever convened abroad, held there because conditions in China after the 1927 purge made a secret gathering at home impossible.

ch01.anchor: Wang Jiaxiang, director of the Red Army's General Political Department
ch01.note: Wang Jiaxiang (1906–1974), a Moscow-trained cadre whose crucial support helped tip the Zunyi Conference to Mao Zedong; he later served as the People's Republic's first ambassador to the Soviet Union.

ch01.anchor: Deng Fa, who had once gone to the Soviet Union to study security work
ch01.note: Deng Fa (1906–1946), a Guangdong worker-organizer and Soviet-trained security man who became the first director of the State Political Security Bureau. He died in the April 1946 plane crash near Yan'an that also killed Bo Gu and Ye Ting.

ch01.anchor: set out on the Long March that the purges
ch01.note: The Long March (1934–1936), the fighting retreat of some six thousand miles by which the Red Army broke out of the Nationalists' encirclement of its southern bases and, decimated, reached the safety of northern Shaanxi; it is the founding epic of the Chinese Communists and the setting for much of this chapter.

ch01.anchor: some Chinese students at Sun Yat-sen University
ch01.note: Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow (1925–1930), a Comintern school that trained a generation of Chinese revolutionaries — among them Wang Ming's Moscow-loyal “28 Bolsheviks” — and where the Stalin–Trotsky quarrel split the Chinese students too.

ch01.anchor: the struggle against the Reorganization Clique one of its central tasks
ch01.note: The Reorganization Clique (改组派) was a dissident faction within the Nationalist Party in the late 1920s, associated with Wang Jingwei, that opposed Chiang Kai-shek; the Communist leadership's insistence on treating it as a chief enemy is cited here as part of the era's misdirected “Left” zeal.

ch01.anchor: Mo Xiong, a Guangdong veteran of long standing
ch01.note: Mo Xiong, a Nationalist officer of Guangdong background who secretly aided the Communists; the intelligence he passed — including advance word of the Nationalists' fifth encirclement plan — is credited with helping the Red Army break out to begin the Long March.

ch01.anchor: the Red Star Medal was conferred
ch01.note: The Red Star Medal, instituted in 1933, was the highest military decoration of the Chinese Soviet Republic, awarded in three classes for distinguished service in the Red Army.

ch01.anchor: Henry Stimson ordered the "American Black Chamber" closed
ch01.note: The “American Black Chamber” was the United States' first peacetime code-breaking unit, run by Herbert Yardley, which had cracked Japanese and other diplomatic ciphers. Secretary of State Henry Stimson shut it down in 1929, reportedly with the words “gentlemen do not read each other's mail” — the author's pointed contrast with the value the Red Army placed on its own codebreakers. CORROBORATED.

ch01.anchor: The Four Crossings of the Chishui were the proudest stroke
ch01.note: The Four Crossings of the Chishui River, in early 1935 during the Long March, were a series of feint back-and-forth river crossings by which Mao Zedong's Red Army slipped repeatedly through converging Nationalist armies; they are celebrated as his tactical masterpiece.

ch01.anchor: When Lu Xun had cured meat carried to Mao Zedong
ch01.note: Lu Xun (1881–1936), the towering figure of modern Chinese literature and a fierce social critic; sympathetic to the Communist cause in his last years though never a Party member, he became, after his death, an all-but-official cultural saint of the movement.

ch01.anchor: the story of the master builder Lu Ban
ch01.note: Lu Ban, the semi-legendary master carpenter of ancient China (traditionally dated to the fifth century BCE), revered ever since as the patron of builders and craftsmen; his name stands for consummate, exactly-fitted skill.

ch01.anchor: a Long March of ten thousand li
ch01.note: A li is the Chinese mile, now standardized at about half a kilometer; “ten thousand li” is a set phrase for an immense distance, and the March is known in Chinese as the “Long March of twenty-five thousand li.”

ch01.anchor: Li Weihan, head of the Central Organization Department
ch01.note: Li Weihan (1896–1984), a founding-generation Communist long in charge of Party organization and, later, of united-front work; he took part here in reversing the wrongful purge in northern Shaanxi.

ch01.anchor: Zhang Wentian, general secretary of the CCP
ch01.note: Zhang Wentian (1900–1976), pen name Luo Fu, a Moscow-trained leader who became the Party's nominal general secretary after the Zunyi Conference threw its support to Mao Zedong; later a diplomat, he was purged after criticizing Mao in 1959.

ch01.anchor: Liu Zhidan, Gao Gang, Xi Zhongxun, Ma Wenrui, and the other founders
ch01.note: The founders of the Communist base in the northwest, arrested here in the very purge the arriving Party Center halted. Liu Zhidan (1903–1936), its principal leader, was cleared and then killed in battle the next year, becoming a revered martyr (Zhidan county bears his name). Gao Gang (1905–1954) rose after 1949 to rule the Northeast, then fell in the new state's first great purge and took his own life. (Xi Zhongxun, later father of Xi Jinping, is treated more fully in a later chapter.)

ch01.anchor: the northern Shaanxi base founded by Xie Zichang and others
ch01.note: Xie Zichang (1897–1935), co-founder with Liu Zhidan of the Red base in northern Shaanxi; gravely wounded in the fighting of 1934, he died in early 1935, just before the events of this section. The county of Zichang is named for him. CORROBORATED.

ch01.anchor: Xu Haidong led the 25th Red Army into northern Shaanxi
ch01.note: Xu Haidong (1900–1970), a Red Army commander of worker origins whose 25th Army, marching separately, reached northern Shaanxi in 1935 ahead of the main force; later a senior PLA general.

ch01.anchor: a security cadre sharing a name with a cruel official of the Tang
ch01.note: The Tang-dynasty Zhou Xing was a notorious judge-torturer under the empress Wu Zetian, remembered chiefly for the idiom “please step into the jar” (请君入瓮): asked by a fellow inquisitor how to make a suspect talk, Zhou proposed roasting him in a great jar — whereupon the questioner invited Zhou himself to step in. The security man's sharing the name is the author's grim joke.

ch01.anchor: the Comintern held its Seventh Congress
ch01.note: The Seventh and last World Congress of the Comintern, Moscow 1935, which abandoned its sectarian line for the “popular front” against fascism; this shift was the external impetus for the Chinese Communists' turn from class war to an anti-Japanese national united front.

ch01.anchor: (the "August 1 Declaration"),
ch01.note: The manifesto of August 1, 1935 (drafted by the Party's Comintern delegation), calling on Nationalists and Communists to stop fighting each other and unite against Japan; it announced the coming shift to the second united front.

ch01.anchor: sent Zhang Hao home to restore contact
ch01.note: Zhang Hao, the Party name of Lin Yuying (1897–1942), a labor organizer and cousin of the general Lin Biao. Returning overland from Moscow in 1935 with the Comintern's new line committed to memory, he brought both instructions and, decisively, the Comintern's authority, which helped Mao Zedong block Zhang Guotao's rival Party Center.

ch01.anchor: holding the Comintern's imperial sword
ch01.note: “Imperial sword” renders shangfang baojian, the emperor's own sword of office, which conferred on its bearer the authority to act in the sovereign's name and even to execute without prior leave; figuratively, unchallengeable backing from the very top.

ch01.anchor: his brother-in-law T.V. Soong
ch01.note: T.V. Soong (Song Ziwen, 1894–1971), a Harvard-trained financier and brother of Song Qingling and of Chiang Kai-shek's wife, Soong May-ling; he served the Nationalist government as finance minister and, later, premier and foreign minister.

ch01.anchor: her eldest sister's husband, H.H. Kung
ch01.note: H.H. Kung (Kong Xiangxi, 1881–1967), husband of the eldest Soong sister, Ai-ling, and reputedly a lineal descendant of Confucius; a banker who long served as the Nationalist government's finance minister and premier.

ch01.anchor: entrusted Dong Jianwu with carrying a letter
ch01.note: Dong Jianwu, a secret Communist who operated under the cover of a Christian pastor — the “Red Pastor” — and had once served in the Special Branch; being also a former classmate of T.V. Soong, he was a courier acceptable to both sides.

ch01.anchor: in the company of Feng Xuefeng
ch01.note: Feng Xuefeng (1903–1976), a Communist writer and literary theorist who made the Long March; he served as the Party's chief link to Lu Xun and the left-wing writers of Shanghai.

ch01.anchor: joining with Cai Tingkai's 19th Route Army against Chiang
ch01.note: Cai Tingkai's 19th Route Army had won national fame resisting the Japanese assault on Shanghai in 1932. In November 1933 its generals broke with Chiang Kai-shek and set up a rival “Fujian People's Government,” seeking common cause with the Red Army; the Communists' “Left” leadership spurned the overture, and Chiang crushed the revolt by early 1934. CORROBORATED.

ch01.anchor: Yang Hucheng, commander of the Northwest Army, had long leaned toward the Communists
ch01.note: Yang Hucheng (1893–1949), commander of the Northwestern (17th Route) Army at Xi'an and, with Zhang Xueliang, co-author of the 1936 Xi'an Incident. Chiang Kai-shek imprisoned him for more than a decade afterward and had him and his family killed in 1949, on the eve of the Nationalist collapse.

ch01.anchor: gave his own flesh to save a dove
ch01.note: An allusion to a Buddhist jataka tale in which a compassionate king (the Buddha in a former life) cuts flesh from his own body to ransom a dove being hunted by a hawk. The legend is offered as the origin of Yan'an's old name, Fushi.

ch01.anchor: the celebrated Song figure Fan Zhongyan
ch01.note: Fan Zhongyan (989–1052), a revered Northern Song statesman, general, and writer; the maxim quoted — to worry before all the world worries and take joy only after it does — comes from his essay “On Yueyang Tower,” the classic expression of the selfless official's ideal.

ch01.anchor: the Nationalist government's Executive Yuan
ch01.note: The Executive Yuan, the cabinet and highest administrative organ of the Republic of China's government under the Nationalists; its formal approval gave the Border Region a color of legality within the national state.

ch02.anchor: sent off a feather-dispatch
ch02.note: A jimao xin (鸡毛信), or “chicken-feather letter”: an urgent dispatch with one or more chicken feathers fastened to it, the feathers signalling that it was to be carried at top speed, day and night, changing runners as needed. The device was old and widespread in rural China and became a staple of Communist wartime lore.

ch02.anchor: The great Laoshan
ch02.note: The Laoshan Incident (劳山事件) of 25 April 1937, in which bandits ambushed Zhou Enlai’s convoy in the hills south of Yan’an. Zhou’s adjutant Chen Youcai, dressed in a Western suit as a decoy, was killed; the ambushers took him for the important man and found Zhou’s calling cards on the body. The account is broadly corroborated. Two small internal discrepancies in the source are worth noting: its photo caption dates the affair 24 April against the 25th given in the text, and it twice names the ambush site “Yanqiushan” (沿湫山) while calling the affair after Laoshan.

ch02.anchor: Deng, Mao, Xie, and Gu
ch02.note: Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zetan (Mao Zedong’s younger brother), Xie Weijun, and Gu Bo, four cadres of the Jiangxi Soviet condemned together in 1933 as followers of a “Luo Ming line” and punished for their closeness to Mao Zedong, who was then out of power. All but Deng Xiaoping died within a few years; Deng’s later rehabilitation and rise are among the ironies the author leaves unspoken.

ch02.anchor: Elder Brothers Society
ch02.note: The Gelaohui (哥老会), a sworn-brotherhood secret society widespread in the Chinese countryside from the nineteenth century. Belonging to neither party, such societies commanded real local loyalty and armed men, and both Nationalists and Communists by turns courted and feared them.

ch02.anchor: Vigorous Action Society
ch02.note: The Lixingshe (力行社, “Vigorous Action Society”) was the secret inner core of the Chinese Renaissance Society, popularly the “Blue Shirts,” a militarist, nationalist body founded in 1932 by Whampoa officers loyal to Chiang Kai-shek and often likened to the fascist movements of the day. Its Special Services Department under Dai Li grew into the military secret service later called Juntong.

ch02.anchor: the disease in our vitals
ch02.note: Japan a passing skin ailment, the Communists a disease in the heart and vitals (疥癣之患 / 心腹大患): the metaphor recurs in accounts of Chiang Kai-shek’s strategic priorities and captures the weight he gave the internal enemy over the invader. The exact wording varies among sources; the sense is well attested.

ch02.anchor: three-in-one alignment
ch02.note: The “three-in-one” (三位一体) alignment of late 1936 joined the Communists, Zhang Xueliang’s Northeast Army, and Yang Hucheng’s Northwestern Army in a common front in the northwest, the coalition behind the Xi’an Incident. With Zhang detained and Yang forced abroad afterward and their armies moved away, it dissolved, leaving the Communists without their two military partners, as the author says.

ch02.anchor: The heavy work of the military blockade fell to Hu Zongnan
ch02.note: Hu Zongnan (1896–1962), Chiang Kai-shek’s favored Whampoa protégé and the senior Nationalist commander in the northwest, nicknamed the “King of the Northwest.” From 1939 the bulk of his large force blockaded and menaced the Border Region rather than fighting Japan, a diversion of strength the Communists never forgot; in 1947 his troops briefly captured Yan’an.

ch02.anchor: worthy of the opera
ch02.note: At the Crossroads (三岔口, Sanchakou) is a celebrated Peking-opera scene in which two men fight in total darkness, each blind to the other, their groping mock-combat performed in full stage light. The image, of allies and enemies grappling in the dark on the same ground, is the author’s figure for the tangled traffic of the blockade years.

ch02.anchor: the new climate of "reform and opening"
ch02.note: The author writes literally “the new situation of reform and opening” (改革开放), the fixed slogan for the era of economic liberalization that began in 1978, some four decades after these events. The anachronism is his own, a playful borrowing: the united front “opened” the sealed Nationalist-Communist front, and that opening, he suggests, only multiplied the covert contest. It is in no sense a term of the 1930s.

ch02.anchor: swore to be loyal to Marshal Mao
ch02.note: Xu Shiyou (1906–1985), a hot-tempered general of the Fourth Front Army, trained as a boy at the Shaolin monastery and later a senior PLA commander. The story of Mao Zedong disarming his rage by handing him a loaded pistol is often told, and stands for Mao’s careful winning-over of the Fourth Front Army cadres after Zhang Guotao’s fall.

ch02.anchor: The tomb of the Yellow Emperor, Xuanyuan
ch02.note: The Mausoleum of the Yellow Emperor at Huangling honors the legendary ancestor of the Chinese people and is a national shrine; sacrifices there at Qingming, the tomb-sweeping festival, are an old imperial rite revived to invoke national unity. At the joint Nationalist-Communist sacrifice of April 1938 Mao Zedong composed a sacrificial ode, a set-piece of the united-front moment.

ch02.anchor: criticism of Zhang Guotao
ch02.note: Zhang Guotao (1897–1979), a founder of the CCP and commander of the powerful Fourth Front Army, had been Mao Zedong’s chief rival for leadership on the Long March; his bid failed and his army was broken. The Yan’an criticism recounted here drove his defection to the Nationalists in April 1938, which ended his Communist career; he later emigrated and died in Canada. That not even his bodyguard would follow him is the author’s pointed detail.

ch02.anchor: better to kill a thousand by mistake than let one slip through
ch02.note: A byword for the Nationalist white terror against Communists from 1927 on. The 1929 “Communist Surrender Law” and its fanxingyuan (反省院, “houses of reflection,” or repentance houses), detention centers meant to make captured Communists recant, marked a shift from mass killing to the subtler policy of turning prisoners, which, as the author notes, produced the very turncoats who later staffed the Nationalist services.

ch02.anchor: one cannot avoid speaking of this Kang Sheng
ch02.note: This unusually harsh portrait of Kang Sheng (1898–1975) reflects the verdict reached after his death. Once the CCP’s intelligence and security chief, he became the driving figure of the Yan’an “Rescue Campaign” (see Chapter 9) and, decades later, a chief instrument of the Cultural Revolution’s persecutions. He died laden with honors, but in 1980 the Party posthumously expelled him and withdrew his eulogy. The author’s open contempt is itself striking in a book so sympathetic to most of its subjects.

ch02.anchor: Dong Biwu, Lin Boqu, Xie Juezai, and Xu Teli
ch02.note: By custom only a handful of the Yan’an leadership, revered for their age and seniority, were addressed as “Elder.” These four, together with Wu Yuzhang, were known as the “Five Elders of Yan’an” (延安五老). That the much younger Kang Sheng could claim the title is the author’s sardonic point.

ch02.anchor: wrongly branded an "inner traitor,"
ch02.note: Pan Hannian’s fall came in 1955: arrested as an “inner traitor,” he was imprisoned for having concealed a secret wartime meeting with the collaborationist Wang Jingwei. He died in disgrace in 1977 and was rehabilitated in 1982, as the author records. The case is among the best-known miscarriages of the Maoist security system, and the sympathy here is that of his old comrades of the Special Branch.

ch02.anchor: would later compose "Snow."
ch02.note: “Snow” (沁园春·雪, to the tune Qinyuanchun), Mao Zedong’s most famous poem, written in the winter of 1936 after the Long March reached northern Shaanxi; surveying the snow-bound land, it moves to a sweeping claim on China’s history and future. Its publication in Chongqing in 1945, during the peace talks, caused a sensation.

ch02.anchor: the thirty-eighth of the Meiji era
ch02.note: The rifle was the Japanese Arisaka Type 38, adopted in the thirty-eighth year of the Meiji reign (1905); Chinese soldiers called it the “Type-38 big cover” for its sliding bolt-cover. The nickname carried over to the cadres who joined the revolution around 1938, the so-called “'38-style.”

ch02.anchor: the Whampoa Academy of Communist intelligence and security
ch02.note: The Whampoa Military Academy, founded near Guangzhou in 1924 during the first Nationalist–Communist alliance, trained the officer corps of the National Revolutionary Army; its graduates and instructors became commanders on both sides of the later civil war. To dub the Qilipu camp a “Whampoa” is to claim that prestige for the Communist security service.

ch02.anchor: his report on the Three People's Principles Youth League
ch02.note: The Three People's Principles Youth League (Sanqingtuan) was the Nationalists' youth organization, founded in 1938 to gather young people under Chiang Kai-shek's leadership and folded back into the Kuomintang in 1947.

ch02.anchor: An important leader of security work, Wang Dongxing
ch02.note: Wang Dongxing (1916–2015) rose from this beginning to run Mao Zedong's personal security for decades as head of the Central Guard Bureau, and became a CCP vice-chairman in the interregnum after Mao's death.

ch02.anchor: Ling Yun entered in 1941
ch02.note: Ling Yun (1917–2018), a career counter-espionage officer, would become the first Minister of State Security when that ministry was created in 1983.

ch02.anchor: the Rectification Movement overtook it
ch02.note: The Yan'an Rectification (zhengfeng), launched in 1942, was Mao Zedong's campaign to remold the Party's thinking and consolidate his leadership. Its “cadre screening” (shen'gan) phase shaded into the coercive spy-hunt of the “Rescue Campaign” (see Chapter 9).

ch02.anchor: Deng Xiaoping, too, had the matter of a wife to settle.
ch02.note: Deng Xiaoping (1904–1997), here a mid-ranking political officer just out of disgrace, would emerge after Mao Zedong's death as China's paramount leader and the architect of its “reform and opening.”

ch02.anchor: the Comintern's military adviser to the Party, Li De
ch02.note: Li De was the Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), a German Comintern agent and the only Westerner to make the Long March. As military adviser he shared the blame for the rigid positional tactics that cost the Central Soviet its base in 1934.

ch02.anchor: This Pu Qiongying was Zhuo Lin.
ch02.note: Zhuo Lin (1916–2009), born Pu Qiongying, daughter of a wealthy Yunnan ham merchant. She married Deng Xiaoping in Yan'an in 1939 and remained his wife for the rest of his life.

ch02.anchor: Mao Zedong's marriage to Jiang Qing
ch02.note: Jiang Qing (1914–1991), a Shanghai film actress who reached Yan'an in 1937 and became Mao Zedong's fourth wife. The Party leadership is said to have consented only on condition that she keep out of politics; she went on to be a chief instigator of the Cultural Revolution and a member of the “Gang of Four,” convicted after Mao's death.

ch02.anchor: read out a letter from Mao Zedong
ch02.note: The 1937 trial and execution of Huang Kegong, a decorated Red Army officer who shot a young woman for refusing him, became a celebrated demonstration of “equality before the law” in Yan'an. Mao Zedong's letter to the court, quoted here, is much reproduced; the case is well documented (CORROBORATED), though it was also put to propaganda use from the first.

ch02.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek's own book, China's Destiny
ch02.note: China's Destiny (Zhongguo zhi mingyun, 1943), a nationalist tract issued under Chiang Kai-shek's name; its attacks on “alien” ideologies were widely read as aimed at the Communists, who answered it in kind.

ch02.anchor: more promise than Li Zicheng
ch02.note: Li Zicheng, the northern-Shaanxi rebel whose peasant army took Beijing in 1644 and toppled the Ming, only to lose the city within weeks (see the fuller note in Chapter 1). The comparison means that this movement, unlike his, would hold what it won.

ch02.anchor: Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun
ch02.note: Mao Zedong's dictum of 1927. The author caps it with a coinage of his own — that leadership grows out of the haft of the knife, the knife being the security and police power — echoing this chapter's play on the “gun” and the “knife.”

ch02.anchor: The Zunyi Conference of 1935
ch02.note: The enlarged Politburo meeting at Zunyi in January 1935, midway through the Long March, at which Mao Zedong won effective control of the Red Army and the Party — the pivot the author treats as the start of the CCP's correction of its own course.

ch02.anchor: the Wang Jingwei puppet regime
ch02.note: Wang Jingwei (1883–1944), once a leading figure of the Nationalists, went over to the Japanese and in 1940 headed a collaborationist government at Nanjing that claimed to be the true Republic of China. “Puppet” (wei) is the standard word for it on both sides of the later divide.

ch02.anchor: Before the Battle of Tai'erzhuang
ch02.note: The Battle of Tai'erzhuang, in southern Shandong in the spring of 1938, was one of China's first major victories over the Japanese army, won by Nationalist forces under Li Zongren.

ch02.anchor: his merits always outweighed his faults
ch02.note: Deng Xiaoping's phrasing anticipates the verdict the Party would formally reach on Mao Zedong in 1981 — that his contributions outweighed his mistakes — a judgment Deng himself did much to shape.

ch02.anchor: the Nationalist representative Gu Zhutong
ch02.note: Gu Zhutong (1893–1987), a senior Nationalist general of Chiang Kai-shek's inner circle. He commanded the Central Army's peaceful entry into Xi'an and took the surrender of the Northeast Army there in February 1937, and later led the Third War Zone against Japan; here he is the Nationalists' negotiator opposite Zhou Enlai.

ch02.anchor: Zhang Yunyi, deputy chief of staff
ch02.note: Zhang Yunyi (1892–1974), a veteran Red Army commander of the Baise Uprising and the Red 7th Army; in 1955 he was made one of the ten Senior Generals (da jiang), the rank just below marshal.

ch02.anchor: the Northwest Security Bureau's special-service detail
ch02.note: The Red Army's traveling security organ. Founded in the Jiangxi Soviet in 1931 as the State Political Security Bureau (modeled on the Soviet GPU), it was renamed the Northwest Security Bureau after the Long March reached northern Shaanxi, and was the forerunner of the Border Region Security Office set up later in this chapter.

ch02.anchor: Qing troops marched to crush a Muslim uprising
ch02.note: The great Hui (Chinese Muslim) revolts that swept the northwest in the 1860s and 1870s, put down by Qing armies with enormous loss of life. Laoshan's bloody past is the author's foreshadowing.

ch02.anchor: the Red Army University the students
ch02.note: Founded in 1936 at the Communists' base and renamed in 1937 the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University (Kangda), which appears elsewhere in this chapter as the Resistance University and the Anti-Japanese University. It trained tens of thousands of cadres and officers in the Yan'an years.

ch02.anchor: Liu Bocheng, the chief of staff
ch02.note: Liu Bocheng (1892–1986), a famed Red Army commander known as the “One-Eyed Dragon” for a battle wound; later one of the ten marshals of the People's Republic.

ch02.anchor: Zhang Wentian, Zhu De, and Li Fuchun
ch02.note: Zhang Wentian (1900–1976), a Moscow-trained leader who was the CCP's nominal general secretary through the later 1930s, by which time real authority had passed to Mao Zedong; he served afterward as a diplomat and was purged in 1959.

ch02.anchor: Li Fuchun stood craning
ch02.note: Li Fuchun (1900–1975), a veteran administrator and economic planner, later a vice-premier of the People's Republic; he appears again in this chapter as a lecturer to the security trainees.

ch02.anchor: bad blood between Hui and Han
ch02.note: The Hui are Chinese-speaking Muslims, long settled across the northwest and distinct from the Han majority; stirring up Hui–Han enmity was a standing tactic of local strongmen.

ch02.anchor: in the sing-song of clapper ballads
ch02.note: Kuaiban, a rapid rhymed patter chanted to the beat of bamboo clappers—a popular street-storytelling form, used here to spread defeatist tales of Communists changing sides.

ch02.anchor: the Border Region government's education chief
ch02.note: The Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia (Shaan-Gan-Ning) Border Region was the Communists' wartime base around Yan'an. During the united front it was nominally a special region under the Nationalist central government while being governed in fact by the CCP; it is the setting of most of this book.

ch02.anchor: Liao Chengzhi and Zhu Guang
ch02.note: Liao Chengzhi (1908–1983), son of the assassinated Nationalist-left leader Liao Zhongkai; a prominent Communist who later ran the Party's overseas-Chinese and Japan affairs.

ch02.anchor: Ding Ling taught literature
ch02.note: Ding Ling (1904–1986), a celebrated woman writer who had come to Yan'an; best known for the novel The Sun Shines over the Sanggan River, she was denounced in later campaigns.

ch02.anchor: off to Lushan for training
ch02.note: Mount Lu (Lushan) in Jiangxi, where Chiang Kai-shek ran officer-training corps in the 1930s; the point is that teachers came back from this Nationalist indoctrination talking reaction.

ch02.anchor: Trotskyites, he suspected
ch02.note: Followers of Leon Trotsky, Stalin's defeated and exiled rival. In Chinese Communist usage “Trotskyite” became a floating accusation of treachery, and the charge that Trotskyites were secretly enemy agents would drive the purges recounted later in this book.

ch02.anchor: Zhu De and Liu Shaoqi to his right
ch02.note: Liu Shaoqi (1898–1969), the CCP's leading organizer of clandestine work in the Nationalist-held “White areas”; after 1949 head of state of the People's Republic, he was purged and hounded to death in the Cultural Revolution.

ch02.anchor: the Yulin uprising during the War of Liberation
ch02.note: “War of Liberation” (jiefang zhanzheng) is the Communist name for the civil war against the Nationalists, roughly 1946–1949, which ended in the founding of the People's Republic.

ch02.anchor: with Zhu Jiahua as director
ch02.note: Zhu Jiahua (1893–1963), a German-trained geologist and Nationalist organization minister; as head of the party's organization apparatus he was the nominal director of Zhongtong and the chief rival of the Chen brothers' “CC Clique.”

ch02.anchor: Zhou Enlai as chairman and Zhang Hao
ch02.note: Zhang Hao (1897–1942), Party name of Lin Yuying, a cousin of Lin Biao; returning from Moscow in 1935 as the Comintern's envoy, he was the man whose word brought Zhang Guotao to accept the Party Center's leadership.

ch02.anchor: a trusted general, Jiang Dingwen
ch02.note: Jiang Dingwen (1895–1974), a senior general of Chiang Kai-shek's Whampoa clique who headed the Nationalists' Xi'an (and Tianshui) field headquarters overseeing the northwest.

ch02.anchor: a blockaded belt a hundred li deep
ch02.note: A li is the Chinese mile, about half a kilometer, so a hundred li is some fifty kilometers. The unit recurs throughout, as in the “25,000-li Long March.”

ch02.anchor: the forces of Deng Baoshan, Gao Shuangcheng
ch02.note: Deng Baoshan (1894–1968), the Nationalist general holding Yulin north of the Border Region; friendly to the Communists, he quietly opened trade and river crossings for them, as this chapter relates, and in 1949 helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Beiping.

ch02.anchor: Zhou Enlai, Ren Bishi, and other Communist leaders
ch02.note: Ren Bishi (1904–1950), one of the CCP's top leaders of this period and later one of the “five great secretaries”; worn out by the revolution, he died in 1950, the first of that inner circle to go.

ch02.anchor: Feng Xuefeng slipped from northern Shaanxi to Shanghai
ch02.note: Feng Xuefeng (1903–1976), a writer and literary theorist close to Lu Xun and a veteran of the Long March; here he re-links the Party Center with its underground in Shanghai.

ch02.anchor: Peng Dehuai, Liu Bocheng, Chen Yi
ch02.note: Peng Dehuai (1898–1974) and Chen Yi (1901–1972), two of the foremost Communist commanders and, later, marshals of the People's Republic; Peng went on to command in Korea and serve as defense minister before his 1959 purge, Chen to become foreign minister.

ch02.anchor: its commander-in-chief Xu Xiangqian escaped
ch02.note: Xu Xiangqian (1901–1990), commander of the Western Route Army and later one of the ten marshals; he alone of its leaders made his way back after that army's destruction.

ch02.anchor: toward Xinjiang under Li Xiannian
ch02.note: Li Xiannian (1909–1992), who led the Western Route Army's survivors out to Xinjiang; a lifelong senior figure, he served as President of the People's Republic from 1983 to 1988.

ch02.anchor: The Xinjiang warlord Sheng Shicai
ch02.note: Sheng Shicai (1897–1970), the warlord who ruled Xinjiang from 1933; for years he courted the neighboring Soviet Union and tolerated the Communists before turning violently against them in 1942.

ch02.anchor: Mao gave Luo Ruiqing precise orders
ch02.note: Luo Ruiqing (1906–1978), a leading Communist security officer; after 1949 the first Minister of Public Security and later PLA chief of staff, before his purge in 1966 (see the “Peng, Luo, Lu, and Yang” case, Chapter 12).

ch02.anchor: come to the Yangtze Bureau
ch02.note: The Yangtze (Changjiang) Bureau, the CCP's regional headquarters at Wuhan in 1937–1938, headed by Wang Ming; it directed the Party's work across central China in the first year of the war.

ch02.anchor: Wang Ming, Zhou Enlai, Bo Gu, and Li Kenong
ch02.note: Bo Gu (1907–1946), Party name of Qin Bangxian; a Moscow-trained leader of the “28 Bolsheviks” who headed the CCP before losing power to Mao at the 1935 Zunyi Conference. He died in the same 1946 plane crash as several other returning leaders.

ch02.anchor: the people of Hadapu were looking to take in sons-in-law
ch02.note: Hadapu, a town in southern Gansu the Long March reached in September 1935; it was here, from an old newspaper, that the leadership learned a Red base still survived in northern Shaanxi. The point is that exhausted marchers deserted to marry into the local families.

ch02.anchor: The army commander Xu Haidong
ch02.note: Xu Haidong (1900–1970), a hard-fighting commander of the Red 25th and 15th Army Corps, from a Hubei potter's family; later made one of the ten Senior Generals in 1955.

ch02.anchor: The CCP Central Social Affairs Department
ch02.note: The Social Affairs Department (社会部, Shehuibu) was the CCP's central intelligence and security organ, founded in February 1939 under Kang Sheng. The innocuous name—borrowed from a civil-administration office of the Nationalist government—was itself a cover; within the Party it was known as Zhongshebu and kept secret.

ch02.anchor: Kong Yuan, and Zeng Xisheng
ch02.note: Kong Yuan (1906–1990), an intelligence official who after 1949 headed the Central Investigation Department; and Zeng Xisheng (1904–1968), chief of the Military Commission's Second Bureau—the Communists' radio-interception and codebreaking service—and later the Party boss of Anhui.

ch02.anchor: Deng Zhongxia and Qu Qiubai
ch02.note: Deng Zhongxia (1894–1933), a pioneer of the Communist labor movement, and Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), an early general secretary of the CCP and noted writer—both later captured and executed by the Nationalists.

ch02.anchor: the three armed uprisings of the Shanghai workers
ch02.note: The three workers' armed risings in Shanghai of 1926–1927, organized by the Communists with Zhou Enlai among the leaders; the third, in March 1927, briefly seized the city—shortly before Chiang Kai-shek's April purge turned on those same workers.

ch02.anchor: a fellow student from Shanghai University, Cao Yi'ou
ch02.note: Cao Yi'ou (1905–1989), Kang Sheng's wife and lifelong political partner; she took an active hand in the Yan'an purges and again in the Cultural Revolution.

ch02.anchor: when Kirov, a member of the Soviet Politburo, was assassinated
ch02.note: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad party chief, was murdered in December 1934; Stalin used the killing as the pretext to launch the Great Purge, in which “Trotskyites” were hunted across the Soviet party.

ch02.anchor: "immortals" come down from the Kunlun Mountains
ch02.note: In Chinese myth the Kunlun range is the dwelling place of the immortals; Mao's florid welcome casts the returnees from Moscow as gods descending from that fabled mountain.

ch02.anchor: At the Comintern's Seventh Congress
ch02.note: The Seventh (and last) World Congress of the Communist International, Moscow, 1935, which proclaimed the “united front” policy of alliance with non-Communist parties against fascism—the line that underlay the second Nationalist-Communist alliance.

ch02.anchor: Deng Fa and Zhou Xing had taken part in the purges
ch02.note: Deng Fa (1906–1946), a Cantonese seaman and labor organizer who headed the State Political Security Bureau in the Jiangxi Soviet; he died in the 1946 air crash that killed several returning Communist leaders.

ch02.anchor: The Comintern's general secretary, Dimitrov
ch02.note: Georgi Dimitrov (1882–1949), the Bulgarian Communist who led the Comintern from 1935; famed for his defiant self-defense at the Nazis' Reichstag-fire trial.

ch02.anchor: the "May Thirtieth" strike
ch02.note: The May Thirtieth Movement of 1925, the wave of anti-imperialist strikes and boycotts that swept China after British-officered police shot Chinese demonstrators in Shanghai; a milestone in the rise of the Communist-led labor movement.

ch02.anchor: Its leaders Guo Moruo and Yu Dafu
ch02.note: The Creation Society, an influential Shanghai literary group of the 1920s. Guo Moruo (1892–1978) was a poet, playwright, and historian who became the foremost cultural official of the People's Republic; Yu Dafu (1896–1945), a celebrated writer, was killed by the Japanese at the war's end.

ch02.anchor: When the Northern Expedition began
ch02.note: The Northern Expedition (1926–1928), the Nationalist military campaign, launched from Guangdong in the first united front with the Communists, that defeated the warlords and nominally reunified China under the Kuomintang.

ch02.anchor: the "League of Left-Wing Writers
ch02.note: The League of Left-Wing Writers, founded in Shanghai in 1930 under Communist guidance with Lu Xun as its figurehead; it made left-wing literature a force in the cities and a target of Nationalist repression.

ch02.anchor: the Red Army's negotiations with the Fujian government
ch02.note: The Fujian People's Government, proclaimed in November 1933 by the Nationalists' 19th Route Army in revolt against Chiang Kai-shek; the Red Army signed a truce with the rebels, though the alliance came to little before Chiang crushed the revolt within weeks.

ch02.anchor: Sun Yat-sen University in the Soviet Union
ch02.note: The Moscow Sun Yat-sen University (1925–1930), founded to train Chinese revolutionaries; its graduates included the “28 Bolsheviks” and, briefly, Chiang Kai-shek's own son.

ch02.anchor: its commander Gao Gang, secretary of the Northwest Bureau
ch02.note: Gao Gang (1905–1954), a founder of the northern-Shaanxi Red base and the leading Communist of the northwest; he rose high after 1949 but fell in 1954, charged with plotting for power, and killed himself.

ch02.anchor: a great many Mauser pistols
ch02.note: The German Mauser C96, the “broomhandle” automatic pistol carried in a wooden holster-stock; imported and copied in huge numbers, it was the prized sidearm of Chinese officers and bodyguards.

ch02.anchor: a Red Army man of the Ningdu Uprising in Jiangxi
ch02.note: At the Ningdu Uprising of December 1931 some 17,000 troops of the Nationalists' 26th Route Army—former Northwest Army men—mutinied in Jiangxi and came over to the Red Army, becoming its 5th Army Corps.

ch02.anchor: the Shaanxi provincial secretary Hu Yaobang
ch02.note: Hu Yaobang (1915–1989), later general secretary of the Party and a leading reformer; his ouster in 1987 and death in April 1989 set off the Tiananmen Square protests.

ch02.anchor: Xie Zichang had launched the "Qingjian Uprising"
ch02.note: Xie Zichang (1897–1935), with Liu Zhidan the founder of the Red Army and Soviet base in northern Shaanxi—the very base that gave the Long March its destination. He was killed in battle in 1935.

ch02.anchor: the officers' school Feng Yuxiang had set up
ch02.note: Feng Yuxiang (1882–1948), the “Christian General,” a powerful northern warlord whose shifting alliances shaped the politics of the 1920s; many later Communist and Nationalist officers passed through his forces.

ch02.anchor: in the battle of Gubeikou
ch02.note: Gubeikou, a strategic pass in the Great Wall northeast of Beijing. The reference is to the 1933 fighting against the Japanese advance south of the Wall, in which Feng Yuxiang raised his short-lived Chahar Anti-Japanese Allied Army.

ch02.anchor: the April 12 coup of 1927
ch02.note: On 12 April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai, disarming the workers' militias and massacring Communists and unionists; the “April 12 coup” ended the first united front and began a decade of Nationalist terror against the CCP.

ch02.anchor: from the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army who had studied
ch02.note: The Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, the Communist-led guerrilla force that fought the Japanese in occupied Manchuria through the 1930s; hard-pressed, many of its cadres withdrew across the border into the Soviet Union.

ch02.anchor: joined Fang Zhimin's Red Army
ch02.note: Fang Zhimin (1899–1935), founder of the Communist base in northeastern Jiangxi; captured by the Nationalists and executed in 1935, he is remembered for the prison essay “Lovable China.”

ch02.anchor: the forced crossing of the Jinsha River
ch02.note: A celebrated feat of the Long March: in May 1935 the Red Army slipped across the Jinsha (the upper Yangtze) in a handful of boats, escaping the pursuing Nationalist armies.

ch02.anchor: the Four Crossings of the Chishui and the storming of Loushan Pass
ch02.note: Celebrated Long March actions of early 1935 under Mao Zedong's command in Guizhou: the storming of Loushan Pass, and the four feints back and forth across the Chishui River that threw off far larger pursuing armies.

ch02.anchor: won by the old cadre He Long
ch02.note: He Long (1896–1969), a founder of the Red Army who led the 1927 Nanchang Uprising and rose to marshal; the woman student he won was Xue Ming. He died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

ch02.anchor: the writers Liu Baiyu and Zhou Libo
ch02.note: Liu Baiyu (1916–2005) and Zhou Libo (1908–1979), well-known Communist writers; Zhou Libo won fame for his land-reform novel The Hurricane.

ch02.anchor: became a Zhongnanhai photographer
ch02.note: Zhongnanhai, the walled lakeside compound beside the old Forbidden City that became the headquarters and residence of the Communist leadership—the seat of power of the People's Republic. The photographer was Hou Bo, who took many of the best-known portraits of Mao.

ch02.anchor: the Lu Xun Academy of Arts
ch02.note: Yan'an's academy of literature and the arts, named for Lu Xun (1881–1936), modern China's most revered writer; it trained the movement's writers, artists, and musicians.

ch02.anchor: the air-defense sentry on Baota Mountain
ch02.note: Baota Shan (“Pagoda Hill”), crowned by a Tang-dynasty pagoda overlooking Yan'an; its silhouette became the emblem of Yan'an and of the Communist revolution itself.

ch02.anchor: the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee in 1938
ch02.note: The enlarged Sixth Plenum of the Party's Sixth Central Committee, held in Yan'an in the autumn of 1938, at which Mao Zedong consolidated his leadership and turned back Wang Ming's rival “Right” line of subordinating the Party to the united front.

ch02.anchor: The purges in the West Hunan-Hubei and the Hubei-Henan-Anhui Soviets
ch02.note: The internal purges of the early 1930s in two Communist base areas—the Xiang-E-Xi (West Hunan–Hubei) Soviet and the E-Yu-Wan (Hubei–Henan–Anhui) Soviet, the latter under Zhang Guotao—in which thousands of Red Army officers and cadres were tortured and killed on fabricated charges. See the “AB Corps” and Futian notes, Chapter 1.

ch02.anchor: "five great secretaries": Mao, Liu, Zhou, Zhu, and Ren
ch02.note: The five members of the Party Secretariat formed in 1943 and confirmed in 1945: Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, Zhu De, and Ren Bishi—the CCP's supreme leadership through the civil war.

ch02.anchor: The neighboring Jin-Sui base area
ch02.note: Communist base areas were named by stringing together one-character abbreviations of the provinces they spanned: Jin (Shanxi), Sui (Suiyuan), Cha (Chahar), Ji (Hebei), Lu (Shandong), Yu (Henan). Thus Jin-Sui is the Shanxi-Suiyuan area, Jin-Cha-Ji the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei area, and so on.

ch02.anchor: Nie Rongzhen was in need of an experienced security cadre
ch02.note: Nie Rongzhen (1899–1992), founder and commander of the Jin-Cha-Ji base behind Japanese lines in North China; later one of the ten marshals of the People's Republic and head of its nuclear-weapons program.

ch02.anchor: worked in the Anyuan coal mine at the age of thirteen
ch02.note: The Anyuan coal mines in Jiangxi were a cradle of the Communist labor movement, site of a famous 1922 miners' strike led by Liu Shaoqi, Li Lisan, and Mao Zedong.

ch02.anchor: freed in 1930 when the Red Army took Changsha
ch02.note: In July 1930 Peng Dehuai's Red Army briefly captured Changsha, the capital of Hunan—the only provincial capital the Communists held in that period, and one they had to abandon within days.

ch02.anchor: editor-in-chief of the New China Daily
ch02.note: The New China Daily (Xinhua Ribao), the Communist Party's openly published newspaper in the Nationalist wartime capital of Chongqing—a legal voice for the Party in enemy territory, and a cover for its intelligence work.

ch03.anchor: the short name *ba-ban*
ch03.note: During the wartime alliance the Nationalists let the Communists keep open liaison offices in the cities they controlled, nominally the rear offices of the Eighth Route Army (the 18th Group Army). The arrangement is what let a Communist establishment operate legally in Nationalist territory; the offices ran open united-front work above the surface and secret intelligence below it.

ch03.anchor: to wear the same Zhongshan suits as government officials
ch03.note: The Zhongshan suit (zhongshanzhuang), named for Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan), was the semi-formal tunic-and-trousers uniform of Republican officialdom, and later the “Mao suit” of the People's Republic. The point is that the Communists now dressed indistinguishably from the officials they worked among.

ch03.anchor: reported the great victory at Pingxingguan
ch03.note: At Pingxingguan in northeast Shanxi, in September 1937, an Eighth Route Army division under Lin Biao ambushed a Japanese column—the Communists' first celebrated battlefield success of the war, and a propaganda coup out of proportion to its scale. CORROBORATED as an event, though its size has long been inflated in the telling.

ch03.anchor: the far country
ch03.note: As glossed earlier, “the far country” (yuanfang) is the Party's code for the Soviet Union and the Comintern in Moscow.

ch03.anchor: "Mengjiang United Autonomous Government
ch03.note: The Japanese puppet regime for Inner Mongolia (Mengjiang, “the Mongol borderland”), set up in 1939 under the Mongol prince Demchugdongrub to detach the region from China.

ch03.anchor: honored it as the "Latter Three Heroes,"
ch03.note: Xiong Xianghui, Chen Zhongjing, and Shen Jian, planted around Hu Zongnan's headquarters. The name deliberately echoes the “Three Heroes of Longtan” (Li Kenong, Qian Zhuangfei, Hu Di) of the early-1930s Special Branch, noted in Chapter 1.

ch03.anchor: be content to serve as an idle chessman
ch03.note: A metaphor from weiqi (go): an “idle stone” (xianqi lengzi) is a piece laid down early, far from the fighting, that looks pointless until, at the decisive moment, it turns the whole board. The author makes it the governing image for the Communists' long-dormant deep-cover agents.

ch03.anchor: You cannot get the tiger's cubs without entering the tiger's lair.
ch03.note: A proverb (bu ru huxue, yan de huzi): nothing worth having is won without entering danger. Zhou Enlai and Dong Biwu gave it to Xiong Xianghui as his watchword.

ch03.anchor: Shen Anna, a native of Taixing in Jiangsu
ch03.note: Shen Anna (1915–2010), later famous as the Communists' “red stenographer,” took shorthand at the Nationalists' confidential meetings for some fourteen years and passed the records to the Party. Her story is well documented in Party histories and her family's own recollections.

ch03.anchor: the largest Party enterprise of all, China Resources, was born
ch03.note: China Resources (Huarun), assembled from the Party's wartime trading firms, went on to become one of the largest state-owned conglomerates of the People's Republic—retail, power, beer, real estate—still active today.

ch03.anchor: his fellow Ningbo townsman Bao Yugang
ch03.note: Bao Yugang (1918–1991), better known in the West as Sir Y. K. Pao, later became the world's largest independent shipowner from Hong Kong. His early dealings with Lu Xuzhang's firm are attested; the passage should not be read as making him a Communist agent.

ch03.anchor: the South Seas overseas-Chinese leader Tan Kah Kee
ch03.note: Tan Kah Kee (Chen Jiageng, 1874–1961), the Singapore rubber magnate and philanthropist who led overseas-Chinese relief for the resistance. His 1940 tour, contrasting a corrupt Chongqing with an austere Yan'an, famously turned him toward the Communists.

ch03.anchor: the great sofa at No. 50 Zengjiayan
ch03.note: Zengjiayan No. 50 in Chongqing was the office of the CCP's Southern Bureau and Zhou Enlai's residence; together with the Hongyan (“Red Crag”) village compound it was the hub of Communist work in the wartime capital, and both are now museums.

ch03.anchor: staged its "scorched-earth resistance" and set fire to the city
ch03.note: The Changsha fire of November 1938 (the “Wenxi fire”): a botched scorched-earth order set on a false alarm burned much of the city and killed thousands of its own people, one of the war's great man-made disasters. CORROBORATED.

ch03.anchor: engineered the New Fourth Army Incident
ch03.note: In January 1941, in southern Anhui, Nationalist forces ambushed the headquarters column of the Communist New Fourth Army, killing or capturing thousands and abolishing the army's designation. It marked the effective end of the united front and is the “second anti-Communist high tide” of the paragraph.

ch03.anchor: the *Yellow River Cantata*
ch03.note: The Yellow River Cantata (1939), words by Guang Weiran and music by Xian Xinghai, became the great musical anthem of the resistance and remains one of the best-known works of modern Chinese music.

ch03.anchor: the Canadian doctor Bethune
ch03.note: Norman Bethune (1890–1939), the Canadian surgeon who served and died with the Eighth Route Army in North China; Mao Zedong's eulogy made him one of the most honored foreigners in Chinese Communist memory.

ch03.anchor: the Vietnamese Communist leader Nguyen Ai Quoc, Ho Chi Minh
ch03.note: Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969) used the name Nguyen Ai Quoc (“Nguyen the Patriot”) in his years as a Comintern agent; he was in and out of south China organizing the Vietnamese revolution before founding the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.

ch03.anchor: Okano Susumu, alias Nosaka Sanzo
ch03.note: Nosaka Sanzo (1892–1993), who used the alias Okano Susumu, spent the war in Yan'an running anti-war work among Japanese prisoners; a founder of the postwar Japanese Communist Party, he was expelled from it at the age of a hundred when Soviet archives exposed his wartime denunciation of a comrade.

ch03.anchor: his one book, *Red Star Over China*
ch03.note: Edgar Snow's Red Star Over China (1937), written after the American journalist reached the Communist base in northern Shaanxi in 1936, was the first sympathetic Western account of Mao Zedong and the Red Army and shaped outside perceptions of the CCP for a generation.

ch03.anchor: Colonel Barrett posted to Yan'an, Major Ou Daiyi to the East River Column
ch03.note: Colonel David D. Barrett led the U.S. Army Observation Group (the “Dixie Mission”) to Yan'an in 1944. “Ou Daiyi” is the source's transliteration of the American officer attached to the East River Column; the name cannot be securely matched to a Western original and is given here as the book renders it.

ch03.anchor: detected the strategic intelligence of Germany's attack on the USSR
ch03.note: The claim that the Communist-linked Yan Baohang gave Moscow advance warning of the June 1941 German invasion is a staple of Chinese intelligence lore. It is UNCORROBORATED in independent sources and rests chiefly on later Chinese accounts; the book presents it as established.

ch03.anchor: successfully rescued eighty-nine British and American prisoners of war
ch03.note: The East River Column's rescues of Allied personnel after the fall of Hong Kong, in cooperation with the British Army Aid Group, are well documented; the figures vary by account. Broadly CORROBORATED.

ch03.anchor: Only in 1988 did a memoir by the former Juntong Northwest district chief reveal the truth
ch03.note: The killing of Xuan Xiafu is the author's clearest “interested witness” set-piece: the account rests on the confession-memoir of the Juntong officer Zhang Yanfo and on Luo Qingchang's later disclosures, both cited in the Principal Sources. That Chiang Kai-shek ordered the killing is CORROBORATED by Zhang's memoir; the deeper motive—fear that Xuan would turn Hu Zongnan—is the Communist side's interpretation, and is presented as fact.

ch03.anchor: which was then named Lihuang County after him
ch03.note: Wei Lihuang's capture of the Communist base town of Jinjiazhai in 1932 led to its renaming as Lihuang County in his honor. After 1947 it was renamed Jinzhai, its present name.

ch03.anchor: a three-sided Executive Headquarters for military mediation
ch03.note: The Executive Headquarters set up in Beiping in January 1946, with Nationalist, Communist, and American members, to supervise the truce after the war; it broke down as the civil war resumed.

ch03.anchor: proposed a "three-thirds system" in building
ch03.note: The “three-thirds system” (sansanzhi): the wartime rule that Communists, non-Party progressives, and other democrats each hold a third of the seats in base-area governments—a united-front device to broaden the Party's support.

ch03.anchor: held property and wives in common
ch03.note: A stock anti-Communist slander of the civil-war years, gongchan gongqi (共产共妻): that the Communists “held property in common” and therefore “held wives in common” too. Playing on the shared character gong (共, “common”) in the word for communism, it painted the Party as an enemy of the family.

ch03.anchor: red-browed, green-eyed
ch03.note: 红眉毛绿眼睛, “red-browed, green-eyed”: the stock description of ogres and demons in Chinese folktale. The author’s point is that Nationalist propaganda had made the Communists out to be literal monsters.

ch03.anchor: folded into the National Revolutionary Army
ch03.note: The National Revolutionary Army was the armed force of the Nationalist state. Under the 1937 alliance the Communists’ Red Army was nominally absorbed into it as the Eighth Route Army in the north and the New Fourth Army in the south, though both stayed under Communist command throughout.

ch03.anchor: the New China News Agency's open dispatches
ch03.note: The New China News Agency (新华社, Xinhua), the CCP’s official news service, founded in the base areas in the 1930s and today the state news agency of the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: the Nationalist center's negotiator, Zhang Chong
ch03.note: Zhang Chong (1904–1941), a senior officer of the Nationalist Zhongtong who had earlier helped engineer the “Wu Hao Incident” forgery against Zhou Enlai (see Chapter 1), then became the Nationalists’ chief liaison to the Communists in the united front. Zhou came to respect him and mourned his death publicly in 1941. He is a different man from the Yunnan army general also named Zhang Chong who appears later in this chapter.

ch03.anchor: Mao Zedong's younger brother Mao Zemin
ch03.note: Mao Zemin (1896–1943), Mao Zedong’s younger brother and the Party’s chief financial and banking organizer; first president of the Chinese Soviet Republic’s national bank. He was arrested and executed in Xinjiang in 1943 by the warlord Sheng Shicai. A different brother from Mao Zetan (Chapter 2).

ch03.anchor: bank president of the Chinese Soviet Republic
ch03.note: The Chinese Soviet Republic (1931–1937) was the Communist state proclaimed at Ruijin in Jiangxi, with Mao Zedong as its chairman; it was dismantled by the Nationalist encirclement campaigns that forced the Long March.

ch03.anchor: into fabi, the Nationalist currency
ch03.note: Fabi (法币, “legal tender”), the unified paper currency the Nationalist government introduced in its 1935 currency reform, replacing the old silver-dollar system.

ch03.anchor: Ye Jianying met the train with a car
ch03.note: Ye Jianying (1897–1986), a Communist general and later marshal of the People’s Republic; here handling liaison and security work, and decades on a decisive figure in the 1976 arrest of the “Gang of Four.”

ch03.anchor: the capital office in Nanjing
ch03.note: Nanjing (“southern capital”) was the seat of the Nationalist government from 1927 until the Japanese captured it in December 1937; hence the CCP’s office there was, in effect, its mission to the capital.

ch03.anchor: his old Nankai teacher Zhang Boling
ch03.note: Zhang Boling (1876–1951), the founder of the Nankai schools and Nankai University in Tianjin, where the young Zhou Enlai had studied; one of the most influential educators of Republican China.

ch03.anchor: the Communist representative Bogu
ch03.note: “Bogu” was Qin Bangxian (1907–1946), a Moscow-trained leader of the “28 Bolsheviks” who had headed the CCP before losing power at the Zunyi Conference of 1935. He died in the “April 8th” air crash of 1946. He appears below under his real name, Qin Bangxian.

ch03.anchor: The eminent professor Wang Kunlun
ch03.note: Wang Kunlun (1902–1985), a Nationalist Party member from 1922 who had secretly joined the Communist Party in 1933 while sitting in the Nationalists’ Legislative Yuan; later a vice-mayor of Beijing and a leader of the Revolutionary Committee of the Nationalist Party.

ch03.anchor: the Communists proposed founding
ch03.note: The New China Daily (新华日报), the CCP’s openly published newspaper, brought out from 1938; the only Communist paper legally circulated in Nationalist-held territory during the war.

ch03.anchor: they would not publish the
ch03.note: The Manifesto of Nationalist-Communist Cooperation was the joint declaration of September 1937 announcing the second united front, in which the CCP pledged to cooperate and the Nationalists conceded its legal existence.

ch03.anchor: the Nationalist propaganda chief Shao Lizi
ch03.note: Shao Lizi (1882–1967), a Nationalist elder and sometime propaganda minister and ambassador; a persistent advocate of peace who joined the Nationalist delegation to the 1949 talks and then stayed on the mainland.

ch03.anchor: the Nationalist elder statesman Yu Youren
ch03.note: Yu Youren (1879–1964), a founding Nationalist, longtime president of the Control Yuan, and one of modern China’s most revered calligraphers, whose brushwork was prized for mastheads and inscriptions.

ch03.anchor: close to the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region
ch03.note: The Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region was the Communists’ principal base area, centered on Yan’an in the arid northwest and straddling parts of the three provinces of its name; from 1937 it was the seat of the CCP Central Committee.

ch03.anchor: ran through Lanzhou in Gansu
ch03.note: Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu province, sits on the Yellow River in the northwest, on the overland road toward Xinjiang and the Soviet Union—hence its use as the Communists’ western window.

ch03.anchor: Wu Xiuquan, fluent in Russian
ch03.note: Wu Xiuquan (1908–1997), a Soviet-trained Communist who had interpreted on the Long March; later a PLA general and senior diplomat of the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: fixed on Ejin Banner
ch03.note: Ejin (Ejina) Banner, a remote desert district in the far west of Inner Mongolia bordering Gansu, astride routes toward the Soviet Union. A “banner” (旗, qi) is the Mongol equivalent of a county in China’s administrative system.

ch03.anchor: a Special Branch veteran, Wang Shiying
ch03.note: Wang Shiying (1905–1968), a Central Special Branch veteran who ran Communist intelligence and united-front work in North China; later a provincial governor, he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

ch03.anchor: Bo Yibo, and many other members arrested
