ch03.note: Bo Yibo (1908–2007), a senior Communist organizer in North China. He and dozens of imprisoned cadres were freed in 1936 under a Party-sanctioned arrangement to sign anti-Communist notices; decades later this was turned against them in the Cultural Revolution as the “Sixty-One Renegades” case. He became a leading economic official and one of the Party’s “Eight Elders.”

ch03.anchor: organized Nan Hanchen
ch03.note: Nan Hanchen (1895–1967), a Special Branch veteran and financial specialist who later served as the Border Region’s finance chief (see below) and became the first governor of the People’s Bank of China.

ch03.anchor: Ji Hongchang, and others
ch03.note: Ji Hongchang (1895–1934), a patriotic general who organized armed anti-Japanese resistance in Chahar after the loss of Manchuria; a secret Communist, he was arrested and executed by the Nationalists in 1934.

ch03.anchor: and work the Second War Zone
ch03.note: The Nationalist government divided the country into large military theaters called war zones. The Second War Zone covered Shanxi and its borders and was commanded by Yan Xishan; the First and Fourth War Zones appear later in the chapter.

ch03.anchor: who held Shanxi as his own domain
ch03.note: Yan Xishan (1883–1960), the “model governor” who ruled Shanxi as a personal fief for decades, trimming his course among the Nationalists, the Communists, and the Japanese.

ch03.anchor: the Central Committee's Yangtze Bureau
ch03.note: The Yangtze Bureau, the CCP organ that directed Party work throughout central and southern China from Wuhan in 1937–38; it was later reconstituted as the Southern Bureau in Chongqing.

ch03.anchor: an old comrade from the Northern Expedition
ch03.note: The Northern Expedition (1926–1928) was the joint Nationalist-Communist military campaign from Guangdong that defeated the northern warlords and brought most of China under nominal Nationalist rule; a shared credential among the older men of both parties.

ch03.anchor: the head of the Xi'an field headquarters, Cheng Qian
ch03.note: Cheng Qian (1882–1968), a senior Nationalist general and elder statesman of Hunan; in 1949 he led the peaceful handover of Hunan to the Communists and afterward held high office in the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: veterans of the 1911 Revolution
ch03.note: The 1911 (Xinhai) Revolution overthrew the Qing dynasty and founded the Republic of China. Having taken part in it conferred a revolutionary seniority that even the Nationalist leadership had to respect.

ch03.anchor: side by side on the Eastern Expedition
ch03.note: The Eastern Expeditions of 1925, in which the young Whampoa cadet army—Chiang Kai-shek commanding, Zhou Enlai in its political department—crushed the Guangdong warlord Chen Jiongming, consolidating the revolutionary base at Guangzhou.

ch03.anchor: Li Jishen, head of the Guilin field headquarters, was firmly for resistance
ch03.note: Li Jishen (1885–1959), a senior Nationalist general long at odds with Chiang Kai-shek; he founded the pro-Communist Revolutionary Committee of the Nationalist Party in 1948 and became a vice-chairman of the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: Hu Yuzhi and Fan Changjiang
ch03.note: Hu Yuzhi (1896–1986), a writer, editor, and Esperantist active in the resistance press, and Fan Changjiang (1909–1970), a celebrated war correspondent and pioneer of modern Chinese journalism; both worked secretly with the Communists.

ch03.anchor: cultural figures such as Chen Hansheng
ch03.note: Chen Hansheng (Chen Han-seng, 1897–2004), a Marxist agrarian economist and secret agent linked to the Soviet spy Richard Sorge’s network in the 1930s; a scholar who lived past a hundred.

ch03.anchor: the Qiongya Column on Hainan Island
ch03.note: The Qiongya Column, the Communist-led guerrilla force on Hainan Island off China’s far south coast, which fought on from the late 1920s through the island’s capture in 1950. (“Qiongya” is the old name for the Hainan region.)

ch03.anchor: Southeast Asia, and the South Seas
ch03.note: “The South Seas” (南洋, Nanyang) is the Chinese term for maritime Southeast Asia—Singapore, Malaya, the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines and beyond—home to the large overseas-Chinese communities that recur through this chapter.

ch03.anchor: the Hebei Peace Preservation commander Zhang Yinwu
ch03.note: Zhang Yinwu, a Nationalist militia commander in Hebei whose June 1939 attacks on Eighth Route Army units were among the first large armed clashes—the “friction”—of the united-front period.

ch03.anchor: Qin Bangxian, Dong Biwu, Wang Ruofei
ch03.note: Wang Ruofei (1896–1946), a senior Communist leader and negotiator; he died with Bogu (Qin Bangxian) and others in the “April 8th” air crash of 1946.

ch03.anchor: Through Feng Yuxiang and Shao Lizi
ch03.note: Feng Yuxiang (1882–1948), the “Christian General,” a powerful warlord who allied by turns with and against Chiang Kai-shek and leaned toward resistance and the Communists in his later years.

ch03.anchor: using Zhang Bojun and Luo Longji
ch03.note: Zhang Bojun (1895–1969) and Luo Longji (1896–1965), leaders of the centrist “third force” parties that made up the Democratic League; both became the most prominent targets of the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign, denounced as the “Zhang-Luo alliance.”

ch03.anchor: through Guo Moruo and Tian Han
ch03.note: Guo Moruo (1892–1978), a leading poet, playwright, and historian close to the Communists, and Tian Han (1898–1968), the dramatist who wrote the words of “The March of the Volunteers,” later the national anthem of the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: under Madame Chiang
ch03.note: “Madame Chiang” was Soong Mei-ling (1898–2003), Chiang Kai-shek’s wife and a formidable presence in Nationalist public life and in wartime diplomacy with the United States; younger sister of Song Qingling, named just below.

ch03.anchor: There were also Song Qingling
ch03.note: Song Qingling (Soong Ching-ling, 1893–1981), the widow of Sun Yat-sen and elder sister of Soong Mei-ling; a lifelong champion of the left who sided openly with the Communists and became an honorary head of state of the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: the Nationalist martyr Liao Zhongkai
ch03.note: Liao Zhongkai (1877–1925), a leading left-wing Nationalist and architect of the first alliance with the Communists, assassinated in 1925. His son Liao Chengzhi ran the Communists’ overseas-Chinese work and his widow He Xiangning (named below) was herself a noted revolutionary and painter.

ch03.anchor: The China Democratic League was the third great party
ch03.note: The China Democratic League, an alliance of centrist intellectuals’ groups formed in 1941; the largest of the “third force” minor parties that sought a middle path between the Nationalists and Communists.

ch03.anchor: the Revolutionary Committee of the Nationalist Party
ch03.note: Founded in Hong Kong in 1948 under Li Jishen, this pro-Communist breakaway from the Kuomintang survives today as one of the officially sanctioned minor parties of the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: he met Liu Wenhui at a secret spot
ch03.note: Liu Wenhui (1895–1976), a Sichuan warlord and governor of Xikang who leaned toward the Communists and declared for them in 1949; afterward a minister in the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: seats on the National Political Council
ch03.note: The People’s Political Council (1938–1948), a wartime advisory assembly that gave seats to the Communists and the minor parties alongside the ruling Nationalists—a rare, if toothless, semi-representative forum.

ch03.anchor: the "Chinese National Liberation Vanguard"
ch03.note: A Communist-led patriotic student organization formed in the wake of the December 9th Movement of 1935 to press for national resistance to Japan.

ch03.anchor: The Nationalist Guangxi-clique general
ch03.note: The Guangxi clique was the powerful regional militarist faction led by Li Zongren and Bai Chongxi, based in the southern province of Guangxi and a standing rival of Chiang Kai-shek within the Nationalist camp.

ch03.anchor: Bai Chongxi was a fine hand at war
ch03.note: Bai Chongxi (1893–1966), the ablest general of the Guangxi clique, a Muslim officer nicknamed “Little Zhuge” after the legendary strategist Zhuge Liang; deputy chief of the Nationalist general staff and later defense minister.

ch03.anchor: Moscow's Sun Yat-sen University
ch03.note: The Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow (1925–1930), a Comintern school that trained young Chinese of both parties; many of the CCP’s Moscow-oriented leaders passed through it.

ch03.anchor: The Shanxi army under Fu Zuoyi
ch03.note: Fu Zuoyi (1895–1974), a leading Nationalist commander in North China; his peaceful surrender handed Beiping (Beijing) to the Communists in 1949, and he served the People’s Republic as water-resources minister.

ch03.anchor: to the Jin-Sui military region
ch03.note: The Jin-Sui (Shanxi-Suiyuan) base area and military region, one of the Communists’ wartime bases in the northwest, guarding the approaches from Yan’an eastward across the Yellow River.

ch03.anchor: Wang Xuewen of the Central Special Branch
ch03.note: Wang Xuewen (1895–1985), a Japan-trained Marxist economist and Special Branch officer who recruited and trained agents such as Shen Anna; he later directed the Communists’ work among enemy troops.

ch03.anchor: the trust of the governor Zhu Jiahua
ch03.note: Zhu Jiahua (1893–1963), a Nationalist administrator and organization minister—here governor of Zhejiang, later secretary-general of the party’s central headquarters—and a rival of the CC Clique.

ch03.anchor: launched the Northeast Salvation Association
ch03.note: The Northeast National Salvation Association, formed in 1935 by exiled Northeasterners to relieve refugees driven out by the Japanese seizure of Manchuria and to press for its recovery.

ch03.anchor: The Northeastern Army elder Gao Chongmin
ch03.note: Gao Chongmin (1891–1971), a leading Northeastern patriot and a bridge between the Communists and the Northeastern and Northwestern armies in the run-up to the Xi’an Incident.

ch03.anchor: In Shanghai, Chen Yun
ch03.note: Chen Yun (1905–1995), here a young underground organizer in Shanghai, later one of the CCP’s most senior leaders and the Party’s foremost economic strategist for half a century.

ch03.anchor: the Guangdong militarist Chen Jitang
ch03.note: Chen Jitang (1890–1954), the warlord who ruled Guangdong in the early 1930s; his secret understanding with the Communists let the Red Army slip through his lines during the 1934 Long March breakout.

ch03.anchor: two and a half more than commander He Long
ch03.note: He Long (1896–1969), a founder of the Red Army and later a marshal of the People’s Republic; he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

ch03.anchor: When Peng Pai launched the peasant uprising
ch03.note: Peng Pai (1896–1929), the pioneer of the Communist peasant movement, who led the Hailufeng soviet in Guangdong—the first rural soviet in China—and was executed by the Nationalists in 1929.

ch03.anchor: his old friend Tao Xingzhi
ch03.note: Tao Xingzhi (1891–1946), an influential progressive educator who gave his life to mass and rural schooling; he died in Shanghai in 1946, worn down by hardship, as the passage says.

ch03.anchor: the richest were the Ningbo men
ch03.note: Natives of Ningbo, a port in Zhejiang near Shanghai, were famous as the dominant merchant and banking community of modern Shanghai—the “Ningbo gang” of the city’s commerce.

ch03.anchor: a National Salvation Association of all circles
ch03.note: The National Salvation Association movement of 1936, a broad patriotic front demanding an end to civil war and resistance to Japan; the arrest of its leaders produced the celebrated case of the “Seven Gentlemen.”

ch03.anchor: called Guangda Huaxing
ch03.note: Guangda Huaxing, a Shanghai medicine-trading firm founded in 1932 and run from 1937 as a secret Communist enterprise, funding and covering the Party’s intelligence work in Nationalist territory.

ch03.anchor: an insurance company jointly with Lu Zuofu
ch03.note: Lu Zuofu (1893–1952), the industrialist who built the Minsheng Shipping Company into China’s largest domestic shipping line and organized the famous wartime evacuation of factories up the Yangtze past the gorges.

ch03.anchor: the lotus of the eighth month, rising from the mud unstained
ch03.note: An allusion to the Song scholar Zhou Dunyi’s essay “On the Love of the Lotus,” which praises the flower for “rising from the mud yet remaining unstained” (出淤泥而不染)—the classic emblem of purity kept amid corruption.

ch03.anchor: graduates of the Yunnan Military Academy
ch03.note: The Yunnan Military Academy at Kunming (founded 1909) was among the most important officer schools of the early Republic; it trained many Chinese commanders and a notable number of foreign cadets.

ch03.anchor: Korea's Choe Yong-gon and Yi Beom-seok
ch03.note: Two cadets who became national figures: Choe Yong-gon (1900–1976), later a founding marshal and head of state of North Korea, and Yi Beom-seok (1900–1972), later the first prime minister of South Korea; Vo Hai Thu became a Vietnamese revolutionary leader.

ch03.anchor: the Qing suppression of the Taiping Rebellion
ch03.note: The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), the enormous civil war that nearly toppled the Qing dynasty; its bloody suppression and the devastation of the southern provinces drove waves of Chinese to emigrate overseas.

ch03.anchor: the perilous Yunnan-Burma Road
ch03.note: The Burma Road, hacked over the mountains from Kunming to British Burma in 1937–38; it was wartime China’s chief overland lifeline for foreign supplies until the Japanese severed it in 1942.

ch03.anchor: the East River Column, the Qiongya Column
ch03.note: The East River Column, the Communist-led guerrilla force of the East River region of Guangdong, operating in the countryside around the Pearl River delta and Hong Kong; it becomes central to the wartime intelligence cooperation described later in this section.

ch03.anchor: The Filipino overseas Chinese Ye Fei
ch03.note: Ye Fei (1914–1999), born in the Philippines, a Communist commander who rose to full general and later admiral and held senior posts in the People’s Republic.

ch03.anchor: the Nationalist elders Lin Sen
ch03.note: Lin Sen (1868–1943), the nominal head of state (Chairman of the National Government) from 1931 until his death in 1943—a largely ceremonial figure while Chiang Kai-shek held the real power.

ch03.anchor: Force 136, formed jointly
ch03.note: Force 136 was the Far Eastern arm of Britain’s Special Operations Executive, which ran sabotage and guerrilla operations behind Japanese lines across Southeast Asia.

ch03.anchor: Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere
ch03.note: Japan’s propaganda name for the bloc of Asian lands it aimed to dominate, advertised as liberation from Western colonialism but amounting in practice to a Japanese empire.

ch03.anchor: patriotic soldiers like Aung San
ch03.note: Aung San (1915–1947), the leader of Burma’s independence movement and founder of its army; he sought first Japanese and then Allied backing, and was assassinated in 1947 on the eve of independence.

ch03.anchor: Kim Il-sung, Choe Yong-gon, Kim Chaek
ch03.note: Korean Communist guerrilla leaders who fought the Japanese in Manchuria. Kim Il-sung (1912–1994) went on to found and rule North Korea; Kim Chaek became one of its senior military and industrial figures.

ch03.anchor: the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army
ch03.note: The Communist-led guerrilla army that resisted Japanese rule in Manchuria through the 1930s, drawing in both Chinese and Korean fighters; it was largely broken up by Japanese counter-insurgency by the early 1940s.

ch03.anchor: the exile government of the Republic of Korea
ch03.note: The Korean Provisional Government, the exile administration first formed in Shanghai in 1919 and based during the war in Chongqing, where it received Nationalist support.

ch03.anchor: the American general Stilwell
ch03.note: General Joseph Stilwell (1883–1946), commander of U.S. forces in the China-Burma-India theater and Chiang Kai-shek’s Allied chief of staff. His feuds with Chiang, and his wish to arm the Communists’ effective troops, led to his recall in 1944.

ch03.anchor: Yuan Geng, who led the East River Column's intelligence men
ch03.note: Yuan Geng (1917–2016), an East River Column intelligence officer who half a century later founded the Shekou industrial zone at Shenzhen, one of the pioneering experiments of the reform era.

ch03.anchor: the former head of the Central Communications Bureau, Wu Defeng
ch03.note: Wu Defeng (1896–1976), a founder of the Party’s courier and intelligence systems who ran the hidden Xi’an intelligence station under a family cover; once police chief of Wuhan in the 1926–27 alliance, he later held senior legal posts.

ch03.anchor: Dong Biwu and Chen Tanqiu
ch03.note: Chen Tanqiu (1896–1943), one of the delegates to the CCP’s founding congress of 1921; like Mao Zemin, he was executed in Xinjiang in 1943.

ch03.anchor: the Red Army veteran Luo Qingchang
ch03.note: Luo Qingchang (1918–2014), a young Yan’an-trained intelligence officer and close aide to Zhou Enlai; later minister of the Central Investigation Department, and one of the author’s principal interviewees for this book.

ch03.anchor: to the governor Jiang Dingwen
ch03.note: Jiang Dingwen (1895–1974), a senior general of Chiang’s Whampoa clique and head of the Xi’an field headquarters; it was he who carried out Chiang Kai-shek’s secret order to kill Xuan Xiafu, the subject of this section.

ch03.anchor: a "Red Gang lodge master"
ch03.note: The Red Gang (红帮, Hong Bang) was a widespread sworn-brotherhood secret society; a “lodge master” was a senior, respected initiate, a useful cover identity for an agent.

ch03.anchor: Sun Weiru, Zhao Shoushan
ch03.note: Zhao Shoushan (1894–1965), commander of the Northwestern Army’s 38th Army and secretly guided by the Communists (see the fuller account in section 7); he defected to them and later governed Qinghai and then Shaanxi.

ch03.anchor: When Ye Ting was appointed commander of the New Fourth Army
ch03.note: Ye Ting (1896–1946), a famed general who commanded the New Fourth Army; captured in the 1941 Incident, he was freed in 1946 and died soon after in the same air crash that killed Wang Ruofei and Bogu.

ch03.anchor: Yang Gongsu had once been a Communist agent
ch03.note: Yang Gongsu, later a diplomat of the People’s Republic long involved in Tibetan affairs and an ambassador; the author draws on his unusually candid memoir, cited in the Principal Sources.

ch03.anchor: deputy commander-in-chief Peng Dehuai
ch03.note: Peng Dehuai (1898–1974), one of the Communists’ foremost field commanders and later a marshal and defense minister of the People’s Republic; purged in 1959 for criticizing the Great Leap Forward, he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

ch03.anchor: The senior advisers of the 129th Division
ch03.note: The Eighth Route Army was organized into three divisions—the 115th, 120th, and 129th. The 129th, in the Taihang mountains, was led by Liu Bocheng and Deng Xiaoping.

ch03.anchor: the Fourth Front Army's E-Yu-Wan base area
ch03.note: The E-Yu-Wan base area, a major early Communist base on the borders of Hubei, Henan, and Anhui—the characters E (鄂), Yu (豫), and Wan (皖) being the classical abbreviations of those three provinces.

ch03.anchor: Deng Baoshan to the north at Yulin
ch03.note: Deng Baoshan (1894–1968), the Nationalist general holding Yulin, north of the Border Region; friendly with the Communists from his time in Yan’an, he later helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Beiping.

ch03.anchor: joined the Revolutionary Alliance in his youth
ch03.note: The Revolutionary Alliance (同盟会, Tongmenghui), Sun Yat-sen’s revolutionary organization founded in 1905, whose members carried out the 1911 Revolution; membership marked a man as a founding revolutionary of the Republic.

ch03.anchor: got from the resistance university
ch03.note: The “resistance university” was Kangda (抗大), the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University at Yan’an, founded in 1936—the Communists’ principal school for training officers and cadres.

ch03.anchor: Deng Yingchao embraced her happily
ch03.note: Deng Yingchao (1904–1992), a pioneering woman revolutionary and Zhou Enlai’s wife, prominent in the Party’s women’s and united-front work; here handling the deep-cover agent Shen Anna.

ch04.anchor: threw up a strange thing: a "dual regime."
ch04.note: The shuangchong zhengquan or “dual regime” was a peculiarity of the wartime united front. Because the Nationalist central government held de jure sovereignty, it insisted on appointing the magistrates and prefectural commissioners of the twenty-three counties it recognized as the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region, while the Communists, who held the ground in fact, appointed their own; many counties thus had two rival administrations at once, each claiming legitimacy. Pulling out these Nationalist “nails,” as the chapter title has it, is the story of the Communists dismantling that rival apparatus between 1939 and 1941. (Printed p. 135.)

ch04.anchor: resolved to "restrict the activities of alien parties,"
ch04.note: The Fifth Plenum of the Nationalist Party’s Fifth Central Executive Committee (Chongqing, January 1939) adopted the policy of “restricting the activities of alien parties” (xianzhi yidang huodong) and a companion program of dissolving the Communists by political means, marking Chiang Kai-shek’s turn from the 1937 alliance back toward containment of the CCP. The shift is a fixed marker in histories of the united front; corroborated. (Printed p. 139.)

ch04.anchor: "Friction," a term from physics
ch04.note: “Friction” (moca) became the accepted term, on both sides, for the running armed clashes between Nationalist and Communist forces from 1939 to 1943, and “the struggle against friction” (fan moca) for the Communist response. The author’s conceit that Mao coined the political use of the word is his own flourish; by 1940 the usage was in any case common Party vocabulary. (Printed p. 139.)

ch04.anchor: Xi Zhongxun, secretary of the Guanzhong sub-committee
ch04.note: Xi Zhongxun (1913–2002), here the young secretary of the Guanzhong sub-committee, later became a vice-premier of the People’s Republic; he was purged for sixteen years from 1962 over the novel Liu Zhidan, and after 1978 governed Guangdong, where he championed the first Special Economic Zones. He is the father of Xi Jinping. The particulars the author gives—Youth League at thirteen, the Liangdang mutiny (a 1932 revolt he helped lead among Nationalist-controlled troops) at eighteen, chairman of the Shaan-Gan Border Soviet at twenty-one—are corroborated in the standard biographies. (Printed pp. 139–140.)

ch04.anchor: Du Bincheng, the secretary-general of the Shaanxi provincial government
ch04.note: Du Bincheng (1888–1947), a noted Shaanxi educator and a founding leader of the China Democratic League, served as secretary-general of the provincial government after the Xi’an Incident. In March 1947 Hu Zongnan had him arrested on fabricated charges; he was shot at Xi’an’s Yuxiang Gate that October, and Mao Zedong wrote his memorial inscription. Corroborated. (Printed p. 138.)

ch04.anchor: setting up baojia units in secret
ch04.note: The baojia was an old system of mutual-surveillance household registration, grouping families into units collectively answerable for one another’s conduct; the Nationalist government revived it in the 1930s as an instrument of local control and counter-insurgency. (Printed p. 137.)

ch04.anchor: "Memorial Meeting for the Martyrs of the Pingjiang Massacre."
ch04.note: On June 12, 1939, troops of Yang Sen’s Nationalist 27th Group Army surrounded the New Fourth Army’s rear liaison office at Pingjiang in Hunan and killed six Communist personnel, among them Tu Zhengkun and Luo Ziming. The killings, and the Yan’an memorial of August 1, became a rallying point of the anti-friction campaign. Corroborated. (Printed p. 139.)

ch04.anchor: this Magistrate Ma Yuzhang, appointed by the Nationalists
ch04.note: Ma Yuzhang, of the great landlord Ma clan of Yangjiagou in Mizhi, held the Nationalists’ Fushi county magistracy while secretly a Communist, and when the Nationalist county government was expelled he stayed on to become deputy mayor and then mayor of Yan’an. By the author’s interviews his cover was so tightly held that even Luo Qingchang, the later intelligence minister, learned of it only decades afterward; during the Cultural Revolution his descendants were persecuted as landlord kin. The account rests on the family and Party-history testimony the author gathered and is otherwise thinly documented. (Printed pp. 138, 147.)

ch04.anchor: specially appointed He Shaonan "administrative inspection commissioner."
ch04.note: He Shaonan, the Nationalists’ “administrative inspection commissioner” for Suide, built a rival security force and a campaign of harassment that the Border Region nicknamed “Commissioner Friction.” His public undoing on corruption charges, driven by Wang Zhen’s 359th Brigade over the winter of 1939–40, is a set piece of Party history; that he embezzled relief funds is the Communist account of it. Corroborated in outline. (Printed p. 143.)

ch04.anchor: Wang Zhen, commander of the 359th Brigade
ch04.note: Wang Zhen (1908–1993) commanded the 359th Brigade, celebrated for reclaiming the Nanniwan wastes during the wartime blockade; he later led armies into Xinjiang and from 1988 served as vice-president of the People’s Republic. Corroborated. (Printed p. 144.)

ch04.anchor: whom he sent off to Ma Hongkui.
ch04.note: Ma Hongkui (1892–1970) ruled Ningxia as a family fief, one of the Muslim “Ma clique” warlords of the northwest and a standing enemy of the Communists on the Border Region’s western flank. (Printed p. 142.)

ch04.anchor: earned himself the nickname "Red Sherlock Holmes."
ch04.note: Bu Lu’s real name was Chen Bo (1909–1972). After 1949 he became the founding head of public security in Guangzhou, but in 1951 he and Chen Kun were arrested in what became known as the “two Chens case,” accused by Public Security Minister Luo Ruiqing of being enemy agents—the first great frame-up of the new state’s own security apparatus. Sentenced to ten years and then held under labor reform, Chen Bo died in 1972 and was posthumously cleared in 1980. The “Red Sherlock Holmes” celebrated here was thus consumed by the very machinery he had helped to build. Corroborated. (Printed p. 143.)

ch04.anchor: This too would be the height of benevolence and the fullness of righteousness.
ch04.note: The closing flourish—gai yi ren zhi zhi, yi zhi jin ye—dresses a blunt ultimatum in the courtly idiom of the Confucian classics; “ren zhi yi jin,” benevolence and righteousness carried to their limit, is proverbial. Sent over Xiao Jinguang’s name, the telegram was, the author says, drafted by Mao Zedong himself. (Printed p. 145.)

ch04.anchor: the "Anti-Traitor Committee,"
ch04.note: Chujian, literally “rooting out traitors,” was the Communist term for counter-espionage and the hunt for collaborators and enemy agents; the mass “Anti-Traitor Committees” extended it into a village-level surveillance network. The word and its apparatus give Chapter 7 its title. (Printed p. 146.)

ch04.anchor: developing the great rear
ch04.note: The “great rear” (大后方, da houfang): the vast unoccupied interior of southwestern and northwestern China—Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou, Gansu, and beyond—that became the Nationalist government’s base once the coast and the eastern cities fell to Japan. Marching his central armies into it let Chiang Kai-shek extend his authority over regions that warlords had long held on their own account.

ch04.anchor: a local earth-god shrine
ch04.note: The earth god (土地, Tudi) is the local tutelary deity of Chinese folk religion, the lowest rank of the celestial bureaucracy, charged with a single village or plot of ground. Small earth-god shrines stood in nearly every settlement, which is what made one an unremarkable place to leave a signal.

ch04.anchor: Phoenix Hill, where Mao lived
ch04.note: Phoenix Hill (凤凰山), in the town of Yan’an, was the first seat of the CCP Central Committee after it reached the city in January 1937. Mao Zedong lived there, in cave dwellings dug into the slope, from early 1937 until November 1938, when Japanese bombing drove the leadership out to Yangjialing on the city’s edge.

ch04.anchor: the Central Auditorium at Yangjialing
ch04.note: Yangjialing (杨家岭), a village on the northwestern edge of Yan’an, was the seat of the CCP Central Committee from late 1938. Its Central Auditorium (中央大礼堂), completed in 1942, was the largest hall in the base area and the site of the Party’s Seventh Congress in 1945.

ch04.anchor: Kuang Yumin's cave dwelling
ch04.note: A cave dwelling (窑洞, yaodong) is the characteristic home of the Loess Plateau of northern Shaanxi: a vaulted room dug straight into a hillside of firm, dry loess, or built up in masonry to the same arched shape. Warm in winter and cool in summer, yaodong housed nearly everyone in the Yan’an region, Mao Zedong and the Party leadership included.

ch04.anchor: Zhang Yinwu, commander-in-chief of the Hebei People's Militia
ch04.note: Zhang Yinwu (1891–1949), a Hebei-born Nationalist general, commanded the province’s “People’s Militia” and was among the most aggressive of the anti-Communist “friction” commanders. The attack at Shen County described here, in June 1939, killed several hundred Eighth Route Army personnel. He refused to give up his arms when the Communists took Beiping and was arrested early in 1949, dying in custody that year. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: Mao Zedong put it this way
ch04.note: The dictum, 人不犯我，我不犯人；人若犯我，我必犯人 — “If no one attacks me, I attack no one; if someone attacks me, I will certainly attack back” — is one of Mao Zedong’s most quoted formulas, framing every Communist blow as retaliation. It recurs, word for word, near the end of the chapter.

ch04.anchor: The ever pro-German Chiang Kai-shek
ch04.note: From the late 1920s until 1938 Chiang Kai-shek leaned on a mission of German military advisers—Max Bauer, Hans von Seeckt, and Alexander von Falkenhausen among them—who reorganized his best divisions and helped design the “encirclement” campaigns against the Red Army. That tie, and his admiration for German methods, is what the author means by “ever pro-German”; it lapsed only as Berlin drew closer to Tokyo. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: the diehards' slaughter of the war-disabled
ch04.note: “Diehards” (顽固派, wangupai) was the Communists’ standard name, during the united front, for the anti-Communist hardliners in the Nationalist camp—those bent on suppressing the CCP even at the cost of the common resistance. Mao distinguished them from the “middle” and “progressive” Nationalist forces the Party hoped to win or hold.

ch04.anchor: the Eighth Route Army's rear garrison corps
ch04.note: Xiao Jinguang (1903–1989) was posted to Yan’an in 1937 and commanded the Eighth Route Army’s rear garrison, the force charged with defending the Border Region and the Party Center; much of Yan’an’s open correspondence with the Nationalists went out over his name. He later became the founding commander of the People’s Liberation Army Navy (1950–1980) and the only officer ever to hold its highest rank.

ch04.anchor: a hundred-odd li from Yan'an
ch04.note: A li (里) is the traditional Chinese unit of distance, fixed in the twentieth century at half a kilometer (about a third of a mile); “a hundred-odd li” is therefore some fifty-odd kilometers.

ch04.anchor: a reporter for the
ch04.note: The Central Daily News (中央日报, Zhongyang Ribao) was the official newspaper of the Nationalist Party; a correspondent’s credentials made a convenient cover for a Zhongtong agent moving from county to county.

ch04.anchor: the Second War Zone command
ch04.note: A “war zone” (战区, zhanqu) was one of the large regional commands into which the Nationalist government divided the front against Japan, each under a commander-in-chief responsible for every force within it. The Second War Zone, covering Shanxi, was Yan Xishan’s domain, and the Eighth Route Army was nominally subordinate to it; the First War Zone (below), on the Yellow River line, was Cheng Qian’s.

ch04.anchor: Cheng Qian, commander of the Nationalists' First War Zone
ch04.note: Cheng Qian (1882–1968), a senior Nationalist general and a Hunan native, commanded the First War Zone. In August 1949 he led the peaceful handover of Changsha to the Communists, and went on to hold high office in the People’s Republic, including the governorship of his home province. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: uniting democratic personages
ch04.note: “Democratic personages” (民主人士) was the Communists’ term for prominent non-Communists—independent intellectuals, professionals, and public men—whom the Party drew to its side through “united front” work. Winning and keeping such figures was treated as a distinct branch of Party labor, separate from work among its own members and the masses.

ch04.anchor: a vice-chairman of the national CPPCC
ch04.note: The CPPCC, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, is the united-front advisory body that gathers the CCP together with the minor “democratic parties” and non-Party notables. Founded in 1949, it holds no legislative power but confers standing, and a vice-chairmanship of its national committee is a senior honorary post. The mention leaps ahead to Wang Feng’s later career.

ch04.anchor: a war of public opinion and a war of law
ch04.note: An anachronism the author flags himself (“in a modern coloring”): “public-opinion warfare” (舆论战) and “legal warfare” (法律战, lawfare) are two of the “Three Warfares,” a doctrine the People’s Liberation Army formally adopted only in 2003. He reads the wartime tactic—win the propaganda battle and the legal argument, then strike—as an early instance of it. Interested witness.

ch05.anchor: the anniversary of the Mukden Incident in 1940
ch05.note: The Mukden (or September 18) Incident of 1931, when the Japanese Kwantung Army staged a pretext to seize Manchuria; its anniversary, jiu-yi-ba (“nine-one-eight”), became a fixed date of national mourning and defiance, which is why the author reckons the Party’s decisions by it.

ch05.anchor: a "Draft Understanding" with the American secretary of state, Hull
ch05.note: The Hull–Nomura talks of 1941, in which a privately drafted “Draft Understanding” briefly raised hopes of a Japanese-American settlement; the negotiations broke down that autumn, months before Pearl Harbor. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: the German friend Anna Wang
ch05.note: Anna Wang (Anneliese Martens, 1907–1990), the German wife of the Communist Wang Bingnan; a journalist and translator active in China’s wartime foreign-friends circles.

ch05.anchor: the battle of Nomonhan in 1937
ch05.note: The Nomonhan Incident—the undeclared border war between Japan and the Soviet Union at Khalkhin Gol—was fought in 1939, not 1937; the source’s date is an error, rendered here as printed. The Soviet victory there is often credited with turning Japan’s expansion south rather than north. CONTRADICTED.

ch05.anchor: the strategic agent Sorge to Shanghai
ch05.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the Soviet military-intelligence officer who ran a ring first in Shanghai and then in Tokyo, and whose warnings of the German attack Stalin also discounted; arrested by the Japanese in 1941 and hanged in 1944. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: the Tokkō, the Special Higher Police
ch05.note: The Tokkō, Japan’s political and “thought” police, charged with surveillance and suppression of suspected subversives; a foreign agent with European features was an obvious target for it.

ch05.anchor: the remnant of the Western Route Army that had reached Xinjiang
ch05.note: The Western Route Army—more than twenty thousand Red Army troops—was destroyed by Muslim cavalry in the Hexi Corridor in the winter of 1936–37; the scattered survivors who reached Xinjiang were the pool from which these Soviet-trained agents were drawn.

ch05.anchor: Vladimirov (Sun Ping), was a Soviet intelligence officer
ch05.note: Pyotr Vladimirov (1905–1953), a Soviet military-intelligence officer and TASS correspondent who used the Chinese name Sun Ping and later served as the Comintern liaison at Yan’an, where he kept a well-known (and much-disputed) diary.

ch05.anchor: the "New Life Movement," Yan was its executive director
ch05.note: The New Life Movement, launched by Chiang Kai-shek and Soong May-ling in 1934, was a state campaign of Confucian-tinged moral and hygienic reform; its prominence gave a well-placed insider like Yan Baohang wide access to the Nationalist elite.

ch05.anchor: Yan Baohang was a Northeasterner from Haicheng
ch05.note: Yan Baohang (1895–1968), a Christian educator and aide to Zhang Xueliang who became a secret Communist inside the Nationalist inner circle. He died in prison in the Cultural Revolution; in 1995 Russia posthumously decorated him for the Barbarossa intelligence. CORROBORATED as to his role and the decoration.

ch05.anchor: Stalin sent the Communists a telegram of thanks
ch05.note: That Yan Baohang obtained the June 22 date and that it was relayed to Moscow is well attested in Chinese sources, and Russia’s 1995 decoration of him is real. But Stalin received many such warnings—from Sorge, from British intercepts, from his own agents—and discounted them all; the Soviet Union was caught grievously unprepared. The claim that this particular warning was believed and acted upon, and the thank-you telegram itself, rest on Chinese accounts and are not corroborated in the Soviet record. The author himself concedes the day’s notice changed little. UNCORROBORATED / CONTESTED.

ch05.anchor: the Japanese Communist leader Okano Susumu
ch05.note: “Okano Susumu” was the wartime alias of Nosaka Sanzō (1892–1993), the Japanese Communist leader who spent the war years at Yan’an running anti-war work among Japanese prisoners.

ch05.anchor: the reference materials on the Japanese prime minister Miki
ch05.note: Miki Takeo was Japanese prime minister in 1974–76; the deathbed anecdote leaps forward to Mao’s final years, decades past the 1940s of the surrounding narrative, to illustrate how deep the habit of “investigation and study” had run.

ch05.anchor: He played the Empty City Stratagem for all it was worth
ch05.note: The Empty City Stratagem is the famous ruse of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which Zhuge Liang, having no troops, throws open the city gates and sits calmly playing the zither, so unnerving the enemy general that he withdraws—bluffing strength from weakness.

ch05.anchor: Wang Jinshan directed the Hanlüe Village ambush
ch05.note: The Hanlüe Village ambush of October 1943, in which Wang Jinshan’s regiment wiped out a touring Japanese officers’ observation party in a single engagement; celebrated as a model ambush of the war behind the lines. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: the Japanese "flower of famous generals," Lieutenant-General Abe Norihide
ch05.note: Abe Norihide, killed at Huangtuling in Laiyuan county in November 1939, was the first and highest-ranking Japanese general slain by the Eighth Route Army; Japanese propaganda had dubbed him “the flower of famous generals.” The engagement was a Jin-Cha-Ji operation; the source credits the local intelligence station with a share of it. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: Kawashima Yoshiko's younger brother Xiandong
ch05.note: Kawashima Yoshiko (1907–1948), born Aisin Gioro Xianyu, was a Qing princess raised in Japan who became a Japanese agent in Manchuria; she was executed by the Nationalists as a collaborator in 1948. Her brother Xiandong worked, instead, for the Communist intelligence group. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: a secret-service organ governing the whole of Central China, the "Ume Kikan."
ch05.note: The “Plum Agency” (Ume Kikan), named for its founder Kagesa’s cover, was the Japanese army organ that arranged Wang Jingwei’s defection and oversaw his regime’s security. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: at No. 76 Jessfield Road
ch05.note: No. 76 Jessfield Road became a byword of terror in occupied Shanghai—the torture-house headquarters of the Wang Jingwei secret service under Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: East Asia Common Culture Academy
ch05.note: The Tōa Dōbun Shoin, a Japanese academy in Shanghai that trained Japanese “China hands” and doubled as a nursery of intelligence officers. It was in fact founded around 1900–1901, not 1905 as the source has it. CONTRADICTED as to the date.

ch05.anchor: his comrade Sun Fengming had braved death to wound Wang Jingwei
ch05.note: At the Nationalists’ Fourth Congress in Nanjing in November 1935, the assassin Sun Fengming—posing as a press photographer—shot and wounded Wang Jingwei; the intended target had been Chiang Kai-shek, who was not on the dais. Hua Kezhi had organized the plot. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: none should be treated with closer intimacy than the spy
ch05.note: From the last chapter of Sun Tzu’s Art of War, “The Use of Spies” (yong jian), on the primacy of trust, reward, and secrecy in running agents.

ch05.anchor: The Duke of Zhou spat out his food
ch05.note: From Cao Cao’s poem “Short Song” (Duan ge xing): the Duke of Zhou is said to have spat out his food to hurry out and receive a worthy caller, so eager was he for talent—the emblem of a leader who wins men’s hearts. Here it stands for the personal loyalty a Communist controller could command.

ch05.anchor: And Guan Lu was given the secret task of turning Li Shiqun
ch05.note: Guan Lu (1907–1982), one of the most admired women poets of the day, paid for this assignment with her name: branded a “collaborator” for her wartime cover, she was later imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case and took her own life soon after her rehabilitation. Her fate became a byword for the private cost of clandestine work.

ch05.anchor: the British foreign secretary Eden
ch05.note: Anthony Eden (1897–1977), Britain's foreign secretary through much of the Second World War and later prime minister (1955–57); here one party to the abortive Anglo-Chinese-Japanese soundings of May 1941.

ch05.anchor: the Chinese ambassador to Britain Guo Taiqi
ch05.note: Guo Taiqi (Quo Tai-chi, 1888–1952), China's ambassador to Britain through the 1930s and, from April 1941, the Nationalist government's foreign minister; he later presided over the first session of the U.N. Security Council in 1946.

ch05.anchor: the Japanese ambassador to Britain Shigemitsu
ch05.note: Shigemitsu Mamoru (1887–1957), Japan's ambassador to Britain until his recall in June 1941; later foreign minister, he signed Japan's surrender aboard the USS Missouri in 1945.

ch05.anchor: the battle of Port Arthur in 1905
ch05.note: The Russo-Japanese War siege of Port Arthur (Lüshun), the Russian naval base at the tip of the Liaodong peninsula in the Northeast; its fall in January 1905 was a decisive Japanese victory. The author's point is that Russia and Japan had contested China's Northeast since the century's start.

ch05.anchor: the Chinese Eastern Railway there
ch05.note: The Chinese Eastern Railway, built by Russia across Manchuria at the turn of the century to shorten its line to Vladivostok; the rights of way and their large Russian-employed workforce gave first tsarist and then Soviet Russia a durable foothold—and an intelligence base—in the Northeast.

ch05.anchor: The Soviet ambassador in Chongqing, Panyushin
ch05.note: Aleksandr Panyushkin (1905–1974), Soviet ambassador to China from 1939 to 1945 and a career intelligence officer; he later headed the foreign-intelligence directorate of the KGB. The book renders his name Panyushin.

ch05.anchor: the military attaché Roshchin
ch05.note: Nikolai Roshchin, a Soviet military officer who served as attaché in wartime China and became, in 1949, the Soviet Union's first ambassador to the newly founded People's Republic.

ch05.anchor: a British Butterfield
ch05.note: Butterfield & Swire (known in Chinese as Taigu), a major British trading and shipping house whose China Navigation Company steamers plied the coast and the Yangtze; an ordinary passage on one drew no attention.

ch05.anchor: at the Paris Cinema on Avenue Joffre
ch05.note: Avenue Joffre (now Huaihai Middle Road), the fashionable main artery of Shanghai's French Concession, lined with shops, cafes, and cinemas and long a center of the city's White Russian émigré community.

ch05.anchor: The Nationalists' four great families
ch05.note: The “four big families” (四大家族)—those of Chiang Kai-shek, T.V. Soong, H.H. Kung, and the Chen brothers (Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu)—were held, in Communist and much popular parlance, to have monopolized the wealth and power of Nationalist China. The label is partly polemical but names the real inner circle of the regime.

ch05.anchor: whose elder brother Sha Menghai
ch05.note: Sha Menghai (1900–1992), of Yinxian in Zhejiang, one of the most celebrated Chinese calligraphers and seal-carvers of the twentieth century; his younger brother, the secret Communist Sha Wenwei (Shi Yong), was placed through his connections on the Nationalist Military Commission's advisory staff.

ch05.anchor: Chen Cheng's aide-de-camp Deng Dazhang
ch05.note: Chen Cheng (1898–1965), one of Chiang Kai-shek's most trusted generals and head of a powerful faction within his army; he later served as premier and vice-president of the Republic of China on Taiwan.

ch05.anchor: Bai Chongxi's secretary Xie Hegeng
ch05.note: Xie Hegeng (1908–1988), a secret Communist who penetrated the Guangxi clique and from 1937 served as Bai Chongxi's personal secretary, carrying a pass that gave him the run of the homes of Bai and Li Zongren; one of the Party's best-known deep-cover agents, and also a poet and writer.

ch05.anchor: at H.H. Kung's, Ji Chaoding
ch05.note: Ji Chaoding (1903–1963), a Columbia-trained economist and secret Communist who worked inside the Nationalist finance ministry as a close aide to its minister, H.H. Kung; author of the influential study Key Economic Areas in Chinese History.

ch05.anchor: the president of the Control Yuan
ch05.note: The Control Yuan, one of the five branches (yuan) of the Nationalist government, charged with censorial oversight—auditing officials and hearing impeachments—in the tradition of the old imperial censorate.

ch05.anchor: the president of the Executive Yuan, Sun Ke
ch05.note: Sun Ke (Sun Fo, 1891–1973), the only son of Sun Yat-sen; he held high Nationalist offices including the presidency of the Executive Yuan (the cabinet) and, later, of the Legislative Yuan.

ch05.anchor: Gui Yongqing said Germany was going to attack
ch05.note: Gui Yongqing (Kuei Yung-ching), a Nationalist general serving as China's military attaché in Germany; it was through his conversation with a German officer in Berlin, the book says, that word of the coming attack on the Soviet Union reached Chongqing.

ch05.anchor: the crown prince, Chiang Ching-kuo
ch05.note: Chiang Ching-kuo (1910–1988), Chiang Kai-shek's eldest son, who had spent twelve years in the Soviet Union; he later succeeded his father as ruler of the Republic of China on Taiwan and served as its president from 1978.

ch05.anchor: secretary of the Xijing city sub-branch
ch05.note: “Xijing,” the Western Capital, was a name for Xi'an, the ancient imperial capital in Shaanxi; it is used here in the title of the Nationalist youth-league branch in the city.

ch05.anchor: the Nationalist secretary-general Chen Bulei
ch05.note: Chen Bulei (1890–1948), a journalist who became Chiang Kai-shek's confidential secretary and chief speechwriter, drafting most of his important proclamations; despairing of the Nationalist cause, he took his own life in November 1948.

ch05.anchor: the intelligence-section chief Zou Dapeng
ch05.note: Zou Dapeng, a Communist intelligence officer of Northeastern background—the text notes he had been secretary of the Party's Manchuria Youth League—who ran intelligence for the 120th Division and later headed the Jiaodong Liaison Department reaching toward the occupied Northeast.

ch05.anchor: Okamura Yasuji's iron-roller mopping-up
ch05.note: Okamura Yasuji (1884–1966), the Japanese general who directed the ferocious “mopping-up” campaigns against the North China bases—associated with the scorched-earth “Three Alls” policy (kill all, burn all, loot all)—and from 1944 commanded all Japanese forces in China.

ch05.anchor: at the decisive battle of Huangqiao
ch05.note: The battle of Huangqiao (“Yellow Bridge”), October 1940 in central Jiangsu, in which the New Fourth Army routed a much larger Nationalist force under the provincial war-zone commander Han Deqin—a clash that helped bring on the New Fourth Army Incident three months later.

ch05.anchor: at the foot of Wutai Mountain
ch05.note: Wutai Mountain (Wutaishan) in northeastern Shanxi, one of the four sacred Buddhist mountains of China; the Communists' Jin-Cha-Ji base grew up in its highland country behind the Japanese lines.

ch05.anchor: relatives of a Tongrentang branch
ch05.note: Tongrentang (同仁堂), the famous Beijing house of traditional Chinese medicine, founded in the seventeenth century and once purveyor to the Qing court; a connection to it made respectable cover for an agent's family.

ch05.anchor: the Yenching University professor Zhang Dongsun
ch05.note: Zhang Dongsun (1886–1973), a leading philosopher and head of the philosophy department at Yenching University—the American missionary university in Beiping—and a prominent figure of the Democratic League; he helped mediate the peaceful Communist takeover of Beiping in 1949.

ch05.anchor: and Michael Lindsay
ch05.note: Michael Lindsay (1909–1994), a British academic teaching at Yenching University who used his foreign status to smuggle radio parts and medicine to the Communists and later served the Eighth Route Army as a radio engineer; he afterward succeeded to a British peerage.

ch05.anchor: the premier, Zheng Xiaoxu
ch05.note: Zheng Xiaoxu (1860–1938), a distinguished late-Qing statesman, poet, and calligrapher who stayed loyal to the deposed dynasty and became “Manchukuo's” first premier; at odds with his Japanese overseers, he was forced out in 1935.

ch05.anchor: changed the premier for Zhang Jinghui
ch05.note: Zhang Jinghui (1871–1959), an old cavalry officer of Zhang Zuolin's who served as premier of “Manchukuo” from 1935 until its collapse in 1945; his son Zhang Mengshi, mentioned later in the chapter, secretly worked for the Communists.

ch05.anchor: Zhang Zuolin, Zhang Zuoxiang
ch05.note: Zhang Zuolin (1875–1928), the “Old Marshal,” the bandit-turned-warlord who ruled Manchuria and for a time the Beijing government; the Japanese Kwantung Army, finding him too independent, blew up his train and killed him in 1928. His son was Zhang Xueliang; with his old lieutenants Zhang Zuoxiang and Zhang Jinghui he made up the “Three Zhangs.”

ch05.anchor: the Manchuria Provincial Committee
ch05.note: The Manchuria Provincial Committee, the Chinese Communist Party's underground regional organization for the Northeast in the late 1920s and 1930s; it built the anti-Japanese guerrilla forces there before Japanese repression, and the severing of its ties to the Party Center, broke it up.

ch05.anchor: launched the Liaoshen Campaign
ch05.note: The Liaoshen Campaign of autumn 1948, the great Communist offensive that destroyed the Nationalist armies in the Northeast and won all of Manchuria—the first of the three decisive campaigns of the civil war.

ch05.anchor: He Yingqin and Yan Xishan
ch05.note: He Yingqin (1890–1987), a Japan-trained senior general, long Chiang Kai-shek's war minister and army chief of staff; in 1945 he formally received the Japanese surrender on China's behalf.

ch05.anchor: Okamura Yasuji and Itagaki Seishirō
ch05.note: Itagaki Seishirō (1885–1948), a Japanese general and a chief planner of the 1931 seizure of Manchuria; later war minister, he was hanged as a war criminal in 1948.

ch05.anchor: the January 28 Incident of 1932
ch05.note: The January 28 Incident of 1932, a fierce but short Japanese assault on the Chinese-held districts of Shanghai, resisted by the Nationalist 19th Route Army; it ended in a truce that demilitarized part of the city.

ch05.anchor: the South Manchuria Railway Company each built
ch05.note: The South Manchuria Railway Company (Mantetsu), the giant Japanese state-backed conglomerate that ran the railways and much of the industry of the Northeast; its research bureau was also a major arm of Japanese intelligence.

ch05.anchor: the Japanese deputy consul-general in Shanghai, Iwai Eiichi
ch05.note: Iwai Eiichi, the Japanese deputy consul-general in Shanghai who ran a foreign-ministry intelligence operation (the “Iwai Agency”) devoted to gathering China's political intelligence; the book recounts how Pan Hannian, through the double agent Yuan Shu, fed it false reports in exchange for its funds.

ch05.anchor: Chen Gongshu tried to kill Li Shiqun
ch05.note: Chen Gongshu, a founding member of Juntong and its most feared assassin, who as head of its Shanghai district waged the running murder-war against the puppet secret service of No. 76; captured in 1941, he went over to the Wang Jingwei side, returned to Juntong after the war, and wrote his memoirs in Taiwan.

ch05.anchor: the Loyal and Righteous National Salvation Army
ch05.note: The Loyal and Righteous National Salvation Army (忠义救国军), a guerrilla and undercover force in the lower Yangtze region run by Dai Li's Juntong; the commission Yuan Shu held in it was one more of his tangle of cover identities.

ch05.anchor: the film director Cai Chusheng
ch05.note: Cai Chusheng (1906–1968), a leading director of Shanghai's leftist cinema and the first Chinese filmmaker to win an international prize, for Song of the Fishermen (1934).

ch05.anchor: Guan Lu, and Eileen Chang
ch05.note: Eileen Chang (Zhang Ailing, 1920–1995), among the most admired of modern Chinese writers, who made her name with stories of love and family set in occupied Shanghai; she later emigrated and died in the United States.

ch05.anchor: for the film Crossroads
ch05.note: Crossroads (Shizi jietou, 1937), a celebrated film of Shanghai's leftist cinema about the struggles of young people in the city; Guan Lu's lyric for its theme song became a nationwide hit.

ch05.anchor: the Communist contacts Xia Yan and Wang Ying
ch05.note: Xia Yan (1900–1995), a prominent leftist playwright and screenwriter of the 1930s Shanghai stage and cinema; after 1949 he became a vice-minister of culture of the People's Republic.

ch05.anchor: and of Doihara's
ch05.note: Doihara Kenji (1883–1948), the Japanese army's most notorious intelligence officer—dubbed the “Lawrence of Manchuria” for his part in seizing the Northeast and installing Puyi—later hanged as a war criminal. The Kōa-in, or East Asia Development Board, was Japan's cabinet agency for the affairs of occupied China.

ch06.anchor: opened in Yan'an a Japanese Workers' and Peasants' School
ch06.note: A real institution (日本工农学校), opened at Yan’an on 15 May 1941 to re-educate Japanese prisoners of war; it was led by the Japanese Communist leader Nosaka Sanzō (who used the alias Okano Susumu, 冯野进). Its graduates carried out antiwar propaganda at the front. CORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: the memorial that the Japanese prime minister Tanaka Giichi had submitted to the Emperor, which said: "To conquer the world, one must first conquer China
ch06.note: The so-called Tanaka Memorial. Its authenticity is rejected by most Japanese and Western historians: no Japanese original has ever surfaced, and it is generally regarded as a fabrication that appeared in China around 1929. Its expansionist program did, however, foreshadow the actual course of Japanese aggression, which is why it was so widely believed. The circulation described here is itself well attested: Yan Baohang obtained a copy and had an English translation distributed to Western delegates at the 1929 IPR conference in Kyoto. CONTRADICTED as a genuine state document; the author reports it, as the Chinese side of the day received it, as authentic.

ch06.anchor: A Survey of China's War-Fighting Strength
ch06.note: The Japanese-language report used the exonym Shina (支那) for China, as in Shina Expeditionary Army and the “China Incident” below; once a neutral term, it had become a slur by this period. It is rendered plainly as “China” throughout.

ch06.anchor: the most highly classified of all the peace operations, "Operation Kiri
ch06.note: Operation Kiri (the Kiri Kōsaku) was a genuine 1940 Japanese channel to Chongqing run by Imai Takeo. The negotiator called “Song Ziliang” used the name of a real Soong brother, but the man at the table was an impostor, an agent of Dai Li’s Juntong; mainstream accounts treat the affair as a Nationalist deception that strung the Japanese along. Pan Hannian did run an intelligence-exchange tie to Iwai Eiichi and did expose the impostor to him. The book’s dramatized version—that Pan cast the man as a Communist plant so the Japanese would fear a Juntong trap—and the credit it gives Pan for collapsing the channel rest on Chinese accounts. PARTLY CORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: Gao Chongwu
ch06.note: So printed in the source. The man is the well-documented Gao Zongwu (高宗武), who with Tao Xisheng defected from the Wang Jingwei camp to Hong Kong and published the draft treaty in January 1940—the “Gao-Tao incident.” The source’s 崩 for 宗 is a misprint.

ch06.anchor: the plan for the "Kwantung Army Special Maneuvers,"
ch06.note: The Kantokuen (関特演) of July 1941 was a real and enormous mobilization—on the order of 700,000 to 800,000 troops—massing the Kwantung Army in the Northeast for a possible strike at the Soviet Union after the German invasion. Japan ultimately shelved it and turned south. CORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: moved the 200,000-strong army defending the eastern front against Japan to the western front, and won at last the defense of Moscow
ch06.note: The Soviet transfer of Far Eastern divisions west in the autumn of 1941 is real and mattered to the defense of Moscow, though modern scholarship qualifies the “Siberian divisions saved Moscow” picture: only some units were genuinely Siberian, and some moves preceded any decisive intelligence. The reporting usually credited for freeing these forces is Sorge’s (and Soviet code-breaking), not Chinese Communist intelligence. The book’s attribution of the decision specifically to the Communists is a Chinese account and is UNCORROBORATED; see the note in Chapter 5 on the Barbarossa warning.

ch06.anchor: On December 7, 1941, Japan will launch surprise attacks at many points across the Pacific
ch06.note: That the Nakanishi–Ozaki network reported Japan would go south, meaning war with the United States and Britain, is well attested; the precise prediction of the Pearl Harbor date recorded here rests on later Chinese accounts (chiefly Nakanishi’s own) and is not independently corroborated. PARTLY CORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: Chi Buzhou broke another special cipher telegram
ch06.note: Chinese accounts credit the Nationalist cryptanalyst Chi Buzhou with reading Japanese diplomatic traffic and forecasting a Sunday attack on Pearl Harbor, a warning said to have been passed to and ignored by the Americans. The story is widely repeated in China but is not corroborated in Western records of the Pearl Harbor intelligence. UNCORROBORATED.

ch06.anchor: so that people call him "the Yue Fei of Japan."
ch06.note: Yue Fei (1103–1142) was a Southern Song general celebrated as the archetype of the loyal soldier who dies for his country; to call the ancestral General Kusunoki Masashige “the Yue Fei of Japan” casts him in the same mold of martyred loyalty.

ch06.anchor: like Zhuge Liang pacifying the Five Routes from the calm of his own home
ch06.note: An allusion to the Romance of the Three Kingdoms: the strategist Zhuge Liang, without stirring from his residence, turns back five invading armies at once by arranging countermeasures in advance—a byword for commanding great events from a quiet center. Zhuge Liang is the same strategist of the Empty City Stratagem (Chapter 5).

ch06.anchor: The greatest sound is silent; the greatest form has no shape.
ch06.note: From Laozi’s Daodejing, chapter 41: the received text reads the greatest sound is faint of voice (大音希声); the source prints 大音无声. The saying is turned here into an emblem of the spy who works unseen and unheard.

ch06.anchor: From the Meiji Restoration onward
ch06.note: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate, restored the emperor as the center of the state, and launched Japan's rapid, state-driven modernization and its emergence as an imperial power — the beginning of the outward expansion the author traces here.

ch06.anchor: Arao Sei, slipped into China
ch06.note: Arao Sei (1859–1896), an army officer regarded as a pioneer of Japanese intelligence work in China; his Hankou branch of the Rakuzendō (楽善堂) pharmacy, a real Japanese firm, served as commercial cover for gathering information.

ch06.anchor: an army captain, Nezu Hajime
ch06.note: Nezu Hajime (1860–1927), army officer and educator who became the guiding director of the East Asia Common Culture Academy in Shanghai, the school that trained Japanese “China hands.”

ch06.anchor: the incorporated East Asia Common Culture Society
ch06.note: The Tōa Dōbunkai, a semi-official Japanese Pan-Asianist body formed in 1898 (from the merger of two earlier societies) whose members ran through Japan's military, political, and academic worlds and helped shape its China policy — the “state-policy society” the author describes, and the parent of the Shanghai academy (glossed in Chapter 5).

ch06.anchor: Inukai Tsuyoshi, later became prime minister
ch06.note: Inukai Tsuyoshi (1855–1932), veteran party politician and a founder of the Pan-Asianist societies; he became prime minister in 1931 and was assassinated by young naval officers in the May 15 Incident of 1932, an event that helped end party government in prewar Japan.

ch06.anchor: Prince Konoe Atsumaro
ch06.note: Prince Konoe Atsumaro (1863–1904), a leading Meiji-era nobleman who founded the East Asia Common Culture Society in 1898; father of the future prime minister Konoe Fumimaro.

ch06.anchor: son Konoe Fumimaro also later became prime minister
ch06.note: Konoe Fumimaro (1891–1945), prime minister three times between 1937 and 1941; on his watch the full war with China began and the alliance with Germany and Italy was formed. He resigned in October 1941, just before Pearl Harbor, and took his own life in 1945 rather than face trial as a war criminal. He figures again below as Ozaki Hotsumi's patron.

ch06.anchor: the state enterprise the South Manchuria Railway
ch06.note: The South Manchuria Railway Company (SMR, 溜铁 Mantetsu), a giant Japanese “state-policy company” founded in 1906 that ran the railways and much of the economy of the Northeast and doubled as an enormous intelligence organ; it is anatomized at length in section 2.

ch06.anchor: Wu Kaixian, chief of Shanghai's Bureau of Social Affairs
ch06.note: Wu Kaixian (1899–1990), a Nationalist politician associated with the CC Clique and long active in Shanghai party and labor affairs; the municipal Bureau of Social Affairs oversaw labor and welfare. The author names him to show that the Japanese academy's Chinese graduates rose in Chinese public life too.

ch06.anchor: Mei Gongbin, a native of Huangmei in Hubei
ch06.note: Mei Gongbin, a Chinese student at the Japanese academy in Shanghai who, far from becoming the pro-Japanese asset the school expected, founded the first Communist Party branch in the city's Xujiahui district from inside its walls. His memoir is among the author's sources.

ch06.anchor: under the Beiyang government
ch06.note: The Beiyang government, the internationally recognized Republican government based at Beijing from 1912 to 1928, dominated by the northern militarist cliques that grew out of Yuan Shikai's Beiyang Army; it had a nominal parliament, the “parliament” referred to here.

ch06.anchor: Shanghai's Xujiahui district
ch06.note: Xujiahui (Zikawei) in the southwest of Shanghai, historically the great center of Jesuit missionary activity in China, with its cathedral, observatory, and libraries; by the 1920s a populous urban district.

ch06.anchor: joined the Communist Youth League
ch06.note: The Communist Youth League, the Party's organization for young people (in this period the Socialist Youth League), from which members “went over” into full Party membership as they came of age.

ch06.anchor: Wang Xuewen walked in through its gates
ch06.note: Wang Xuewen (1895–1985), a Japan-trained Marxist economist and secret Communist who taught inside the Japanese academy in Shanghai and later directed the Eighth Route Army's enemy-army work and the Japanese Workers' and Peasants' School at Yan'an (section 3).

ch06.anchor: admitted to Tokyo Imperial University
ch06.note: Tokyo Imperial University (today the University of Tokyo), founded in 1877, the most prestigious university in Japan and the training ground of its official and intellectual elite.

ch06.anchor: the socialist scholar Kawakami Hajime
ch06.note: Kawakami Hajime (1879–1946), Japan's foremost early Marxist economist and a professor of economics at Kyoto Imperial University; his writings and his translation of Das Kapital shaped a generation of Japanese and Chinese radicals.

ch06.anchor: Nishizato Tatsuo, Ishida Shichirō
ch06.note: Nishizato Tatsuo, a Japanese journalist and graduate of the academy who joined the Communist intelligence network at Nanjing; he was tried with Nakanishi Kō and freed at the war's end in 1945.

ch06.anchor: and Ozaki Shōtarō of the 26th class
ch06.note: Ozaki Shōtarō, a left-leaning graduate of the academy and a member of Nakanishi Kō's network — a different man from the Sorge-ring spy Ozaki Hotsumi, who appears below.

ch06.anchor: Nakanishi Kō and Mizuno Shigeru of the 29th
ch06.note: Nakanishi Kō (1910–1973), the central figure of this chapter: a Japanese Communist and China expert who worked for the South Manchuria Railway's research arm while spying for the Chinese Communists under Pan Hannian's system, and who obtained the strategic intelligence of Japan's turn south. Arrested by the Tokkō and freed at the war's end, he later sat in the Japanese Diet as a Communist.

ch06.anchor: electing Anzai Kuraji as branch secretary
ch06.note: Anzai Kuraji, a Japanese student at the academy who, by the author's account, later became a secretary of the Central Committee of the Japanese Communist Party and a noted friend of China.

ch06.anchor: the Central Committee of the Japanese Communist Party
ch06.note: The Japanese Communist Party, founded in secret in 1922; illegal and heavily suppressed under the prewar state, it operated underground until it was legalized after Japan's defeat in 1945.

ch06.anchor: the Japanese agent Doihara
ch06.note: Doihara Kenji (1883–1948), the army's leading intelligence officer in China, nicknamed the “Lawrence of Manchuria”; a principal plotter of the 1931 Mukden Incident and of the creation of Manchukuo. He was hanged as a war criminal in 1948.

ch06.anchor: the Empress Wanrong
ch06.note: Wanrong (1906–1946), the empress consort of the last Qing emperor Puyi; she followed him to Manchukuo, became addicted to opium, and died in Communist captivity in 1946.

ch06.anchor: Tanaka Ryūkichi, set Japanese ruffians
ch06.note: Tanaka Ryūkichi (1893–1972), a Japanese army officer in Shanghai who, working with Kawashima Yoshiko, staged the street provocations that touched off the January 28 fighting; after the war he turned prosecution witness at the Tokyo war-crimes tribunal.

ch06.anchor: touch off the "January 28 Incident."
ch06.note: The Shanghai (January 28) Incident of 1932: heavy fighting between Japanese forces and the Chinese 19th Route Army in and around Shanghai, a month after the seizure of Manchuria; it ended in a truce that May.

ch06.anchor: Agnes Smedley, who knew China's progressive literary men
ch06.note: Agnes Smedley (1892–1950), an American radical journalist close to China's left-wing writers and revolutionaries; author of the autobiographical novel Daughter of Earth, and a link between Richard Sorge's network and its Chinese and Japanese contacts.

ch06.anchor: Smedley introduced Ozaki Hotsumi
ch06.note: Ozaki Hotsumi (1901–1944), Asahi Shimbun journalist, China expert, and later a private adviser to Prime Minister Konoe — and the key Japanese member of Sorge's spy ring. Arrested in 1941, he was hanged with Sorge in 1944. He is a distinct person from Ozaki Shōtarō above.

ch06.anchor: who in turn introduced Kawai Teikichi
ch06.note: Kawai Teikichi, a Japanese member of the Sorge network whom Agnes Smedley first brought to Sorge in Shanghai.

ch06.anchor: deputy consul-general, Iwai Eiichi
ch06.note: Iwai Eiichi (1899–1980), Japanese deputy consul-general in Shanghai and head of a Foreign Ministry intelligence organ, the “Iwai Kōkan.” Pan Hannian's network ran a channel into his operation, exploited in section 4.

ch06.anchor: correspondent of the Asahi Shimbun
ch06.note: The Asahi Shimbun, founded 1879, one of Japan's largest and most influential national daily newspapers.

ch06.anchor: the League of Left-Wing Writers
ch06.note: The League of Left-Wing Writers, a Communist-led literary organization founded in Shanghai in 1930 under the nominal leadership of Lu Xun; a center of radical culture and a target of Nationalist repression.

ch06.anchor: Lu Xun, Xia Yan, Wang Xuewen
ch06.note: Xia Yan (1900–1995), a Communist playwright, journalist, and film screenwriter, and a leading organizer of the left-wing cultural movement in Shanghai; his memoir is among the author's sources.

ch06.anchor: Wang Xuewen, Tian Han, and others
ch06.note: Tian Han (1898–1968), a major modern playwright and lyricist; he wrote the words of “The March of the Volunteers,” later adopted as the national anthem of the People's Republic of China.

ch06.anchor: This Institute of Pacific Relations had been founded
ch06.note: The Institute of Pacific Relations (IPR), an international academic body founded in 1925 that met in turn around the Pacific rim to study the region's affairs; its findings carried real weight with governments, and in the United States it was later attacked for supposed Communist influence.

ch06.anchor: Yan Huiqing, Jiang Menglin, Hu Shi.
ch06.note: Two of the three named delegates: Yan Huiqing (W. W. Yen, 1877–1950), a much-traveled diplomat who served the Republic as foreign minister, premier, and first ambassador to the Soviet Union; and Jiang Menglin (Chiang Monlin, 1886–1964), a leading educator and long-serving president of Peking University. Hu Shi is identified earlier in the book.

ch06.anchor: After the Russo-Japanese War of 1905
ch06.note: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, in which Japan defeated Tsarist Russia; the peace transferred Russia's leases and railway rights in southern Manchuria to Japan, giving it the foothold from which the SMR and the Kwantung Army grew.

ch06.anchor: the Chinese Eastern Railway that Russia had built
ch06.note: The Chinese Eastern Railway, the trunk line Russia built across Manchuria around 1897–1903 to shorten its route to Vladivostok; its southern branch, below Changchun, passed to Japan after 1905 and became the core of the South Manchuria Railway.

ch06.anchor: the "Kwantung Leased Territory,"
ch06.note: The Kwantung Leased Territory, the tip of the Liaodong peninsula (the ports of Dalian and Lüshun, the old Port Arthur), leased from China first by Russia and then, after 1905, by Japan; it gave the SMR's headquarters city, Dalian, and the “Kwantung” (“east of the pass”) name to the army stationed there.

ch06.anchor: Pine, bamboo, plum, and orchid are the elegant emblems
ch06.note: Pine, bamboo, and plum are the “Three Friends of Winter,” and plum, orchid, bamboo, and chrysanthemum the “Four Gentlemen” of classical Chinese painting — all standing for upright, unbending character. The author's point is the perversity of Japanese spy agencies taking these emblems of virtue as their code names.

ch06.anchor: Song Zheyuan's Northwestern Army
ch06.note: Song Zheyuan (1885–1940), commander of the 29th Army in North China, a force descended from Feng Yuxiang's old Northwestern Army; his troops fought the opening battle at the Marco Polo Bridge in July 1937.

ch06.anchor: a beautiful woman agent, Zheng Pingru
ch06.note: Zheng Pingru (executed 1940), a young Zhongtong agent who, from 1939, drew close to the collaborator Ding Mocun in occupied Shanghai in an attempt to assassinate him; the plot failed in December 1939 and she was seized and shot. Ding Mocun was the first chief of No. 76 and later a minister in the Wang Jingwei regime.

ch06.anchor: the raw material for Eileen Chang's story
ch06.note: Eileen Chang (Zhang Ailing, 1920–1995), one of the most celebrated modern Chinese writers; her novella Lust, Caution drew on the Zheng Pingru affair, and Ang Lee's 2007 film was adapted from it.

ch06.anchor: Through Yuan Shu, reach Iwai Eiichi
ch06.note: Yuan Shu (1911–1987), a left-wing writer turned one of the war's most tangled multiple agents — at once a Communist, a Nationalist Zhongtong man, and on the Japanese payroll — who furnished Pan Hannian's channel into Iwai Eiichi's operation. He was imprisoned along with Pan in 1955.

ch06.anchor: vice-president of the Marx-Lenin Academy
ch06.note: The Marx-Lenin Academy (Marx-Lenin Institute), a senior Party school established at Yan'an in 1938 to train cadres in Communist theory.

ch06.anchor: the Enemy-Army Work Department
ch06.note: The Eighth Route Army's organ for “enemy work” (diren gongzuo): propaganda directed at Japanese troops, and the handling and re-education of prisoners of war — the subject of section 3.

ch06.anchor: 30,000 Polish officers in the Katyn Forest
ch06.note: The Katyn massacre of 1940, in which the Soviet secret police shot captured Polish officers and members of the elite; the total is usually put at about 22,000, not the 30,000 the author gives. The Soviet Union blamed Germany and admitted responsibility only in 1990. CONTRADICTED as to the number.

ch06.anchor: in the camp at Weifang
ch06.note: The Weihsien (Weifang) Internment Camp in Shandong, where Japan held some two thousand Allied civilians during the war; among its inmates was the Olympic champion runner Eric Liddell, who died there in 1945.

ch06.anchor: the Japanese song "Karatachi no Hana,"
ch06.note: “Karatachi no Hana” (“Flowers of the Trifoliate Orange”), a beloved Japanese art song of 1925, set by the composer Yamada Kōsaku to a poem by Kitahara Hakushū.

ch06.anchor: the "New Order in East Asia"
ch06.note: The “New Order in East Asia,” the slogan proclaimed by Prime Minister Konoe in 1938 for a Japanese-led bloc of Japan, Manchukuo, and China; it was the forerunner of the wartime “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere.”

ch06.anchor: the Conference of the Anti-Fascist Peoples of the East
ch06.note: A congress convened at Yan'an in October 1941 that gathered anti-fascist delegates from across East Asia, including Japanese and Korean, to coordinate resistance to Japanese imperialism.

ch06.anchor: Nakanishi Kō studied Mao Zedong's
ch06.note: On Protracted War (Lun chijiu zhan), Mao Zedong's series of lectures of May 1938 analyzing the war with Japan; it argued that China, though weaker, would win a long war fought in three stages — strategic defensive, stalemate, and counter-offensive — the very framework Nakanishi Kō is said to have borrowed for his own analysis.

ch06.anchor: called it an "all but decisive battle."
ch06.note: The Ta Kung Pao (Dagongbao), a leading independent Chinese newspaper founded in 1902, respected for its serious national and political coverage.

ch06.anchor: the SMR or the RAND Corporation
ch06.note: The RAND Corporation, the American think tank founded in 1948 to provide strategic analysis to the U.S. military — an anachronism here, used by the author simply as the type of the modern intelligence-and-policy research institution.

ch06.anchor: the Japanese China Expeditionary Army
ch06.note: The China Expeditionary Army, the unified command of Japanese ground forces in China proper, established in 1939 to coordinate the several armies fighting the war below the Great Wall.

ch06.anchor: finish off the "China Incident."
ch06.note: “The China Incident” (Shina jihen) was Japan's official name for its undeclared war on China from 1937; by calling a full-scale war an “incident,” Japan avoided a formal declaration and its legal consequences, including the reach of American neutrality law.

ch06.anchor: the Chief Cabinet Secretary, Kazami Akira
ch06.note: Kazami Akira (1886–1961), Chief Cabinet Secretary in Prince Konoe's first cabinet (1937–39); a politician of relatively liberal, China-sympathetic leanings.

ch06.anchor: the Japanese cell that Wu Chengfang handled
ch06.note: Wu Chengfang, a Communist intelligence officer under Pan Hannian who ran the network's Japanese cell in Shanghai; imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case and rehabilitated in 1982.

ch06.anchor: handed a copy to Zheng Wendao
ch06.note: Zheng Wendao (1914–1942), Nakanishi Kō's Chinese liaison in Shanghai and the martyr of this chapter's closing section; arrested by the Japanese gendarmerie in 1942, he took his own life to shield the network and to protect Nakanishi Kō.

ch06.anchor: Wang Jinyuan planted at Wang Jingwei's side
ch06.note: Wang Jinyuan, a secret Communist placed as a secretary at Wang Jingwei's side, from which post he fed the puppet regime's top secrets to Pan Hannian's network.

ch06.anchor: the Second Bureau of the Military Commission
ch06.note: The Central Military Commission's Second Bureau, the Communists' radio-interception and code-breaking service, which drew intelligence “from the sky” by monitoring enemy wireless traffic.

ch06.anchor: a new body, the Kōa-in
ch06.note: The Kōa-in (Asia Development Board), a Japanese cabinet organ set up in 1938 to administer the affairs of occupied China; it took most China policy out of the Foreign Ministry's hands and, as the author notes, treated China as a collection of colonies rather than a country.

ch06.anchor: Yu Hanmou in Guangdong
ch06.note: Two of the regional power-holders named: Yu Hanmou (1896–1981), the Nationalist commander who dominated Guangdong, and Xu Chongzhi (1887–1965), a veteran Cantonese general of an earlier generation. Yan Xishan of Shanxi and Long Yun of Yunnan are identified elsewhere in the book. The author's point is that several Nationalist regional bosses had feelers out to Japan at once.

ch06.anchor: among three men: Itagaki, Chiang, and Wang
ch06.note: General Itagaki Seishirō (1885–1948), a chief planner of the 1931 Mukden Incident, briefly war minister, and by this time a senior commander in China; his supposed presence at a secret summit with Chiang Kai-shek and Wang Jingwei made him the intended prize of the sabotage that follows. He was executed as a war criminal in 1948.

ch06.anchor: a classmate of Chiang Ching-kuo
ch06.note: Chiang Ching-kuo (1910–1988), Chiang Kai-shek's eldest son, who studied and lived in the Soviet Union from 1925 to 1937; later he ran the Nationalist secret police and, from 1978, served as president of the Republic of China on Taiwan.

ch06.anchor: the Hongmen brotherhood
