ch06.note: The Hongmen, an old Chinese fraternal secret society with roots in anti-Qing brotherhoods (kin to the Triads and, overseas, the Chee Kung Tong); its networks ran wide among southern and overseas Chinese and could shield — or watch — clandestine dealings.

ch06.anchor: the Chinese classic the Thirty-Six Stratagems
ch06.note: The Thirty-Six Stratagems, a Chinese handbook of military and political ruses. The “Stratagem of Sowing Discord” (lijian ji) means turning one's enemies against one another — here Pan Hannian's playing of the Japanese Foreign Ministry against the army. Chapter 7 refers back to this stratagem.

ch06.anchor: Wang Shiying convened a mass meeting
ch06.note: Wang Shiying (1905–1968), a Central Special Branch veteran who ran Communist intelligence and united-front work in North China; later a provincial governor, he died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

ch06.anchor: the "Red Orchestra,"
ch06.note: The “Red Orchestra” (Rote Kapelle), the name German counter-intelligence gave to the Soviet espionage and resistance networks operating in occupied Western Europe during the war.

ch06.anchor: the Red Army intelligence chief Berzin
ch06.note: Jan (Yan) Berzin (1889–1938), the Latvian founder and long-time head of Soviet military intelligence (the GRU); he was arrested and shot in Stalin's Great Purge in 1938, one of the losses that, as the author says, crippled Soviet foreign networks.

ch06.anchor: General Staff intelligence, Golikov
ch06.note: Filipp Golikov (1900–1980), head of Soviet military intelligence from 1940; to suit Stalin's disbelief he filtered and dismissed the mounting warnings of the coming German attack. He later rose to marshal.

ch06.anchor: the Chinese ambassador to Britain Guo Taiqi
ch06.note: Guo Taiqi (Quo Tai-chi, 1888–1952), China's ambassador to Britain through the 1930s and, from 1941, foreign minister; he later presided over the first session of the U.N. Security Council.

ch06.anchor: the Japanese ambassador to Britain Shigemitsu Mamoru
ch06.note: Shigemitsu Mamoru (1887–1957), a veteran Japanese diplomat who served as ambassador to Britain and, later, foreign minister; it was he who signed Japan's instrument of surrender aboard the USS Missouri in 1945.

ch06.anchor: the army minister, Tōjō Hideki
ch06.note: Tōjō Hideki (1884–1948), the army general who became prime minister in October 1941 and led Japan into the Pacific War; executed as a war criminal in 1948. His rise from war minister to premier marked the army's grip on the state.

ch06.anchor: the decision of Japan's Imperial Conference
ch06.note: The Imperial Conference (gozen kaigi), an extraordinary meeting of Japan's senior ministers and military chiefs held in the presence of the Emperor to ratify the gravest decisions of state.

ch06.anchor: the Central Investigation and Study Bureau was founded
ch06.note: A high-standing intelligence-and-research bureau Mao Zedong set up in 1941 and headed himself; its name embodied his doctrine that “investigation and study” (diaocha yanjiu) was the foundation of sound decision.

ch06.anchor: the Center added a new department
ch06.note: The Central Intelligence Department, established in September 1941 as the Communists' unified strategic-intelligence organ — in practice one body with the Social Affairs Department under two signboards, run day to day by Li Kenong.

ch06.anchor: The People's Commissariat for State Security
ch06.note: The Soviet state-security ministry (the NKGB), which in 1941 was folded back into the vast People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs (the NKVD), the combined security and police commissariat; these were the forerunners of the postwar KGB.

ch06.anchor: Lieutenant-General Imamura, 3 divisions, Malaya
ch06.note: The generals listed were the field commanders of Japan's simultaneous December 1941 offensive across Southeast Asia. Homma Masaharu led the invasion of the Philippines and Imamura Hitoshi the drive into the Dutch East Indies, while General Terauchi Hisaichi commanded the overall Southern Army; the book's assignment of theaters is looser than the historical record.

ch06.anchor: Ambassador Kurusu flies today via Hong Kong
ch06.note: Kurusu Saburō (1886–1954), a Japanese career diplomat who had signed the Tripartite Pact as ambassador to Germany; in November 1941 he was sent to join Ambassador Nomura in the final Washington talks, and was still negotiating when Pearl Harbor was struck.

ch06.anchor: Hitokappu Bay off Etorofu Island
ch06.note: The remote anchorage in the Kuril Islands (Etorofu, now Iturup) where Japan's Pearl Harbor strike force secretly assembled before sailing east across the North Pacific.

ch06.anchor: Wen Yuqing of the Ministry of Communications'
ch06.note: Wen Yuqing, a Nationalist cryptographer who in 1934 urged Chiang Kai-shek to set up a dedicated unit to break Japanese ciphers, and later headed the Military Commission's Technical Research Office that did so.

ch06.anchor: the Office of Strategic Services
ch06.note: The OSS, the United States' first central wartime intelligence agency, created in 1942; disbanded after the war, its lineage led to the founding of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) in 1947.

ch06.anchor: America put the Hull Note to Japan
ch06.note: The “Hull Note” of November 26, 1941, in which the U.S. Secretary of State demanded that Japan withdraw from China and Indochina and abandon the Axis alliance; Japan treated it as an ultimatum and as the point of no return toward war.

ch06.anchor: the three-nation military alliance of Germany, Italy, and Japan
ch06.note: The Tripartite Pact of September 1940, which bound Germany, Italy, and Japan as the “Axis” in a pledge of mutual support; it was, as the author says, what finally hardened American opinion against Japan.

ch06.anchor: a "Declaration of War Against Japan" as early as April 15, 1932
ch06.note: The Chinese Soviet Republic's declaration of war on Japan, issued in April 1932. It was a gesture without military means behind it — the small Jiangxi base could not reach the Japanese — but the author uses it to contrast the Communists' early defiance with Chiang Kai-shek's formal declaration, which came only after Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

ch06.anchor: The courier Zhang Mingda
ch06.note: Zhang Mingda, a courier of the Nakanishi Kō network who escaped the 1942 arrests; he later wrote about the network under the name Fang Zhida, and served in the 1980s as a deputy head of the Central United Front Work Department.

ch06.anchor: attached to Tongji University in Shanghai
ch06.note: Tongji University in Shanghai, founded in 1907 with German backing as a school of medicine and engineering, and long one of China's leading technical universities.

ch06.anchor: Ozaki Hotsumi's younger brother, Ozaki Hotsuki
ch06.note: Ozaki Hotsuki, a literary critic and the younger brother of Ozaki Hotsumi; he devoted much of his writing to his brother's memory and to the Sorge affair, and served as head of the Japan PEN Club, the writers' association. Several of his books are among the author's sources.

ch06.anchor: elected to the House of Councillors
ch06.note: The House of Councillors, the upper house of Japan's postwar parliament, the Diet.

ch07.note: “Rooting out traitors” renders chujian (除奸), literally “to hoe out the traitors”: the wartime name the Communists gave to counter-espionage work. A hanjian (汉奸), the “traitor to the Han” of the following sentences, is a Chinese who collaborates with a foreign invader—here the Japanese. The word carries the author’s side’s full charge, and is kept as he uses it.
The armed unit of the Central Special Branch—also called the “Red Squad”—that hunted down and killed defectors and informers, the “dogs” of the name. It first appears in Chapter 1.

Puyi (1906–1967), the last Qing emperor, abdicated in 1912 and was installed by Japan in 1932 as ruler of the puppet state of Manchukuo. Wang Jingwei headed the Japanese-sponsored regime at Nanjing (see Chapter 2).

ch07.anchor: Wang Kemin, chairman of the Provisional Government council
ch07.note: Wang Kemin (1873–1945) headed the Japanese-sponsored Provisional Government of the Republic of China set up in North China in December 1937.

ch07.anchor: Zuo Quan, was killed in action
ch07.note: Zuo Quan (1905–1942), Soviet-trained deputy chief of staff of the Eighth Route Army, was killed on May 25, 1942, breaking out of a Japanese encirclement at Shiziling during the “May mopping-up” of the Taihang base; he was the highest-ranking Communist commander to die in the war. Corroborated. (The book styles him chief of staff; his post was deputy chief of staff of the forward headquarters.)

ch07.anchor: the "three links": mail, transport, and trade
ch07.note: The “three links” (santong): postal exchange, transport, and trade. The same phrase would become famous decades later in cross-Strait politics.
The Communist term for the civil war of 1927–1937, also called the Agrarian Revolutionary War; the “White areas” were the Nationalist-held regions.

ch07.anchor: Shen Zhiyue, who claimed to have slipped into Yan'an
ch07.note: Shen Zhiyue (1913–1994) did infiltrate Yan’an around 1938 and later became a senior intelligence official in Taiwan, eventually heading the Investigation Bureau. His claim to have been Mao Zedong’s secretary is uncorroborated—the book itself calls it bragging.

ch07.anchor: their bodies in Cao's camp, their hearts with Han
ch07.note: An idiom from the tales of the Three Kingdoms: the general Guan Yu, obliged to serve the warlord Cao Cao, kept his heart loyal to his own lord and the Han cause. It means outward service and inward loyalty.
The faction of the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, which dominated the Nationalist party machine and Zhongtong; its rival, the “Zhu faction,” formed around the organization minister Zhu Jiahua.
The kurou ji, one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: to injure one’s own man so the enemy will trust him—classically the flogging of Huang Gai before the battle of Red Cliffs.

An episode from Romance of the Three Kingdoms: Zhou Yu plants a forged letter for Cao Cao’s envoy Jiang Gan to “steal,” tricking Cao into executing his own two admirals—a byword for the counter-espionage frame (fanjian ji) that turns the enemy’s own spying against him.

ch07.anchor: packing his Sacrifice League with renegade cadres
ch07.note: The Sacrifice League for National Salvation, an anti-Japanese mass organization set up under the Shanxi warlord Yan Xishan in 1936; the Communists infiltrated it deeply and used it, and the “Shanxi New Army” (its Dare-to-Die Columns), to build their own strength.

ch07.anchor: a correspondence between Heaven and man
ch07.note: Tianren ganying, the old Han-Confucian doctrine that Heaven answers a ruler’s conduct with portents and disasters—so that a lightning strike could be read as a verdict on the government.

Jingbing jianzheng, the streamlining of army and administration adopted in the Border Region in 1941–1942 to survive the Nationalist blockade; proposed by the non-party assemblyman Li Dingming and praised by Mao. Corroborated.
A dan (石) is a measure of grain, roughly a picul; a jin (斤), a catty, is about half a kilogram.
The Yan’an self-reliance drive of 1942–1945—land reclamation, spinning, and weaving, most famously by the 359 Brigade at Nanniwan—launched to beat the blockade.
Bianbi, the banknotes issued by the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region Bank, legal tender within the Border Region.

The book prints his name Ma Xiwu (马锡武); the documented judge is 马锡五 (1899–1962), the same romanization. His plain, investigative, mediation-based “Ma Xiwu adjudication method” became a Communist model, and the opera Liu Qiao’er (Chapter 9) derives from one of his judgments. “Blue Sky” (qingtian) is the epithet of the incorruptible Song judge Bao Zheng. Corroborated.

The All-Russian Extraordinary Commission (its Russian initials, ChK), Lenin’s political police founded in December 1917 under Dzerzhinsky, which combined the hunting of counter-revolutionaries with the policing of sabotage. It was the model for Communist security work—and, the author suggests, for its excesses.

ch07.anchor: Xu Jishen and others were ordered to found
ch07.note: Xu Jishen (1901–1931), a Whampoa graduate and Red Army commander in the Hubei-Henan-Anhui base, was executed in an internal purge in 1931 after a Nationalist counter-espionage frame—planted agents who “confessed” him an inside man—cast suspicion on him; he was later rehabilitated as a martyr. Corroborated. (The book dates the base’s founding to 1932; the army and base had in fact taken shape by 1930–1931.)

Zhang Luping (1921–1945) led the underground Communist branch inside Juntong’s Chongqing radio headquarters—with Zhang Weilin, Feng Chuanqing, Zhao Ligeng, Yang Guang, Chen Guozhu, and Wang Xizhen. The group was exposed in 1940, imprisoned, and executed in 1945; their true story surfaced only in the 1980s. Corroborated.

The Sino-American Cooperative Organization (SACO), a joint U.S.-Nationalist intelligence body formed at Chongqing in 1943; its Geleshan compound adjoined the Baigongguan and Zhazidong prisons where the Zhang Luping group and many other Communists were held and, on the eve of liberation, killed.
Deng Yanda (1895–1931), the leftist Nationalist leader and founder of the “Third Party,” was executed on Chiang Kai-shek’s orders in 1931.

ch07.anchor: the counter-espionage stratagem means turning the enemy's agents
ch07.note: Fanjian ji, one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: to turn the enemy’s own agents against him. It is distinct from lijian ji, the stratagem of sowing discord within the enemy (Chapter 6).

Zhiyi, a term coined by Zhao Cangbi (1917–1993), a Border Security cadre who rose to become the PRC’s Minister of Public Security (1977–1983), for the point-against-point contest of stratagems in covert struggle.
Hancheng, a county in the far east of Shaanxi province on the west bank of the Yellow River; its ferry crossings were a main gateway between the Communists' Shaanxi base and the Shanxi front.

ch07.anchor: Yang Qiqing, chief of the Anti-Traitor Department
ch07.note: Yang Qiqing (1911–1978), a Communist counter-espionage officer from Pingjiang in Hunan; here head of the Anti-Traitor (security) Department at the Eighth Route Army's forward headquarters, and after 1949 the first vice-minister of Public Security of the People's Republic. He is the subject of one of the book's principal sources, A Life of Yang Qiqing.

North Shaanxi College (陕北公学, Shaanbei Gongxue), a Communist academy founded at Yan'an in 1937 to train cadres for the resistance; its parade ground was a usual site for Yan'an's mass meetings and public trials.

Lei Jingtian (1904–1959), a veteran revolutionary from Guangxi who served as president of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region High Court from 1937 to 1945; he had presided the year before over the celebrated trial and execution of the Red Army officer Huang Kegong (see Chapter 2).
Cheng Fangwu (1897–1984), a writer and educator, co-founder with Guo Moruo and Yu Dafu of the Creation Society (see Chapter 2); at this time he was principal of North Shaanxi College.
Mo Wenhua (1910–2000), a Red Army political officer from Guangxi and veteran of the 1929 Baise Uprising; later a lieutenant general of the People's Liberation Army.

“Maintenance associations” (維持会, weichihui) were the local caretaker bodies that sprang up across Japanese-occupied areas, staffed by gentry and notables who kept civil order and supplied labor and grain on the occupier's behalf—the lowest and most numerous rung of collaboration.

ch07.anchor: the Japanese North China Area Army's
ch07.note: The North China Area Army (华北方面军) was the standing Japanese army command responsible for occupied North China; its subordinate armies garrisoned Shanxi and the other northern provinces.
Taiyuan is the capital of Shanxi province; the other places named (Fenyang, Lishi, Linfen, and the rest) are towns across Shanxi where the Japanese planted intelligence posts.

These were popular sworn-brotherhood and salvationist religious societies (会道门) of the countryside; the Way of Former Heaven (先天道) was one of the largest of the old redemptive sects. Rooted in local life and often armed, such bodies were courted by turns by the Japanese, the Nationalists, and the Communists.

The red-tasseled spear (红翈枪), a long spear with a tuft of red horsehair below the blade, was the standard weapon of village militia; the children's corps (儿童团) was the boys' auxiliary that stood sentry and checked travel passes at the village entrance.

ch07.anchor: The Eighth Route Army's Shandong Column
ch07.note: The Shandong Column was the Eighth Route Army's principal force in Shandong, the province on China's northeast coast, fighting behind Japanese lines.

ch07.anchor: A young Guangdong man named He Qingyu
ch07.note: He Qingyu, a Communist officer from Guangdong who ran enemy-subversion and liaison work in Shandong; his memoir Years of Beacon Fire is one of the book's principal sources, and he dealt directly with the Japanese agent Mizuhara Kiyoshi of this section.

ch07.anchor: the General Political Department's enemy-work course
ch07.note: “Enemy work” (敌工, digong) was the Communist specialty of subverting the enemy's forces—propaganda aimed at Japanese and puppet troops and the winning-over of collaborator units—taught here in a dedicated course at the army's General Political Department.

The Japanese People's Anti-War League (在华日本人反战同盟) was an organization of Japanese prisoners of war, won over under Communist tutelage, who carried on antiwar propaganda against their former comrades; it was associated with the Japanese Communist leader Nosaka Sanzo (see Chapter 6).
The Yi-Meng mountains (沛蒙山区), the rugged highlands of south-central Shandong named for the Yi River and Mount Meng, were the heartland of the Communist base in the province.

The Japanese “pacification-intensification” campaigns (治安强化运动) of 1941–1942 in North China combined military sweeps, blockade lines, and “model” zones of soft rule, aiming to detach the population from the Communist guerrillas.

ch07.anchor: a good-natured devil had come to Da'anzhuang
ch07.note: “Devil” renders guizi (鬼子), the standard Chinese wartime epithet for the Japanese invader (“Japanese devils”)—which is what makes “a good devil” so jarring a phrase for the villagers to use.

ch07.anchor: and Qin Ping, with an orderly
ch07.note: Qin Ping, a Border Security field officer who recurs throughout this chapter and was among the author's chief interviewees; the book draws on his own memoirs. He later served as a party and security official in the Ministry of Petroleum.

ch07.anchor: of the Tianshui Field Headquarters sent an inspection team
ch07.note: The Tianshui Field Headquarters was a Nationalist regional military command (its seat the Gansu town of Tianshui) that oversaw operations and intelligence directed against the Border Region; compare the Xi'an field headquarters under Jiang Dingwen (Chapter 3).

“Friendly parties” (友党) was the polite fiction of the united-front years—each side officially treating the other as an allied party against Japan—beneath which, as the author says, the covert war went on undiminished.

ch07.anchor: kept receiving rejection slips from the
ch07.note: The Liberation Daily (解放日报) was the Communist Party's principal newspaper at Yan'an, published from 1941; its open, public pages are what let the agent couple signal their arrival by placing an article.

ch07.anchor: at Guanzhong, Longdong, Sanbian, and Suide
ch07.note: The Border Region was ringed by outlying sub-districts, four of which are named here: Guanzhong, the southern salient reaching toward Xi'an; Longdong, eastern Gansu on the west; Sanbian, the sandy northern march; and Suide, the eastern strip along the Yellow River. Each faced Nationalist forces across its border.

ch07.anchor: Xu Mengqiu, a senior Red Army cadre
ch07.note: Xu Mengqiu (1895–1976), a senior Red Army cadre and its “red historian,” chief editor of the Records of the Long March; he lost both legs to frostbite on the March. Detained in Xinjiang and broken under interrogation, he defected in 1943 and became a Juntong general, and died in prison. CORROBORATED.

The “Great Revolution” (大革命) is the Chinese name for the era of the first Nationalist-Communist alliance and the Northern Expedition, roughly 1924–1927, before Chiang Kai-shek's 1927 purge shattered it.

The Northwest Youth National Salvation Association (西北青年救国会) was the Communist-led patriotic youth federation based at Yan'an from 1937. The “Five Youths of the Northwest” were a celebrated group of its young progressive leaders; the source does not name them all.

ch07.anchor: Shi Zhe, chief of the First Bureau
ch07.note: Shi Zhe (1905–1998), a Soviet-trained security officer from Hancheng in Shaanxi who reached Yan'an in 1940 and became Mao Zedong's longtime Russian-language interpreter (and interpreter to Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi, and Zhu De); here a bureau chief of the Border Region Security Office.

Chen Long (1910–1958), originally Liu Hanxing, a Moscow-trained Communist security officer who headed the Social Affairs Department's public-order section; in 1945 Mao Zedong personally chose him to guard him at the Chongqing negotiations. Later a vice-minister of Public Security.

ch07.anchor: The Jidong intelligence station chief, Ren Yuan
ch07.note: Ren Yuan, a Communist intelligence officer from Suide who ran the eastern-Hebei (Jidong) station; his account of his capture by the Japanese and his escape, told in his book The Test, is one of the chapter's principal sources.

The Ji-Re-Liao region spans Hebei (Ji), Rehe or Jehol (Re, a former province), and Liaoning (Liao)—the borderland northeast of Beijing that was the Communists' gateway into Japanese-held Manchuria. “Jidong,” below, is its eastern Hebei portion.

ch07.anchor: The Social Affairs Department secretary Wang Chu
ch07.note: Wang Chu, a Social Affairs Department officer who handled this case; one of the author's interviewees, later a deputy bureau director in the Ministry of Public Security.

ch07.anchor: Liang Ji's father had a schoolmate
ch07.note: Liang Ji, a young Communist who worked as an inside informer against the Nationalist-run postal and telecommunications offices and later in the Yan'an public-security bureau; one of the author's interviewees, afterward a public-security official in Shanghai.

ch07.anchor: director of the Anshan Iron and Steel Works
ch07.note: The Anshan Iron and Steel Works, in Liaoning in the Northeast, was the largest iron-and-steel complex in the country and a showpiece of the early People's Republic—a measure of how far the once-suspected secretary rose.

ch07.anchor: Why doesn't the Thunder God strike Mao Zedong dead?
ch07.note: The Thunder God (雷公, Leigong) is the deity of Chinese folk belief who strikes down the wicked with his thunderbolts; the peasants' taunt asks why Heaven's justice spares Mao Zedong while killing a mere county head.

ch07.anchor: Li Qiming went to Suide to do field work
ch07.note: Li Qiming, a Border Security intelligence officer who ran the Lu Nan network described here; one of the author's interviewees, later a standing secretary of the Yunnan provincial party committee.
Suiyuan was a province of Republican China on the Mongolian steppe northwest of Shanxi; its territory is now part of Inner Mongolia, and its old capital, Guisui, is today Hohhot.

ch07.anchor: Luochuan, lying between Yan'an and Xi'an
ch07.note: Luochuan, a county on the highway midway between Yan'an and Xi'an, was a frontier post of the covert Nationalist-Communist struggle—the point where the two sides' apparatus met and probed each other.

Zhao Qufei, the Border Security field-team head whose counter-espionage coups at Luochuan are told here; one of the author's interviewees, later deputy governor of Heilongjiang province and head of its Public Security Department.

ch07.anchor: followed Xu Jianguo to work in Jin-Cha-Ji
ch07.note: Xu Jianguo, a Communist security official who directed intelligence and security work in the Jin-Cha-Ji (Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei) base area behind Japanese lines; later a senior public-security figure of the People's Republic.

ch08.note: “Expendable agents” renders 死间 (sijian), literally “dead agents”—one of the five kinds of spy in Sun Tzu’s Art of War, the doomed agent fed false information and sent knowing he is likely to be caught and killed. Juntong used the term for the men it planted to burrow into the Communist base areas, as Sun Tzu’s spy-types are glossed earlier in the book.

The haidi (海底, literally “sea bottom”) was Juntong jargon for the secret personal dossier each agent compiled and memorized: his real and cover names, his permanent and mailing addresses, the cover names of his contacts, the cipher for their correspondence, and his oath. The original stayed on file at the training class, and all later clandestine contact was keyed to it.

The Renaissance Society (复兴社) was an outer organ of the Nationalist “Blue Shirts,” the network of Chiang Kai-shek loyalists built in the early 1930s around the inner Vigorous Action Society (力行社), noted earlier in the book. Its members served as Nationalist party and security cadres.

Ren Zhuoxuan (任卓宣, 1896–1990), pen name Ye Qing, was an early Communist—once head of the Party’s Paris branch—who, after his arrest, defected and became the Nationalists’ foremost anti-Communist theorist and a propaganda official. Kang Sheng cites his career as the model of a turncoat put to use. (Corroborated.)

The chapter gives several figures because they count different things from different sources. The 32 agents of the core Yan’an “Dai case” (1 who came forward, 20 found by investigation, 11 named by others) are the single case cracked in 1942; a later recollection puts the Yan’an arrests at forty-odd and the whole Yan’an-period haul at 55; the 631 trained over nine sessions is the Gansu investigators’ 1955 count for the entire class, close to Cheng Muyi’s own captured report of 670, against 320 known earlier and 160 newly found. The book does not reconcile the tallies.

The People’s Liberation Army’s assault on Yijiangshan (一江山), a small island off the Zhejiang coast held by the Nationalists, in January 1955 was China’s first combined army-navy-air amphibious landing; the captured documents included Cheng Muyi’s report. (Corroborated.)
The Bureau of Confidential Investigation (保密局, Baomiju) was the postwar successor to Juntong, formed in 1946 under the Defense Ministry; that renaming is why the wartime Juntong is meant here.

Baigongguan (白公馆, the “White Mansion”), a villa at Geleshan outside Chongqing, served Juntong as a prison and as part of its Chongqing training apparatus; it belonged to the SACO complex noted in Chapter 7, where many captured Communists were held and killed.

ch08.anchor: the 385th Brigade under Wang Weizhou, with Geng Biao as his deputy
ch08.note: The 385th Brigade of the Eighth Route Army's 129th Division doubled as the Longdong Military District, the force guarding the Border Region's western approaches from its garrison in eastern Gansu. Wang Weizhou (1887–1970) was a veteran Communist commander from Sichuan; his deputy Geng Biao (1909–2000) later became a diplomat, a vice-premier, and—in 1981–82—the People's Republic's minister of national defense.

The “Premier” (总理, zongli) was Sun Yat-sen, founder of the Nationalist Party and of the Republic, a title the party kept for him alone after his death in 1925. His deathbed testament, exhorting his followers to complete the revolution, was recited as a ritual at the opening of Nationalist meetings and ceremonies—here it heads the curriculum.

The “Director-General” (总裁, zongcai) was Chiang Kai-shek, who took that title as leader of the Nationalist Party in 1938, the senior title of “Premier” being reserved for the dead Sun Yat-sen. Elsewhere in the book Chiang is styled the “Generalissimo.”

ch08.anchor: communism and the Three People's Principles
ch08.note: The Three People's Principles (三民主义, Sanmin zhuyi)—nationalism, democracy, and the people's livelihood—were Sun Yat-sen's political doctrine and the official ideology of the Nationalist state, set here against communism as its rival creed.

ch08.anchor: Turning from the dark to the light
ch08.note: Renders 弃暗投明 (qi an tou ming), “forsake the dark and turn to the light”—the set phrase, used on both sides, for a man abandoning a wrong allegiance for a right one.

ch08.anchor: Cheng Muyi, chief of Juntong's Northwest Special Investigation Station
ch08.note: Cheng Muyi ran Juntong's Xi'an-based Northwest Special Reconnaissance Station and, under the cover name Cheng Yi, was the working director of the Hanzhong class—the mastermind of the whole penetration effort this chapter recounts. He later fled to Taiwan; a report of his captured in 1955 (see below) would reopen the case.

Renders 天之骄子 (tian zhi jiao zi), literally the “proud sons of Heaven”—a phrase first used in the Book of Han for the Xiongnu nomads, now meaning those specially favored by fortune. The author's irony is that these “expendable agents” were treated as a pampered elite.

ch08.anchor: startle the snake in the grass
ch08.note: The idiom 打草惊蛇 (da cao jing she), “beat the grass and startle the snake”: to alert one's quarry by a careless move. The security men hold back from seizing Qi Sanyi lest they scare off the larger network behind him.

Renders 青面獠牙 (qing mian liao ya), “green-faced and fang-toothed,” the stock description of a hideous demon. The Hanzhong class had taught its students to expect the Communists as literal monsters; the agents planted in Yan'an found ordinary people instead.

ch08.anchor: I set out to paint a tiger and made a cur
ch08.note: The idiom 画虎不成反类犬 (hua hu bu cheng fan lei quan), “to try to paint a tiger and end up with a dog”: to attempt something beyond one's powers and produce a ludicrous failure. The repentant agent means that his grand resolve had come to nothing.

ch08.anchor: a performance of the self-injury ruse
ch08.note: The “self-injury ruse” (苦肉计, kurou ji) is one of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: to injure oneself, or feign injury, in order to win an enemy's trust—famously the beating Huang Gai took in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms to make his surrender to Cao Cao convincing. The fear is that the agents' surrender might be just such a planted deception.

ch08.anchor: loose a tiger back to the mountain
ch08.note: The idiom 放虎归山 (fang hu gui shan), “to let the tiger back to the mountain”: to release a dangerous enemy to make trouble again. Zhao Xiu, judged less reliable than the rest, could not be allowed to return to Nationalist Xi'an.

ch08.anchor: but for the master's face, I'd have thrashed it with a stick
ch08.note: An allusion to the proverb 打狗看主人 (“when you beat a dog, look to its master”): one should weigh a man's powerful patron before striking at him. The turncoat means that only his regard for the Party—“the master”—stayed his hand, a backhanded profession of loyalty.

Shen Zui (1914–1996) was a senior Juntong officer whose memoirs, written after his 1949 capture and years of imprisonment, became among the most widely read insider accounts of the Nationalist secret service—which makes their silence on the Hanzhong class, the author's point here, all the more telling.

ch09.anchor: because of a famous speech of Kang Sheng's
ch09.note: The “Rescue Campaign” (qiangjiu yundong) was the coercive spy-hunt into which the Yan’an Rectification’s cadre-screening phase escalated in 1943. Kang Sheng, chairing it from the Central Social Affairs Department, cast the purge as the “rescue” of misled youths from espionage; in practice it ran on forced confessions and manufactured evidence. Scholarship on the period—Gao Hua’s How the Red Sun Rose, Dai Qing’s study of Wang Shiwei, Chen Yung-fa’s work, which the author himself cites—finds the great majority of the thousands accused innocent; Mao soon conceded that real agents were “only a very few.” CORROBORATED: the campaign drew in on the order of 30,000 cadres, and the Party later disowned it. The author’s own verdict, that it prefigured the Cultural Revolution, matches the scholarly mainstream.

ch09.anchor: the very begetter of the Rescue Campaign
ch09.note: That Kang Sheng drove the campaign is the single most scrutinized fact of this chapter, and the consensus is firm (on the man, see the note at Chapter 2). It was he who generalized Zhang Keqin’s coerced confession into the “Red-Flag Party” theory, gave the July 1943 “Rescue the Fallen” speech, and let his wife Cao Yi’ou run the campaign in Yan’an county in person. In 1980 the Party posthumously expelled him and named him, with Lin Biao and Jiang Qing, a chief author of the era’s persecutions. CORROBORATED. The author assigns him the blame plainly—unusual candor for so Party-sympathetic a book, and consistent with the record.

ch09.anchor: On February 17 Wang Shiwei published
ch09.note: Wang Shiwei (1906–1947), a writer and translator at the Central Research Institute, whose essay “Wild Lily” (野百合花) attacked the privilege and hierarchy of Yan’an’s elite. He was made the literary target of the Rectification, denounced as a “Trotskyite,” and imprisoned. CONTRADICTED, and gravely: the “living memorial” scene later in this chapter shows him alive and “living well” in 1944, but Wang Shiwei was in fact secretly killed during the Communists’ retreat from Yan’an on 1 July 1947, his body thrown down a well. In February 1991 the Ministry of Public Security overturned the verdict, called the killing a wartime error, and rehabilitated him. The author’s text holds to the 1944 moment; the record does not end there.

ch09.anchor: put nearly three hundred Huxi cadres to death
ch09.note: The Huxi (“west-of-the-lake”) anti-Trotskyist purge of late 1939, in the base area west of Weishan Lake on the Shandong–Jiangsu border, is a documented atrocity in Party historiography: on fabricated charges of a Trotskyite ring, several hundred cadres were tortured and killed before Luo Ronghuan and Guo Hongtao rode in to stop it. The Party Center’s February 1941 “Decision on the Anti-Traitor Errors in the Huxi Border Region,” which the author cites, formally condemned it. CORROBORATED.

ch09.anchor: Root Out the Trotskyite Bandits
ch09.note: Kang Sheng’s article, published in Liberation in early 1938, notoriously branded Chen Duxiu—co-founder and first general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, by then close to the Trotskyists—a paid agent of Japanese intelligence. The charge was baseless and never substantiated; historians read it as a political smear. It set the “Trotskyite equals Japanese spy” template the later purges would exploit.

ch09.anchor: Kawashima Yoshiko in disguise
ch09.note: Kawashima Yoshiko (1907–1948), born Aisin Gioro Xianyu, a Manchu princess raised in Japan who became a Japanese intelligence agent famed as the “Eastern Jewel.” The Nationalist government executed her for treason in Beiping in 1948. The rumor that Wang Zunji “was really Kawashima Yoshiko in disguise” the author offers as a specimen of the fantastical charges the campaign bred.

ch09.anchor: her uncle, Wang Kemin
ch09.note: Wang Kemin (1873–1945), a Beiping banker who headed the Japanese-sponsored Provisional Government of North China and then chaired its successor, the North China Political Council—among the most senior collaborators of the occupation. Arrested after Japan’s surrender, he died in a Beiping prison in December 1945.

ch09.anchor: the Communists' Southern Committee had been wrecked
ch09.note: The wrecking of the Southern Committee (南委) in 1942 was one of the gravest penetrations the CCP underground suffered in the war. Zhongtong turned captured cadres in Jiangxi and rolled the network up through Guangdong and Guangxi; by the author’s account the whole Jiangxi provincial organization was gutted and over two thousand members arrested. The secretary, Fang Fang, escaped; the deputy secretary Zhang Wenbin died in prison in 1944. CORROBORATED in the standard accounts.

ch09.anchor: waved the red flag to oppose the red flag
ch09.note: This forced confession by Zhang Keqin, a young Gansu cadre broken after three days and nights of interrogation in early 1943, was the spark Kang Sheng seized: he generalized it into the theory of a “Red-Flag Party” (红旗党), a supposed Nationalist front “flying the red flag to oppose the red flag,” and extended the hunt to underground organizations across a dozen provinces. The “Red-Flag Party” was a fabrication; on 9 September 1981 the Party Center formally rehabilitated the organizations so charged—the document the author cites from the biography of Sun Zuobin. CORROBORATED.

ch09.anchor: The Injustice to Dou E
ch09.note: The Injustice to Dou E (答娴冠), Guan Hanqing’s Yuan-dynasty tragedy. Wrongly condemned and beheaded, the chaste widow Dou E swears three portents will prove her innocence, one of them snow falling in the sixth month of summer. “Snow in June” became the stock image of a great injustice crying out to Heaven, which is why the author reads Yan’an’s freak April snow as an omen.

ch09.anchor: the Comintern declared its own dissolution
ch09.note: The Communist International dissolved itself in May 1943, a wartime gesture by Stalin to reassure his Western allies. Chiang Kai-shek seized on it to argue that the Chinese Communists, their “higher body” gone, should dissolve too.

ch09.anchor: doffing his cap and bowing
ch09.note: Mao Zedong’s public apology for the campaign’s excesses is attested in several participants’ memoirs. In October 1943 he laid down the corrective “not one to be killed, and most not to be arrested” (一个不杀，大部不抓), and at the Seventh Congress in 1945 he apologized again for the wrongs of the vetting. CORROBORATED. Historians add that the gesture cost him little: the blame fell to Kang Sheng, and Mao’s own authority emerged from the Rectification enlarged.

ch09.anchor: Pan Hannian, deputy head of the Social Affairs Department
ch09.note: Pan Hannian (1906–1977), the CCP’s master intelligence operative (Chapters 5–6). The campaign’s shadow reached far past 1943: as the author’s own sources note, Pan never reported a 1943 meeting into which the collaborationist Wang Jingwei had drawn him, and in 1955 that silence was used to charge him as a traitor. He and Yang Fan, named here, were imprisoned for life; Pan died in a labor camp in 1977. The Party rehabilitated both in 1982, ruling the charges a fabrication. CORROBORATED.

ch09.anchor: Jiang Nanxiang wrote to Liu Shaoqi
ch09.note: Jiang Nanxiang (1913–1988), a leader of the 1935 December 9th student movement and later the People’s Republic’s minister of higher education and president of Tsinghua University. His March 1945 “Opinion on the Rescue Campaign” is remembered as one of the earliest reasoned repudiations of the campaign from within the Party.

ch09.anchor: with the famous actress Xin Fengxia
ch09.note: The opera grew from a real 1943 Longdong case: the marriage-freedom suit of the peasant girl Feng Zhiqin (childhood name Feng Peng’er), decided by Judge Ma Xiwu. Reworked as the pingju Liu Qiao’er and, with Xin Fengxia (1927–1998) in the title role, made into a hugely popular 1956 film, it became the best-known celebration of the 1950 Marriage Law. Feng Zhiqin was still living when the author wrote.

ch09.anchor: only Xiong Dazheng, the most deeply implicated
ch09.note: Xiong Dazheng—better known as Xiong Dazhen (熊大缝); the source prints a homophone variant—was a Western-trained physicist and a favored student of Ye Qishun who left Tsinghua to build munitions for the Jin-Cha-Ji resistance. Accused as a “Nationalist agent” in a 1939 anti-espionage purge, he was killed by his escorts during a transfer. His case, like the Huxi purge, is a documented instance of “coerce, confess, believe” predating the Rescue Campaign; he was rehabilitated in the 1980s. CORROBORATED.

ch09.anchor: at his old home in Wenzhou
ch09.note: Wenzhou, a port city on the coast of southern Zhejiang province.

ch09.anchor: at Yan'an's New Market
ch09.note: The New Market (新市场) was the commercial and entertainment quarter of Yan’an town, its shops, stalls, and theaters. It recurs in this chapter as the place people called an “agents’ market,” and later as the spot where the opera Liu Qiao’er dared to sell tickets.

ch09.anchor: Thoughts on March 8
ch09.note: Ding Ling’s essay “Thoughts on March 8” (三八节有感), published on International Women’s Day 1942, protested the persistence of male privilege and the hard lot of women even in revolutionary Yan’an; with Wang Shiwei’s “Wild Lily” it made her a target of the Rectification. It appeared in the Liberation Daily (解放日报), the CCP’s principal newspaper in Yan’an, which recurs throughout this chapter.

ch09.anchor: on the wall paper
ch09.note: A “wall paper,” or wall newspaper (墙报), was a hand-written sheet of news and opinion posted for all to read—a cheap, semi-official public forum, and a forerunner of the big-character posters (dazibao) of later campaigns. “Arrow and Target” and “Light Cavalry,” named here, were two such Yan’an wall papers.

ch09.anchor: On May 2 Mao Zedong convened the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art
ch09.note: Mao Zedong’s Talks at the Yan’an Forum on Literature and Art (May 1942) laid down that art must serve the workers, peasants, soldiers, and the Party; they became the governing doctrine of literature and art in Communist China for decades, and the charter against which writers like Wang Shiwei and Ding Ling were judged.

ch09.anchor: the Party Center set up a General Study Committee
ch09.note: The Central General Study Committee (中央总学委) was the body formed in June 1942 to direct the Rectification across the whole Party. That Kang Sheng, the security chief, was made its deputy under Mao is what let him fold the spy-hunt into the campaign, as the next sentences explain.

ch09.anchor: Small Broadcast
ch09.note: “Small broadcast” (小广播) was the Yan’an term for word-of-mouth rumor and unofficial news—the gossip network, as against the Party’s authorized “big broadcast.” The campaign treated it as a channel by which agents gathered secrets and spread “plausible rumors.”

ch09.anchor: Lin Lifu had been a
ch09.note: Lin Lifu (林里夫), a veteran of the Shanghai underground held by the Border Security for some seven years, is one of the chapter’s central old-case figures and, through his widow and his own memoirs, one of the author’s sources. By the book’s account he became after 1949 an economist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and an early advocate of economic accounting in socialist enterprises; branded in 1957 as part of the “Di Chaobai–Lin Lifu anti-Party clique,” he was cleared only in 1984. He never stopped charging that Kang Sheng was himself a turncoat.

ch09.anchor: the Chinese National Armed Self-Defense Committee
ch09.note: The Chinese National Armed Self-Defense Committee (中国民族武装自卫委员会) was a Communist-led anti-Japanese mass organization of the early 1930s, centered in Shanghai; its exposure and collapse scattered its underground cadres.

ch09.anchor: a man named He Guiren
ch09.note: He Guiren, another of the old-case prisoners, is described here as a foreign-educated intellectual of eminent family—grandson of a man who had taught the scholar Zhang Taiyan (see next note), son of a Qing Hanlin scholar, born in England, a doctor of law, and briefly one of Mao Zedong’s secretaries—held for years on Kang Sheng’s order. His fate is drawn from the memoir of his fellow prisoner Lin Lifu, who believed he was put to death during the civil war; the book presents the account as Lin’s.

ch09.anchor: Zhang Taiyan's teacher
ch09.note: Zhang Taiyan (章太炎, also Zhang Binglin, 1869–1936), one of modern China’s greatest classical scholars and philologists and a fierce anti-Manchu revolutionary; to have taught him marked He Guiren’s grandfather as a scholar of the first rank.

ch09.anchor: a Hanlin scholar of the Qing
ch09.note: The Hanlin Academy (翰林院) was the empire’s most prestigious body of scholar-officials, entered only by the highest examination graduates; a “Hanlin scholar” stood at the summit of the old learned elite.

ch09.anchor: his real name was Wang Fanxi
ch09.note: Wang Fanxi (王凡西), a leading figure of China’s small Trotskyist movement and later a memoirist in exile—the “Shanghai Wang Wenyuan,” a genuine Trotskyist Central Committee member, as against the innocent Yan’an namesake the passage is about.

ch09.anchor: Li Yuchao's ties to him were close
ch09.note: Li Yuchao, a Special Branch veteran and a fellow townsman, schoolmate, and colleague of Kang Sheng. In 1931, when Gu Shunzhang’s defection put a price on Zhou Enlai’s head, Zhou and his wife are said to have taken refuge in Li’s home; trusted once so far, he was examined all the same on reaching Yan’an.

ch09.anchor: Luo Ronghuan, the 115th's political commissar
ch09.note: Luo Ronghuan (罗荣朸, 1902–1963), political commissar of the 115th Division and the leading Communist figure in the Shandong base area; in 1955 he was made one of the ten marshals of the People’s Republic.

ch09.anchor: the wife of Lü Zhengcao, the Jizhong military commander
ch09.note: Lü Zhengcao (吕正操, 1904–2009), commander of the Jizhong (central Hebei) base area behind Japanese lines, famed for its railway guerrillas; a former Northeast Army officer, he later served as railways minister and, dying at 105, was the last survivor of the People’s Liberation Army’s original generals.

ch09.anchor: sent his organization chief Guo Qian to Jiangxi
ch09.note: Guo Qian, organization chief of the Southern Committee, was captured and turned, and became a chief instrument of Zhongtong’s destruction of the Communist underground in the south. As the chapter reveals later, he resurfaced in Taiwan as the scholar “Guo Hualun,” author of a much-cited history of the Chinese Communist Party (published in English under the name Warren Kuo). Corroborated in outline: Warren Kuo (Guo Hualun) was a former Communist who wrote such a history in Taipei.

ch09.anchor: Kang Sheng summoned Zhou Xing and Shi Zhe
ch09.note: Shi Zhe (师哲, 1905–1998), a Soviet-trained cadre moved to the Border Security in 1943 and later Mao Zedong’s Russian-language interpreter. His memoir Peaks and Valleys is a principal source for this chapter and, the author notes, the first to link the Hanzhong-class case to the Rescue Campaign.

ch09.anchor: sent to the Administrative Academy for collective training
ch09.note: The Yan’an Administrative Academy (行政学院) was where cadres of the Border Region government were gathered for “collective training”—in the campaign, a euphemism for detention and examination.

ch09.anchor: holding them at Zaoyuan
ch09.note: Zaoyuan (梱园), a compound northwest of Yan’an town that housed the Party Center’s secretariat and the Social Affairs Department; it recurs below as the site of confession rallies and of the department’s own art troupe.

ch09.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek and He Yingqin
ch09.note: He Yingqin (何应钦, 1890–1987), Chiang Kai-shek’s long-serving chief of staff and minister of war, one of the most senior figures of the Nationalist high command; briefly premier of the Republic of China in 1949.

ch09.anchor: The Nationalists' third anti-Communist upsurge
ch09.note: The last of three Nationalist “anti-Communist upsurges” of the united-front years—after the friction of 1939–40 and the New Fourth Army Incident of January 1941 (see earlier chapters)—this one, in July 1943, saw Hu Zongnan poised to strike the Border Region before pressure at home and abroad made Chiang draw back.

ch09.anchor: magic weapons like the Heaven-Toppling Seal
ch09.note: The Heaven-Toppling Seal (翻天印) is a magic weapon in the classic Ming novel Investiture of the Gods (封神演义), a stone seal hurled from the sky to crush an enemy; the author means that Kang Sheng always had another devastating “proof” to fling down.

ch09.anchor: the tiger bench
ch09.note: The “tiger bench” (老虎凡) was a notorious torture: the victim was bound seated with the legs held flat on a bench while bricks were forced under the ankles, bending the knees backward. It was a byword for the cruelty of the Nationalist secret services.

ch09.anchor: Li Kenong questioned Huang Gang himself
ch09.note: Huang Gang (黄钢), a writer on the Liberation Daily and the orphaned son of an early Party martyr, was “rescued” into a false confession as a Nationalist agent and then cleared. He went on to specialize in writing on the intelligence front and wrote the screenplay for the film The Unfailing Radio Waves.

ch09.anchor: cared for from childhood by Yun Daiying
ch09.note: Yun Daiying (恋代英, 1895–1931), one of the most influential early Communist youth leaders and editor of the journal China Youth; captured and executed by the Nationalists in 1931, he became a revered martyr—which is why the boy he had reared counted as a “red seedling.”

ch09.anchor: the Nationalist propaganda chief Zhang Daofan
ch09.note: Zhang Daofan (张道藩, 1897–1968), a Nationalist politician, playwright, and the party’s leading figure in propaganda and cultural affairs; later president of the Legislative Yuan on Taiwan.

ch09.anchor: Suide was a newly won part of the base area
ch09.note: Suide (绑德), a prefecture in the far north of Shaanxi, taken into the Border Region only in 1940; Xi Zhongxun was its Party secretary. Its recent Nationalist past made its cadres and schools a special object of suspicion in the campaign.

ch09.anchor: Zhao Chaogou of the
ch09.note: Zhao Chaogou (赵超构, 1910–1992), a well-known journalist of the Chongqing Xinmin press; his 1944 reports from Yan’an, later collected as Yan’an, One Month, were a sensation in the Nationalist areas.

ch09.anchor: raised a yangge-opera movement
ch09.note: The yangge (稻歌) is a boisterous folk song-and-dance of northern China, danced at festival time. The “yangge movement” of 1943–44, prompted by Mao’s Yan’an Forum talks, reworked it into a vehicle for revolutionary propaganda and became one of the signature cultural forms of the base area.

ch09.anchor: they wrote a qinqiang libretto
ch09.note: Qinqiang (秦腔), the vigorous, high-pitched traditional opera of Shaanxi and the northwest, one of the oldest of China’s regional operatic styles.

ch09.anchor: The Shaanbei storyteller Han Qixiang
ch09.note: Han Qixiang (韩起祥, 1915–1989), the celebrated blind storyteller of northern Shaanxi, who chanted shuoshu ballads to his own three-stringed sanxian; the Communists made him a model folk artist of the Yan’an years.

ch09.anchor: the first to be let out was Li Rui
ch09.note: Li Rui (李锐, 1917–2019), here the first prisoner freed in the screening. He became a part-time secretary to Mao Zedong in 1958, was purged the next year for criticizing the Great Leap Forward, and in his long later life was the most prominent liberal critic and Party historian among the Communist elders.

ch09.anchor: elected a delegate to the Seventh Party Congress
ch09.note: The CCP’s Seventh National Congress (April–June 1945, at Yangjialing in Yan’an), the Party’s first congress in seventeen years; it confirmed Mao Zedong’s supremacy, enshrined “Mao Zedong Thought,” and set the Party’s course for the final drive to power. Whether the many still-tainted cadres could be seated as delegates is the problem of this section.

ch09.anchor: non-Party public figure Xu Fanting
ch09.note: Xu Fanting (续范亭, 1893–1947), a patriotic general and old Nationalist who in 1935, in despair at the government’s failure to resist Japan, tried to disembowel himself before Sun Yat-sen’s tomb in Nanjing; he later drew close to the Communists in the northwest.

ch09.anchor: Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of the Party
ch09.note: The “Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of the Party,” adopted in April 1945, was the capstone of the Rectification: it fixed the official verdict on the Party’s past struggles—condemning the earlier “Left” lines and vindicating Mao’s—and so cemented his authority on the eve of the Seventh Congress.

ch09.anchor: Mao Zedong Thought
ch09.note: “Mao Zedong Thought” (毛泽东思想), the fusion of Marxism-Leninism with the “concrete practice of the Chinese revolution,” was written into the Party constitution at the Seventh Congress in 1945 as the guide for all Party work—the formal elevation of Mao’s thought to doctrine.

ch09.anchor: Chen Yongfa
ch09.note: Chen Yung-fa (陈永发, b. 1944), a leading Taiwanese historian of the Chinese Communist revolution; his The Shadow of Yan’an (1990) is the major scholarly study of the cadre-vetting and Rescue Campaign, drawing on the Social Affairs Department’s own internal journal. Academia Sinica (中央研究院) is Taiwan’s national research academy—here a Nationalist-side source the author openly relies on for this sensitive chapter.

ch10.anchor: under the table their intelligence services were already kicking each other
ch10.note: “The open scheme” renders 阳谋 yangmou, coined as the mirror of 阴谋 yinmou, “plot”: a design carried out in the open rather than in secret. The chapter’s “open scheme” is the postwar contest in which the two sides maneuvered openly — above all in the Chongqing peace talks — while each raced in secret for military position.

ch10.anchor: arrived by air in Chongqing
ch10.note: The Chongqing negotiations (28 August–10 October 1945) were a genuine historic event: Chiang Kai-shek invited Mao Zedong to talks, Mao flew to the Nationalist capital under American escort, and the two sides signed the Double-Tenth Agreement. The risk to Mao’s person was real, and his safety a preoccupation of the CCP security apparatus. Corroborated; the framing here as a “play performed in earnest” is the author’s.

ch10.anchor: a modern-day Feast at Hongmen
ch10.note: 鸿门宴, the banquet of 206 BC at which Xiang Yu’s followers schemed to assassinate his rival Liu Bang, who slipped away; a byword for a banquet that is a deadly trap.

ch10.anchor: buffoons out of the tale of Jiang Gan
ch10.note: In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Jiang Gan is sent to spy on the Wu strategist Zhou Yu before the Battle of Red Cliffs, is fed a forged letter, and is gulled into having his own side’s admirals killed — the archetype of the spy turned against his master. Zhou Yu, named just below, is the brilliant young Wu commander who engineers the deception.

ch10.anchor: On September 5, 1945, Japan surrendered.
ch10.note: The date is as printed, and is anomalous. Japan announced its acceptance of the Potsdam terms on 15 August 1945; the instrument of surrender was signed aboard the USS Missouri on 2 September; and the surrender of Japanese forces in the China theater was received at Nanjing on 9 September — the date the book itself gives correctly two paragraphs below. No standard milestone falls on 5 September; treat it as the author’s slip.

ch10.anchor: north of the 16th parallel was China's to receive
ch10.note: Under the Allied surrender arrangements, Chinese forces took the Japanese surrender across China (apart from the Soviet-occupied Northeast), on Taiwan, and in French Indochina north of the 16th parallel; the zone south of it went to the British. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: forced Long Yun out of Yunnan
ch10.note: Long Yun (1884–1962), the “King of Yunnan,” had ruled the province semi-autonomously since 1927. On Chiang’s order Du Yuming’s troops surrounded his headquarters on Wuhua Mountain on 3 October 1945 and forced him to Chongqing, where he was kept under virtual house arrest; in 1948 he fled to Hong Kong and sided with the Communists. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: the Vietnamese emperor Bao Dai
ch10.note: Bao Dai (1913–1997), last emperor of the Nguyen dynasty, abdicated on 25 August 1945 in favor of Ho Chi Minh’s provisional government and briefly served it as “supreme adviser.”

ch10.anchor: no Sino-Japanese dispute over the Diaoyu Islands today
ch10.note: An editorial aside of the author’s, reading a present-day territorial quarrel back onto 1945. The status of the Diaoyu (Senkaku) islands was not part of the surrender arrangements the passage describes; the remark reflects the book’s contemporary nationalist vantage rather than the historical record. Interested witness.

ch10.anchor: known within the trade as "strategic spies."
ch10.note: 冷藏间谋 (“cold-storage” or “refrigerated” spy) and 战略间谋 (“strategic spy”) both name an agent planted deep in the enemy camp and left dormant, doing no active work, until a decisive moment makes him worth the risk of activation.

ch10.anchor: the time had come to bring out Yan Youwen
ch10.note: Yan Youwen (1914–1962), a secret CCP member planted years before as aide and press chief to Fu Zuoyi. His intelligence, and his later persuasion, helped bring about the peaceful surrender of Beiping in 1949. His Party membership was kept secret even from his family; branded a “reactionary warlord” and persecuted, he was publicly acknowledged as a CCP intelligence officer only in 1993. Corroborated: the book cites his daughter and his case officer Luo Qingchang.

ch10.anchor: hailed them as the "Latter Three Heroes."
ch10.note: 后三杰. Xiong Xianghui (1919–2005), placed by Zhou Enlai as Hu Zongnan’s confidential secretary and later a senior PRC diplomat, together with Chen Zhongjing and Shen Jian, formed the trio that penetrated Hu Zongnan’s headquarters and gave early warning of the 1947 attack on Yan’an. The name deliberately echoes the “Three Heroes of Longtan” (Qian Zhuangfei, Li Kenong, Hu Di) of the early 1930s (see ch. 1). Corroborated; Xiong’s own memoir, My Life in Diplomacy and Intelligence, is the principal source, and the episode is standard in accounts of CCP intelligence.

ch10.anchor: was Zhou Enlai's tesuji indeed
ch10.note: 手筋 (Japanese tesuji), a term from the board game go for a deft, precisely placed stone that turns a position; here, the perfectly timed use of a long-buried agent.

ch10.anchor: loudly singing the Empty Fort
ch10.note: 空城计, the ruse attributed to Zhuge Liang in the Three Kingdoms tale: with the city all but undefended, he flings the gates open and sits playing the zither, so that the stronger enemy suspects an ambush and withdraws. In 1943 the CCP publicized Hu Zongnan’s planned attack in order to deter it; by 1947, the passage notes, the bluff no longer sufficed.

ch10.anchor: declared his revolt at Handan
ch10.note: Gao Shuxun (1898–1972), a former Northwest Army general, defected with the New 8th Army during the Handan campaign on 30 October 1945. Mao turned his name into a slogan, the “Gao Shuxun Movement,” encouraging Nationalist officers to revolt rather than fight the civil war. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: these revolted units had not yet raised the Communist banner
ch10.note: At this stage the CCP called the fighting a “war of self-defense,” not yet a “war of liberation,” and the defecting units took “democratic” names to appeal to the broad popular longing for peace and against Chiang’s one-party rule. The CCP’s own main force in the Northeast was likewise styled the “Northeast Democratic Allied Army.” The framing is the CCP’s; the passage reports it faithfully.

ch10.anchor: it sent a Red Army cadre, Li Bai.
ch10.note: Li Bai (1910–1949), the CCP’s clandestine radio operator in Shanghai, was arrested and executed by the Nationalists in May 1949 on the eve of the city’s fall; he later became famous as the model for the hero of the film The Unfailing Radio Waves (永不消逝的电波).

ch10.anchor: The Shaanbei people call such a withdrawal
ch10.note: 跑反 paofan, a north-Shaanxi term for the flight of a whole population, families and belongings and all, ahead of an oncoming army.

ch10.anchor: that very night Wang Shiwei was put to death.
ch10.note: Wang Shiwei (1906–1947), the writer whose 1942 essay “Wild Lily” attacked privilege in Yan’an and made him the literary target of the Rectification (see ch. 9), was killed here during the retreat; the book's text says only that he was “put to death,” while by most later accounts his body was thrown down a dry well. In February 1991 the verdict was overturned and the killing officially called a wartime error. The chapter’s own accounting below — 2,296 killed in the Border Region in 1947, more than half of them wrongly — is an unusually candid reckoning for this book.

ch10.anchor: with its own "house law": "enter alive, leave only dead."
ch10.note: 生进死出, Juntong’s motto for the lifelong loyalty it claimed: a man admitted while living could leave only as a corpse.

ch10.anchor: seized by the home-returning corps
ch10.note: 还乡团 (huanxiangtuan), landlord-led militias that came back in the wake of the Nationalist advance to retake land distributed under CCP land reform and to take revenge on those who had carried it out.

ch10.anchor: Wu Manyou, a Border Region model laborer
ch10.note: Wu Manyou was the most celebrated model farmer of the wartime Border Region and a poster figure of Yan’an’s production drive. His 1947 capture and the broadcasts he then made for the Nationalists were a grave embarrassment; returned to Yan’an after 1949, he died in obscurity and was quietly dropped from the model-laborer story. Corroborated in outline.

ch10.anchor: with the wrong character
ch10.note: The performer's surname is 章 (Zhang); the monument miscarves it as the common homophone 张 (Zhang). The two characters are plainly different in Chinese but identical in pinyin, so the slip — the author's whole point — vanishes in romanization. He appears earlier in this chapter as the Border Security yangge troupe's well-known performer.

ch10.anchor: fought for fifteen years
ch10.note: The book reckons the war's length inconsistently. This chapter opens by calling it “fourteen bitter years” (counting from the 1931 Mukden Incident to 1945); “fifteen years” here is the author's own figure, given as printed. The “eight years” spoken of elsewhere is the older conventional span, counted from the 1937 Marco Polo Bridge Incident. No one count is corrected against the others.

ch10.anchor: became the Nationalists' open intelligence officers in Yan'an
ch10.note: Three officers were posted, one to each of the Eighth Route Army's three divisions, and the account here and below slips between “the three” and “the two”: by the 1945 scenes only two are named and shadowed, Zhou Liwu and Luo Bolun. Both counts stand as the source gives them.

ch11.anchor: you will win a hundred.
ch11.note: Mao is playing on Sun Tzu's Art of War: the original reads "know the enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will never be in peril" (bai zhan bu dai). Mao's substitution of "win a hundred" (bai zhan bai sheng) turns a promise of safety into a promise of victory.

ch11.anchor: This too was electronic warfare.
ch11.note: The "electronic warfare" of 1947 was radio: the Nationalists used American direction-finding sets to locate Communist transmitters, and the Communists answered with radio silence, relaying, and deception. The technology was decades short of what the term means today; the author uses it for effect.

ch11.anchor: Hu Zongnan's army of 230,000 men
ch11.note: Estimates of the force Hu Zongnan committed to the northern-Shaanxi campaign vary from about 230,000 to 250,000; the direct assault on Yan'an in March 1947 used a smaller spearhead. The book's figure is at the low end of the range and is broadly corroborated.

ch11.anchor: at Wayaobao his men wiped out the Nationalist 135th Brigade
ch11.note: The historical record places the annihilation of the Reorganized 135th Brigade (about 4,700 men) at Yangmahe on April 14, 1947, a few miles from Wayaobao (the seat of Zichang county). It was the second of the "three victories in three battles" in northern Shaanxi, after Qinghuabian and before Panlong. The book's "Wayaobao" names the general area rather than the exact battlefield.

ch11.anchor: the Wang Shijian intelligence system
ch11.note: Wang Shijian ran the Communists' largest behind-the-lines network in the north. In September 1947 the arrest and defection of a radio operator, Li Zhengxuan, let Juntong trace and seize Wang himself, and with him more than a hundred agents, the Five Martyrs of North China among them. It was the gravest Communist intelligence loss of the civil war.

ch11.anchor: Dai Li was killed in a plane crash on March 16, 1946
ch11.note: Corroborated. Dai Li, the feared chief of Juntong, died when his aircraft crashed near Nanjing in fog on March 17, 1946 (the book gives March 16); his death broke the personal machine he had built and hastened Juntong's reorganization.

ch11.anchor: Guo Ruguai in the Ministry of National Defense's operations department
ch11.note: Guo Ruguai, operations chief in the Nationalist high command, passed the Communists whole operational plans through the civil war. Suspected but never caught, he was posthumously confirmed as a long-serving Communist agent; the account here is corroborated.

ch11.anchor: Wei Lihuang's personally endorsed originals
ch11.note: Whether Wei Lihuang deliberately served the Communists is genuinely contested. Some Communist elders later called him a secret Party member, and his passivity in the Liaoshen campaign helped the outcome; other historians read his caution as an ordinary general's wish to preserve his forces, not collusion. No documentary proof has been released. The book gives the partisan reading; the record is divided.

ch11.anchor: one more heavy charge, that of
ch11.note: "Turning" (cefan) means inducing an enemy officer or unit to defect. The renamings the author traces—Destruction Department, Enemy Work Department, Nationalist-Army Work Department, Liaison Department—mark a real shift in doctrine, from wrecking the enemy army to winning it over whole, which culminates in the mass defections of 1948–49.

ch11.anchor: The highest realm of the Chinese strategist is not slaughter
ch11.note: The section title and this line quote Sun Tzu: "to subdue the enemy without fighting is the finest skill of all." The closing phrase, zhi ge wei wu, "to stop the fighting is the true martial virtue," is a classical gloss on the character for "martial" (wu), analyzed as "stop" plus "weapon."

ch11.anchor: Han Liancheng, vanished from the field
ch11.note: Han Liancheng, the "invisible general," was a secret Communist inside the Nationalist high command. His disappearance from the Reorganized 46th Division at Laiwu in February 1947 helped collapse the Nationalist line; he surfaced only later as a PLA officer. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: the great scholar who drafted this manifesto for him, Yan Youwen
ch11.note: One of the best-documented ironies of the period: Fu Zuoyi's fierce open telegram against Mao was ghostwritten by his own secretary Yan Youwen, a secret Communist, who wrote it deliberately harsh on Zhou Enlai's instruction, to inflame the Liberated Areas and swell Fu's conceit.

ch11.anchor: the manifesto Chen Lin drafted against Cao Cao in the Three Kingdoms
ch11.note: Two famous denunciatory manifestos (xi) of Chinese letters: Chen Lin's third-century proclamation against the warlord Cao Cao, and the Tang poet Luo Binwang's against the usurping empress Wu Zetian. To liken Fu Zuoyi's telegram to them is high praise for its rhetoric.

ch11.anchor: four statues: Wu Shi, Zhu Feng, Chen Baocang, and Nie Xi
ch11.note: The Wu Shi case, the Communists' deepest penetration of Nationalist Taiwan. Wu Shi, a lieutenant general and deputy chief of the general staff, passed Taiwan's defense plans to the mainland; the courier Zhu Feng, the lieutenant general Chen Baocang, and the lieutenant colonel Nie Xi were his group. All four were shot at Machangding in Taipei on June 10, 1950. They are commemorated at the Nameless Heroes Plaza opened in the Western Hills of Beijing in 2013. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: The wind blows chill over the Yi River
ch11.note: The parting song of the assassin Jing Ke, who in 227 BC set out to kill the king of Qin knowing he would not return: "The wind blows chill, the Yi River is cold; once the brave man leaves, he comes back no more." Wu Shi recites it on the eve of a mission he expects will cost his life.

ch11.anchor: In East China there was the martyr Li Bai
ch11.note: Li Bai (no relation to the Tang poet) was a Communist radio operator in Shanghai, seized and executed just before the city fell in 1949. His story became the celebrated film The Unfailing Radio Wave.

ch11.anchor: the rape of the Peking University student Shen Chong
ch11.note: The Shen Chong incident: the rape of a Peking University student by U.S. Marines in Beiping on Christmas Eve 1946 touched off nationwide anti-American student protests, which the Communists turned into a "second front" in the cities.

ch11.anchor: beat back Lin Biao's forces at the battle of Siping
ch11.note: At Siping in 1947 Chen Mingren's stubborn defense inflicted heavy losses on Lin Biao's army, one of the rare Nationalist successes of the Northeast war. Two years later Chen led his troops over to the Communists in Hunan, the propaganda value of a Central Army general defecting being the point the author makes here.

ch11.anchor: used fellow-townsman ties to recruit Liu Jinchang
ch11.note: The source names both the Nationalist Baoding station chief and the deserter he recruits "Liu Jinchang." This is almost certainly a slip in the original; the two are distinct people. Rendered as printed.

ch11.anchor: it produced the Nationalist commander-in-chief Chiang Kai-shek
ch11.note: The Baoding Military Academy (1902–1923) trained many of the Nationalists' senior generals, Wu Shi and Bai Chongxi among them, both full graduates. Chiang Kai-shek's tie to it is looser: he passed through a Baoding army preparatory class in 1906 and then left for Japan's Shinbu Gakkō without completing the officer course, so sources differ on whether to count him a Baoding alumnus. That is why the same paragraph can both credit the academy with “producing” him and add, a few lines on, that his real schooling was the Japanese officers' school.

ch11.anchor: Just let her stay in Taiwan
ch11.note: The testament refers to her own remains in the third person — “her” — as the original does (就让她在台湾吧). Xiao Minghua was executed in Taipei in 1950, aged 28; her wish was that her remains be left in Taiwan, though in 1982 they were brought back to the mainland.

ch13.anchor: set up a National Security Commission
ch13.note: The Central National Security Commission, established in 2013 under Party general secretary Xi Jinping, consolidating oversight of internal and external security. The book's second edition, from which this afterword comes, was written in its wake.
Qiangli jigou, the “organs of force” or “power organs”: the army, police, and security services, the coercive arms of the state; the phrase parallels the Russian siloviki.

ch13.anchor: the founding of the state on September 30, 1949
ch13.note: The People's Republic was proclaimed on October 1, 1949; September 30 was the close of the first Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, which elected the new government. The author dates the founding from that eve.

ch13.anchor: the crushing of the "Gang of Four"
ch13.note: Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen, the radical leadership faction blamed for the Cultural Revolution, arrested in October 1976, a month after Mao's death.

ch12.anchor: three days' free plunder
ch12.note: When Zeng Guofan's Hunan Army stormed Nanjing (Tianjing), the capital of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, in 1864, the victorious troops sacked the city. Da suo san ri (“a great search of three days”) was the customary license to loot a captured city.

ch12.anchor: jokingly called "the Hundred-and-Eight Heroes."
ch12.note: An allusion to Shuihu zhuan (Water Margin), the classic novel whose 108 outlaw-heroes gather at the marsh stronghold of Liangshan. The 101 trainees plus 7 instructors made 108. In the roster, “(f.)” marks the trainees the source flags as women (女), whose given names do not otherwise show gender in romanization.

ch12.anchor: reactionary party, corps, and agent organizations
ch12.note: “Party and corps” renders dang-tuan: the Nationalist Party (Kuomintang) and its Three People's Principles Youth Corps, whose members were registered and screened by the new authorities after the takeover.

ch12.anchor: the rinsed mutton of the Donglaishun
ch12.note: The Donglaishun, a celebrated Beijing restaurant founded in 1903 and famous for shuan yangrou, thin-sliced mutton rinsed briefly in a communal pot of simmering broth.

ch12.anchor: poking fun at the Yiguandao
ch12.note: The Yiguandao (“Way of Pervading Unity”), a popular syncretic religious sect with a mass following, banned and violently suppressed as a “reactionary secret society” in the campaigns of 1950–1951.

ch12.anchor: The French military attaché, Lei Meng
ch12.note: The French military attaché's name survives here only in Chinese transliteration (雷蒙, Lei Meng); his name in French is not established, so the romanization is provisional.

ch12.anchor: Farewell, Leighton Stuart!
ch12.note: John Leighton Stuart (1876–1962), American missionary-educator, founding president of Yenching University, and U.S. ambassador to China from 1946 to 1949. Mao's essay “Farewell, Leighton Stuart!” (August 1949) mocked him as the embodiment of a failed American China policy; it long remained a set text in Chinese schools.

ch12.anchor: contact with the Panchen Lama's establishment
ch12.note: The tenth Panchen Lama (1938–1989), the second-ranking figure of Tibetan Buddhism after the Dalai Lama, whose seat was then at Xiangride in Qinghai. The xingyuan was his personal establishment or court; the Kashag was the governing council of the Tibetan government in Lhasa.

ch12.anchor: granted the rank of Senior General in 1955
ch12.note: In the People's Liberation Army ranks conferred in 1955, da jiang (“Senior General”) stood just below marshal; ten officers held it. It outranked shang jiang (“General”), the rank later cited for Li Kenong.

ch12.anchor: "the Eight Vajra Warriors."
ch12.note: Ba da jingang, the eight guardian-warrior kings of Buddhist iconography; used here half in jest for the ministry's eight formidable deputy ministers.

ch12.anchor: earliest "counter-terror" rule anywhere in the world
ch12.note: The author's claim, and a rhetorical one. No external scholarship treats a 1950 internal CCP intelligence guideline as the world's first counter-terrorism measure, and “counter-terrorism” in the modern sense is anachronistic here. UNCORROBORATED; the passage reflects the author's framing, written after the 2001 attacks, rather than a documented first.

ch12.anchor: Light and dark had changed places
ch12.note: The chapter's title, ming an yi wei: the “light” (the open, the state) and the “dark” (the hidden, the clandestine services) trade places, as the Party's once-secret apparatus comes into the open as the public-security organs of a ruling state and, in the campaigns that follow, is turned against its own.

ch12.anchor: the great Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries
ch12.note: The zhenfan campaign of 1950–1953, which the author presents here as a triumph of public order. Its scale was far bloodier than the text lets on: deputy public-security minister Xu Zirong's 1954 report counted about 712,000 executed, 1,290,000 imprisoned, and 1,200,000 placed under control; Mao himself later spoke of some 700,000 killed. Historians' estimates of the executions run from about 500,000–720,000 at the low end to two or three million. CORROBORATED as a mass campaign of execution; the book's framing omits the toll.

ch12.anchor: China became the safest great country in the world.
ch12.note: The author's partisan verdict. Low reported ordinary crime in the Mao years coexisted with waves of state-driven political violence — the very campaigns and purges this chapter goes on to describe — so “safest” measures only one kind of safety. The judgment is the author's, not a neutral finding.

ch12.anchor: the new China's first unjust, false, and wrongful case
ch12.note: On Pan Hannian, see the notes at Chapters 2 and 9. He and the Shanghai police chief Yang Fan were arrested in 1955 and both were posthumously rehabilitated in the 1980s. That the author — himself a sympathetic insider — flatly calls these “unjust, false, and wrongful cases” reflects the settled post-Mao verdict.

ch12.anchor: Toppling "Peng, Luo, Lu, and Yang"
ch12.note: Peng Zhen, Luo Ruiqing, Lu Dingyi, and Yang Shangkun, four senior officials purged together in 1965–66 as the “Peng-Luo-Lu-Yang anti-Party clique,” an opening move of the Cultural Revolution.

ch12.anchor: Smash the police, procuratorate, and courts!
ch12.note: The Cultural Revolution slogan za lan gong-jian-fa: smash the gong (public security, the police), the jian (the procuratorate), and the fa (the courts). Mao spoke of having the legal apparatus “beaten to a pulp”; from 1967 the procuratorate and courts effectively collapsed and the security leadership was purged wholesale. CORROBORATED as to the slogan and the wholesale purge; the casualty figures that follow are the public-security system's own post-Mao reckoning.

ch12.anchor: excavating a cultural gene
ch12.note: The book's closing figure, which answers the mining metaphor of its Preface: the “cultural gene” is the inherited character — the habits, methods, and instincts — that the author sees carried down through the Communists' intelligence tradition. The image is his own, meant as heritage rather than biology.

ch12.anchor: the Asian-African Conference
ch12.note: The 1955 Bandung Conference. En route, an Air India plane, the Kashmir Princess, chartered for the Chinese delegation, was destroyed by a bomb planted by a Nationalist agent; sixteen people died, but Zhou Enlai had changed his travel plans and was not aboard.

ch12.anchor: won back the returning "acting president."
ch12.note: Li Zongren (see above in this chapter), who had been the Republic of China's acting president in 1949, returned to the mainland from exile in the United States in 1965, a propaganda coup the CCP's united-front and intelligence organs worked to bring about.

ch12.anchor: the greatest spy has no name
ch12.note: The first two clauses adapt Laozi (Daodejing, ch. 41): “the greatest sound is faint of voice, the greatest form has no shape” (see the note at Chapter 6). “The greatest spy has no name” is the author's own coinage completing the parallel.

ch12.anchor: the ancient capital of six dynasties
ch12.note: The source calls Xi'an the capital of “six dynasties” (六朝古都), but that is by convention the epithet of Nanjing, whose Six Dynasties ruled from there in the third to sixth centuries. Xi'an (ancient Chang'an) is usually called the capital of thirteen dynasties, from the Western Zhou through the Tang. The author's “six” is given as printed.

ch12.anchor: intelligence, security, safety, and public-security work
ch12.note: The near-synonyms translate four distinct Chinese terms that the source lists separately: 情报 (intelligence), 保卫 (protective or internal security — the “security” of this book's own title), 安全 (state security, later the Ministry of State Security's domain), and 公安 (public security, the police). English runs the middle two together; the original keeps them apart.
